questions.q: Assume the §448 gross receipts threshold for 2025 is $31 million. Bolt Corp., a C corporation that is not a tax shelter, had gross receipts of $28 million in 2022, $32 million in 2023 and $34 million in 2024. May Bolt use the cash method for 2025?
choices: Yes, because only the immediately preceding year is tested
No, because C corporations may never use the cash method
Yes, because its 2022 gross receipts were under $31 million
No, because its average annual gross receipts for 2022 through 2024 exceed $31 million
questions.exp: The §448 test uses average annual gross receipts for the three prior years: ($28M + $32M + $34M) / 3 = $31.33 million, which exceeds $31 million, so Bolt must use accrual. C corporations under the threshold may use the cash method, so the 'never' choice is wrong.

questions.q: MedGroup, a qualified personal service corporation providing health services, has average annual gross receipts of $50 million. It is not a tax shelter. Which accounting method rule applies?
choices: It must use accrual because its receipts exceed the §448 threshold
It may use the cash method only if it has no inventory
It must use the hybrid method
It may use the cash method regardless of its gross receipts
questions.exp: Qualified personal service corporations are excepted from the §448 accrual requirement whatever their size. Tax shelters, by contrast, may never use the cash method.

questions.q: Hauler Co., a calendar-year accrual taxpayer, received freight services in December 2025 and paid the $40,000 invoice on February 20, 2026. The expense recurs every year, Hauler consistently treats such items under the recurring item exception, and the amount is not material. When is the expense deductible?
choices: 2026, when paid, because economic performance is payment
2026, because the invoice was received in 2026
2025 only if paid by January 15, 2026
2025, under the recurring item exception, because the services were performed and the item was paid within 8.5 months after year-end
questions.exp: For services provided to the taxpayer, economic performance occurs as the services are performed (December 2025), and the recurring item exception also allows deduction when payment is made within 8.5 months after year-end. Treating payment as the economic performance event applies to items such as tort liabilities, not purchased services.

questions.q: Crane Inc., a calendar-year accrual taxpayer, accrued $400,000 of year-end bonuses to unrelated employees on December 31, 2025. It paid $300,000 on March 10, 2026 and $100,000 on April 20, 2026. How much may Crane deduct for 2025?
questions.exp: Compensation paid within 2.5 months after year-end (by March 15, 2026) is not deferred compensation and is deductible when accrued, so $300,000 is deductible in 2025. The $100,000 paid later is deferred compensation, deductible in 2026.

questions.q: Lynx Corp., a calendar-year accrual taxpayer, accrued a $50,000 bonus on December 31, 2025 for its president, a cash-method individual who owns 60% of its stock. The bonus was paid January 10, 2026. When may Lynx deduct it?
choices: 2025, because it was paid within 2.5 months
2025, under the recurring item exception
Never, because it is a constructive dividend
2026, when the president includes it in income
questions.exp: Under §267, an accrual payor cannot deduct an amount owed to a related cash-method payee (here, a more-than-50% shareholder) until the payee includes it in income. The 2.5-month rule does not override §267.

questions.q: On November 1, 2025, Fixit Corp., a calendar-year accrual taxpayer with an applicable financial statement, received $24,000 for a 24-month service contract and recognized $2,000 of revenue in its 2025 financial statements. Fixit uses the deferral method under §451. How much does it include in 2025 gross income?
questions.exp: Under the one-year deferral method, Fixit includes the amount recognized in its AFS for 2025 ($2,000) and the remaining $22,000 in 2026, even though the contract runs into 2027. The full-inclusion trap ignores the available deferral.

questions.q: On December 1, 2025, Landco, a calendar-year accrual taxpayer, received $36,000 of advance rent covering the next three years from a commercial tenant. How much rent must Landco include in 2025 gross income?
questions.exp: Rent is excluded from the advance payment deferral rules, so prepaid rent is income when received under the claim-of-right doctrine. The $13,000 trap applies the one-year deferral method, which is not available for rent.

questions.q: On July 1, 2025, a cash-method calendar-year business pays $24,000 for a 24-month insurance policy running July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2027. How much may it deduct in 2025?
questions.exp: The 12-month rule does not apply because the benefit extends beyond 12 months, so the prepayment is capitalized and deducted ratably: $24,000 x 6 / 24 = $6,000. A 12-month policy would have been fully deductible.

questions.q: Trim Co. changes from the cash to the accrual method with IRS consent, effective for 2025. At the start of 2025 it had $300,000 of accounts receivable and $120,000 of accounts payable not previously reported. Under the general §481 spread rules, how much of the adjustment is included in 2025 income?
questions.exp: The net §481 adjustment is $300,000 - $120,000 = +$180,000, and a positive adjustment from a voluntary change is generally spread over four years, $45,000 per year. Including the full $180,000 is the trap; that treatment applies to negative adjustments.

questions.q: A taxpayer voluntarily changes an accounting method with IRS consent, producing a negative §481 adjustment of $120,000. How is the adjustment taken into account?
choices: Entirely in the year of change
$30,000 per year over four years
Through amended returns for the prior years
Over 15 years
questions.exp: Negative §481 adjustments are generally taken entirely in the year of change, while positive adjustments are spread over four years. A method change never requires amending prior returns.

questions.q: Zed Corp., a calendar-year taxpayer, is making an automatic change in accounting method for its 2025 tax year. What is the filing requirement for Form 3115?
choices: File it any time before the statute of limitations expires for 2025
No form is required for automatic changes
Attach the original to the timely filed (including extensions) 2025 return and file a copy with the IRS
File the original with the IRS national office before the end of 2025
questions.exp: For automatic changes, the original Form 3115 goes with the timely filed return for the year of change, including extensions, and a signed copy is filed separately with the IRS. Filing before the end of the year of change is the rule for non-automatic changes.

questions.q: Which of the following is a change in accounting method that requires IRS consent?
choices: Correcting a posting error that put a sale in the wrong year
Correcting a math error in last year's depreciation computation
Switching inventory valuation from FIFO to LIFO
Reporting income differently because the terms of the company's sales contracts changed
questions.exp: A change in the overall method or in the treatment of a material item, such as inventory identification, is a method change. Correcting math or posting errors and responding to changed facts are not method changes.

questions.q: Assume the 2025 gross receipts threshold for small business taxpayers is $31 million. Shopco, a retailer with average gross receipts of $12 million, does not want to keep a full inventory accounting system. What does §471 allow?
choices: It must keep inventories under the full absorption method
It may deduct all inventory purchases when paid, with no tracking
It must use LIFO
It may treat inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies, or follow the method used in its books and records
questions.exp: Small business taxpayers below the threshold may account for inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies (deducted when sold or used) or conform to their AFS or books and records. Deducting purchases when paid, with no tracking at all, is not permitted.

questions.q: Maker Co. is subject to §263A uniform capitalization. Production-year costs include direct materials $500,000, direct labor $300,000, factory overhead $200,000, warehousing of raw materials $50,000, marketing $80,000 and selling commissions $40,000. All units produced remain in ending inventory. What amount must be capitalized to inventory?
questions.exp: UNICAP capitalizes direct costs and allocable indirect costs, including storage: $500,000 + $300,000 + $200,000 + $50,000 = $1,050,000. Marketing and selling costs are never capitalized, and the $1,000,000 trap leaves out storage.

questions.q: Vale Corp. uses LIFO for its inventory. At year-end, its inventory cost is $400,000 and market value is $360,000. At what amount is ending inventory reported for tax purposes?
questions.exp: Taxpayers using LIFO must value inventory at cost and may not use lower of cost or market. A FIFO taxpayer could have written it down to $360,000.

questions.q: Gator Co. elects LIFO for federal income tax purposes. Which requirement applies?
choices: It generally must also use LIFO for financial reports to shareholders, partners and creditors
It must obtain a ruling before each year's use
It may use FIFO for its financial statements to shareholders
It must use LIFO for state tax returns only
questions.exp: The LIFO conformity rule of §472 requires LIFO in financial reports to owners and creditors, with limited exceptions such as supplemental disclosures. Using FIFO in primary statements would end the LIFO election.

questions.q: Ann, not a dealer, sells investment land with a basis of $200,000 for $500,000. She receives $100,000 in 2025 and a note for the balance, payable with adequate interest over the next four years. Using the installment method, how much gain does she recognize in 2025?
questions.exp: The gross profit percentage is $300,000 / $500,000 = 60%, and 60% x $100,000 = $60,000. The $40,000 trap treats the payment as first a recovery of basis (40%).

questions.q: Builder Co., a large contractor, must use the percentage-of-completion method. A contract's price is $10,000,000 and estimated total cost is $8,000,000. Costs incurred in 2025, the first year, are $3,200,000. How much gross profit does it report in 2025?
questions.exp: Completion is $3,200,000 / $8,000,000 = 40%; revenue is 40% x $10,000,000 = $4,000,000, less $3,200,000 of cost, for $800,000 of gross profit. The $4,000,000 trap reports revenue rather than gross profit.

questions.q: Assume the 2025 small business gross receipts threshold is $31 million. Which contractor may use the completed-contract method for a new construction contract instead of percentage of completion?
choices: A contractor with $40 million of average receipts building a bridge expected to take 12 months
A contractor with $90 million of average receipts building an office tower expected to take 18 months
Any contractor, for a contract expected to take more than two years
A contractor with $20 million of average gross receipts building a warehouse expected to be finished within two years
questions.exp: The small contractor exception in §460 requires both average gross receipts under the threshold and expected completion within two years. Home construction contracts are exempt separately, but none of the other choices qualify.

questions.q: Cobb Corp., an accrual taxpayer, increased its allowance for doubtful accounts by $50,000 for book purposes this year. During the year, it wrote off $30,000 of specific accounts that became wholly worthless. What is Cobb's tax bad debt deduction?
questions.exp: §166 requires the specific charge-off method for non-bank taxpayers, so only the $30,000 actually written off is deductible. The $50,000 book provision is a reserve and is not deductible.

questions.q: Dr. Ray, a cash-method calendar-year taxpayer, received a $12,000 patient check on December 31, 2025, after the bank closed, and deposited it on January 2, 2026. When must he report the income?
choices: In the year the check clears
2026, because the bank was closed
2026, when deposited
2025, because a check is income when received, even if deposited later
questions.exp: Cash-method taxpayers include payments when actually or constructively received, and receiving a good check is receipt. Deposit timing does not defer the income.

questions.q: A partnership's partners are Corp A (fiscal year ending June 30) with a 55% interest in profits and capital, and three individuals (calendar year) holding the other 45%. What is the partnership's required tax year?
choices: June 30 fiscal year
The year that results in the least aggregate deferral
Any year the partnership elects
Calendar year
questions.exp: Under §706, a partnership must use the majority interest tax year, meaning the year of partners owning more than 50% of profits and capital; Corp A's 55% means June 30. Least aggregate deferral applies only when neither the majority interest test nor the principal partners test settles the year.

questions.q: A partnership's profits interests are held by A, 45% (year ending June 30), B, 45% (calendar year), and C, 10% (year ending March 31). No majority interest year or principal partner year exists. Which year gives the least aggregate deferral?
choices: March 31
December 31
September 30
June 30
questions.exp: Deferral scores: June 30 = 45% x 6 + 10% x 9 = 3.6; December 31 = 45% x 6 + 10% x 3 = 3.0; March 31 = 45% x 3 + 45% x 9 = 5.4. December 31 is the smallest. The June 30 trap ignores how far C's year is from it.

questions.q: An S corporation wants to adopt a natural business year ending April 30 under the 25% gross receipts test. Its gross receipts for March and April as a percentage of the 12-month total were 26%, 27% and 24% for the three most recent years. What is the result?
choices: It does not qualify, because the 25% test must be met in each of the three years
It qualifies, because the most recent year exceeds 25%
It qualifies, because the average exceeds 25%
It qualifies, because two of the three years exceed 25%
questions.exp: The natural business year test requires that at least 25% of gross receipts fall in the last two months of the proposed year in each of the three preceding 12-month periods, and 24% fails. The average does not count, so the 'average exceeds 25%' choice is the trap.

questions.q: A new partnership whose required tax year is the calendar year wants a fiscal year ending September 30 without showing a business purpose. What can it do?
choices: Nothing; a partnership must always use the calendar year
Use September 30 automatically for its first year
Make a §444 election for the September 30 year, which requires required payments that offset the deferral benefit
Use September 30 if the partners agree in writing
questions.exp: §444 allows a year with up to three months of deferral (a September 30 year defers three months relative to December 31), conditioned on the §7519 required payments. A partnership has no free choice of its first year.

questions.q: A personal service corporation with a calendar required year makes a §444 election for a fiscal year ending September 30. What additional requirement applies to the PSC?
choices: It must switch to the accrual method
It must meet minimum distribution requirements for compensation paid to employee-owners during the deferral period, or its deductions are limited
It must make §7519 required payments
It must elect S corporation status
questions.exp: A PSC electing §444 must comply with §280H by paying enough compensation to employee-owners during the deferral period, or its deduction for those payments is limited. Required payments under §7519 apply to partnerships and S corporations.

questions.q: With IRS approval, a C corporation (21% flat rate) changes its tax year, creating a four-month short period with $100,000 of taxable income. What is the tax for the short period?
questions.exp: Annualized income is $100,000 x 12 / 4 = $300,000, the tax on that is $63,000, and the short-period tax is $63,000 x 4 / 12 = $21,000. With a flat rate, annualization gives the same result as 21% x $100,000; $63,000 is the trap of not prorating back.

questions.q: A retailer wants its tax year always to end on the last Saturday of January. Which is correct?
choices: This is not allowed; a tax year must end on the last day of a month
A 52-53 week tax year ending on the same day of the week each year, closest to or last in a month, is allowed if used in the books
It is allowed only for S corporations
It requires a §444 election
questions.exp: §441 allows a 52-53 week year ending on the same weekday that last occurs in a calendar month or falls nearest the month's end, if it matches the taxpayer's books. It is available to all types of taxpayers, so no §444 election is needed.

questions.q: A newly formed C corporation (not a personal service corporation) files its first return using a fiscal year ending March 31. Is IRS approval required?
choices: No, but it must make a §444 election
Yes, because all fiscal years require consent
Yes, unless it shows a business purpose
No, because a new corporation may adopt any permissible tax year on its first timely filed return
questions.exp: A new C corporation adopts its tax year by filing its first return and does not need consent; only later changes do. The required-year and §444 rules apply to partnerships, S corporations and PSCs.

questions.q: Shopco, a calendar-year accrual taxpayer, settled a customer's tort claim in December 2025 for $500,000. It paid $200,000 in December 2025 and $300,000 in February 2026. How much may it deduct in 2025?
questions.exp: For tort liabilities, economic performance occurs only when payment is made, and the recurring item exception is not available for them. Only the $200,000 paid in 2025 is deductible then.

questions.q: Phoneco, an accrual taxpayer, records $120,000 of estimated warranty expense in its books for products sold this year. It paid $70,000 of warranty claims during the year. What is its tax deduction for warranty costs?
questions.exp: Warranty obligations to customers are payment liabilities, and economic performance occurs when they are paid, so only the $70,000 paid is deductible. The $120,000 book estimate is a reserve.

questions.q: Pip Corp., an accrual taxpayer, contests a $90,000 state tax assessment but transfers the full amount to the state in December 2025 while the contest continues into 2026. When may Pip deduct the payment?
choices: Never, because contested liabilities are not deductible
Only when the contest is resolved
Half in 2025 and half in 2026
2025, under §461 rules for contested liabilities paid or transferred while the contest continues
questions.exp: When a taxpayer contests a liability but transfers money to satisfy it, the deduction is allowed in the year of transfer if all other requirements are met. Waiting for resolution is the rule only when no payment has been made.

questions.q: Signco, an accrual taxpayer with an applicable financial statement, completed a project in December 2025 and recognized the revenue in its 2025 audited financial statements. Under the contract, it cannot bill the customer until March 2026. When must Signco include the revenue in income?
choices: 2025, because §451 requires inclusion no later than when it is taken into revenue in the AFS
2025 only if collected within 2.5 months
2026, when it can bill
2026, when payment is received
questions.exp: The AFS income inclusion rule in §451 requires accrual taxpayers with an AFS to include income no later than when it is included in AFS revenue. A billing restriction does not defer it.

questions.q: A calendar-year corporation discovers it has claimed $50,000 of depreciation in prior open and closed years on an asset, when the allowable amount was $80,000. It is still using the asset. What is the most appropriate remedy?
choices: File Form 3115 for an automatic change and take a $30,000 negative §481 adjustment in the current year
Claim the $30,000 when the asset is sold
Nothing can be done for closed years
Amend only the open years
questions.exp: Using an impermissible depreciation method for two or more years is a method of accounting, so the taxpayer may change it automatically and catch up the unclaimed allowable depreciation through a negative §481 adjustment. Because basis is reduced by the allowable amount anyway, waiting until a sale would lose the benefit.

questions.q: On December 1, 2025, Rex, a calendar-year landlord, received from a new tenant $3,000 of rent for December, $3,000 of rent for the last month of the lease, and a $3,000 refundable security deposit. How much must Rex include in 2025 income?
questions.exp: Advance rent, including last month's rent, is income when received, but a security deposit that must be refunded is not income while the landlord may have to return it. So Rex includes $3,000 + $3,000 = $6,000.

questions.q: Kay, a cash-method sole proprietor, bought $5,000 of business supplies on December 28, 2025 using a bank credit card and paid the card bill in January 2026. She also gave a vendor a promissory note for another $4,000 of supplies in December 2025, which she paid in 2026. What may Kay deduct in 2025?
questions.exp: A charge on a third-party credit card is treated as payment when charged, but giving the creditor your own note is not payment. Only the $5,000 credit card purchase is deductible in 2025.

questions.q: Which entity generally must use a calendar tax year, absent a §444 election, a business purpose, or a natural business year?
choices: An estate
A C corporation that is not a personal service corporation
An S corporation
A partnership whose majority partners use a June 30 year
questions.exp: S corporations (and PSCs) are generally required to use a calendar year under §1378. C corporations and estates may choose a fiscal year, and that partnership's required year is June 30.

questions.q: Taxco, a calendar-year accrual corporation, owes $12,000 of real property tax for the local fiscal year July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026, and it has validly elected under §461 to accrue real property taxes ratably over the period they relate to. How much may Taxco deduct for 2025?
questions.exp: Under the ratable accrual election, real property taxes accrue over the period to which they relate: $12,000 x 6 / 12 = $6,000 for July through December 2025. Deducting all $12,000 ignores the election's ratable rule.

questions.q: Ada sells investment land with a $200,000 basis for $500,000 and pays $20,000 of selling expenses. The buyer pays $100,000 down and gives a note for the $400,000 balance, payable over four years with adequate interest. How much gain does Ada recognize in the year of sale under the installment method?
questions.exp: Gross profit is $500,000 − $200,000 − $20,000 = $280,000; the contract price is $500,000, so the gross profit percentage is 56%, and $100,000 × 56% = $56,000. Ignoring the selling expenses gives a 60% ratio and $60,000.

questions.q: Bert sells a building for $800,000. The buyer assumes Bert's $300,000 mortgage, pays $50,000 cash at closing, and signs a $450,000 note. Bert's adjusted basis is $200,000, and there is no depreciation recapture. How much gain does Bert recognize in the year of sale?
questions.exp: Mortgage assumed in excess of basis ($100,000) is treated as a payment in the year of sale and is added to the contract price: $800,000 − $300,000 + $100,000 = $600,000, which equals the $600,000 gross profit (100%). Year-of-sale gain = ($50,000 + $100,000) × 100% = $150,000. Answering $50,000 ignores the deemed payment.

questions.q: Cora sells land for $1,000,000. The buyer assumes a $200,000 mortgage, pays $100,000 down, and gives a $700,000 note. Cora's basis is $400,000. How much gain does she recognize in the year of sale?
questions.exp: Gross profit is $600,000; the contract price excludes the assumed mortgage (it is less than basis): $1,000,000 − $200,000 = $800,000, so the gross profit percentage is 75% and $100,000 × 75% = $75,000. Dividing by the full $1,000,000 selling price gives 60% and understates the gain.

questions.q: Dirk sells business equipment held for four years for $100,000: $20,000 down and an $80,000 note. The equipment cost $90,000, and its adjusted basis is $30,000. How much gain does Dirk recognize in the year of sale?
questions.exp: Under §453(i), all $60,000 of §1245 recapture is recognized in the year of sale and added to basis; the remaining $10,000 gain is reported on the installment method at a 10% gross profit percentage ($10,000 ÷ $100,000): $60,000 + $20,000 × 10% = $62,000. Applying a 70% ratio to the down payment ($14,000) ignores the rule that recapture is recognized up front.

questions.q: Eli sells land to his son on the installment method and reports the gain as payments arrive. Eighteen months later, before Eli has collected the note, the son sells the land to an unrelated buyer for cash. What is the effect on Eli?
choices: The son's resale is treated as a payment to Eli, accelerating Eli's gain
The original sale is disregarded, and the son reports all of the gain
None; Eli continues to report gain as he collects the note
Eli must recognize gain only if the son's resale price exceeds the original price
questions.exp: Under the §453 related-party second-disposition rule, if a related buyer resells within two years of the first sale, the amount realized on the resale (up to the contract price, less payments already received) is treated as received by the original seller. Continuing on the installment method ignores this anti-abuse rule.

questions.q: Fran sold securities this year and has a $400,000 net capital loss from those sales. She also sells investment land at a $350,000 long-term gain, receiving 10% down and a 10-year note. Which approach is most tax-efficient?
choices: Treat the note as a cash equivalent without electing out
Report on the installment method to defer the gain
Report the gain on the installment method but treat it as ordinary income
Elect out of the installment method and recognize the entire gain this year to absorb the capital loss
questions.exp: Electing out under §453 by the return's due date accelerates the $350,000 gain into the year she has a $400,000 capital loss to offset it; otherwise most of the loss would be limited to $3,000 a year against ordinary income. Deferral is usually good, but not when current losses can absorb the gain.

questions.q: Which of the following sales may be reported using the installment method?
choices: An individual's sale of a rental duplex for 20% down and a note
A dealer's sale of residential lots from inventory on a 10-year contract
A retailer's sale of inventory on revolving credit
A sale of publicly traded stock for a five-year note
questions.exp: The installment method under §453 is available for casual sales of real property and non-inventory personal property, such as the duplex. It is barred for sales of publicly traded stock or securities, dealer dispositions, and inventory.

questions.q: Gail holds an installment note with an unpaid balance of $300,000 from a land sale on which her gross profit percentage is 40%. This year she gives the note to her daughter when it is worth $300,000. How much gain does Gail recognize?
questions.exp: Under §453B, a gift of an installment obligation is a disposition that triggers gain equal to the note's FMV less its basis. Her basis is $300,000 × 60% = $180,000, so the gain is $120,000. Recognizing nothing treats the gift like a transfer at death, which is excepted.

questions.q: Hank exchanges investment land with a $200,000 basis and a $500,000 FMV for an office building worth $450,000 plus $50,000 of cash. What are his recognized gain and basis in the building?
choices: $0 gain; $150,000 basis
questions.exp: Realized gain is $300,000, but under §1031 gain is recognized only to the extent of $50,000 of boot. Basis = $200,000 old basis + $50,000 gain recognized − $50,000 boot received = $200,000 (equal to the $450,000 FMV less the $250,000 deferred gain). Adding the gain without subtracting the cash gives $250,000.

questions.q: Ira exchanges a rental building (FMV $1,000,000; adjusted basis $300,000; mortgage $400,000, assumed by the other party) for a warehouse (FMV $900,000) subject to a $300,000 mortgage that Ira assumes. No cash changes hands. What gain does Ira recognize?
questions.exp: Liabilities are netted: Ira was relieved of $400,000 and assumed $300,000, so net liability relief of $100,000 is boot under §1031. His realized gain is $700,000, so $100,000 is recognized. Treating the full $400,000 of relief as boot ignores the netting allowed for liabilities assumed.

questions.q: Jo exchanges a rental property (FMV $600,000; basis $250,000; mortgage $100,000, assumed by the other party) for a property worth $800,000 that is subject to a $330,000 mortgage she assumes, plus $30,000 of cash. What gain does Jo recognize?
questions.exp: Liabilities Jo assumes can offset liabilities she is relieved of, but not cash she receives. Her net liability relief is negative (she assumed more), so only the $30,000 of cash is boot, against $350,000 of realized gain. Answering $0 wrongly nets the extra mortgage she assumed against the cash received.

questions.q: Under current law, which exchange can qualify for nonrecognition under §1031?
choices: An apartment building in Ohio for unimproved land in Texas held for investment
A U.S. office building for a commercial building in Canada
A 30% interest in an LLC taxed as a partnership for a 30% interest in another such LLC
Construction equipment for other construction equipment
questions.exp: Since 2018, §1031 applies only to real property held for business or investment, and improved and unimproved real property are like-kind to each other. Personal property such as equipment and partnership interests do not qualify, and U.S. and foreign real property are not like-kind.

questions.q: Kai, a calendar-year individual, transfers his relinquished property to a qualified intermediary on October 1, 2026, in a deferred like-kind exchange. He will not extend his return, which is due April 15, 2027. What are the last days to identify the replacement property and to receive it?
choices: November 15, 2026, and March 30, 2027
November 15, 2026, and April 15, 2027
October 31, 2026, and March 30, 2027
November 16, 2026, and March 31, 2027
questions.exp: Under §1031, replacement property must be identified within 45 days (November 15, 2026) and received by the earlier of 180 days (March 30, 2027) or the due date, with extensions, of the return for the year of transfer. Because the 180-day deadline comes first, the April 15 due date does not apply.

questions.q: Lena sells her rental property in a planned like-kind exchange, but the closing agent wires the $700,000 of proceeds into Lena's personal account. Thirty days later she uses the funds to buy a replacement rental. What is the result?
choices: The exchange qualifies because the replacement was bought within 45 days
The exchange fails, and the gain is recognized, because Lena actually received the proceeds
The exchange qualifies only for the portion of gain above the cash
The exchange qualifies if she identified the property in writing
questions.exp: Actual or constructive receipt of the sale proceeds turns the transaction into a sale and a reinvestment, not an exchange. A qualified intermediary must hold the funds under Reg. 1.1031(k)-1 safe harbors. Timely identification cannot cure receipt of the cash.

questions.q: Max exchanges a rental property with his sister, each receiving the other's property in a valid like-kind exchange. Eighteen months later, his sister sells the property she received to an unrelated buyer. What is the consequence?
choices: Max recognizes his deferred gain in the year of his sister's sale
Max recognizes his deferred gain in the original exchange year by amending his return
Neither party is affected because each held the property for investment
Only the sister recognizes gain, on her own sale
questions.exp: Under §1031, if either related party disposes of the property received within two years, the deferred gain of both parties is recognized as of the date of that disposition, not retroactively. Max's gain is triggered even though he did not sell.

questions.q: Nina exchanges investment land (basis $150,000; FMV $400,000) for a building worth $380,000 and a pickup truck worth $20,000. What is her basis in the building?
questions.exp: She recognizes $20,000 of gain, equal to the truck boot. Total basis is $150,000 + $20,000 gain = $170,000, of which $20,000 (FMV) goes to the truck and $150,000 to the building. Answering $170,000 assigns the entire basis to the building and none to the truck.

questions.q: Ole exchanges rental property with a $500,000 basis and a $400,000 FMV for another rental property worth $350,000 plus $50,000 cash. What loss does Ole recognize, and what is his basis in the new property?
choices: $0 loss; $500,000 basis
$0 loss; $450,000 basis
questions.exp: Section 1031 prevents loss recognition even when boot is received. Basis = $500,000 − $50,000 cash = $450,000, which preserves the $100,000 deferred loss ($350,000 FMV + $100,000). To deduct the loss, Ole should sell the property outright instead of exchanging it.

questions.q: A fire destroys Pam's warehouse (adjusted basis $400,000). She receives $900,000 of insurance proceeds and, within the replacement period, buys a replacement warehouse for $800,000. She elects §1033 deferral. What are her recognized gain and her basis in the new warehouse?
choices: $0 gain; $300,000 basis
questions.exp: Under §1033, gain is recognized only to the extent the proceeds are not reinvested: $900,000 − $800,000 = $100,000. Basis = $800,000 cost − $400,000 deferred gain = $400,000. Using an $800,000 cost basis ignores the deferred gain.

questions.q: Quinn sells a depreciable building on the installment method to a corporation in which he owns 85% of the stock. Which statement is correct?
choices: The gain is capital gain, but any loss is disallowed
The gain is §1231 gain reported as payments are received
The sale is disregarded because the corporation is controlled
The gain is ordinary income under §1239, and the installment method is generally unavailable, so all payments are treated as received in the year of sale
questions.exp: Section 1239 treats gain on a sale of depreciable property to a more-than-50%-controlled entity as ordinary income, and §453 generally denies installment reporting for such sales unless tax avoidance was not a principal purpose. Reporting §1231 gain on the installment method ignores both rules.

questions.q: Rita sells land for $1,000,000 and receives a 10-year note that states no interest. Which statement about the note is correct?
choices: Rita reports $1,000,000 of selling price and no interest income
The buyer's basis in the land includes the full $1,000,000 and Rita has no interest income
The installment method is unavailable for notes without stated interest
Part of each payment is recharacterized as interest under the imputed interest rules, which reduces Rita's selling price and gain
questions.exp: Under §483 or §1274, a deferred-payment sale without adequate stated interest has interest imputed at the applicable federal rate, which converts part of the principal into ordinary interest income and lowers the selling price used to compute gain. The installment method itself remains available.

questions.q: Sam sold land with an $80,000 basis for $200,000, receiving $50,000 down and a note for the rest (gross profit percentage 60%). After the down payment, the buyer defaulted, and Sam repossessed the land, paying $5,000 of repossession costs. How much gain does Sam recognize on the repossession?
questions.exp: Under §1038, gain on repossession of real property equals cash received before repossession ($50,000) less gain already reported ($50,000 × 60% = $30,000), or $20,000. This is limited to the original gross profit ($120,000) less gain reported ($30,000) and repossession costs ($5,000), or $85,000. The lower amount, $20,000, controls.

questions.q: Tia sells a commercial building held for 10 years on the installment method. Her gain includes $150,000 of unrecaptured §1250 gain and $250,000 of other §1231 gain, and she treats the total as long-term capital gain after netting. How is the gain in each installment payment characterized?
choices: Pro rata between unrecaptured §1250 gain and other gain in each payment
Unrecaptured §1250 gain (taxed at up to 25%) first, until it is used up, then the rest
Other §1231 gain first, then unrecaptured §1250 gain
Entirely as ordinary income until the §1250 portion is recovered
questions.exp: Under Reg. 1.453-12, unrecaptured §1250 gain is taken into account before the lower-taxed long-term gain in installment payments. Prorating each payment is a common assumption but understates the early-year tax. Straight-line real property has no ordinary §1250 recapture.

questions.q: Uma, a real estate developer, subdivides land and sells the lots to home builders. She wants to exchange 10 unsold lots for an apartment building she would hold as a rental. Does the exchange qualify under §1031?
choices: No, because the lots are held primarily for sale
Yes, if the apartment building is held for at least two years
No, because improved real property is not like-kind to unimproved land
Yes, because both are real property
questions.exp: Section 1031 excludes real property held primarily for sale, such as a dealer's inventory lots. Improved and unimproved real property are like-kind, so that is not the obstacle.

questions.q: Victor owns a beach condominium that his family uses occasionally and wants to exchange it under §1031. Under the Rev. Proc. 2008-16 safe harbor, which pattern of use in each of the two years before the exchange best supports investment use?
choices: Personal use for 60 days and no rentals
Rented to his brother at half the market rate for 200 days
Rented at fair rent for 90 days and personal use for 20 days
Rented at fair rent for 10 days and personal use for 10 days
questions.exp: The safe harbor requires rental at fair rent for 14 or more days and personal use no greater than the greater of 14 days or 10% of fair-rental days in each of the two 12-month periods. With 90 rental days, the personal-use limit is 14 days, so 20 days fails. Below-market rentals to family count as personal use.

questions.q: Will sold land last year on the installment method at a 40% gross profit percentage. This year he receives $50,000 of principal and $12,000 of stated interest on the note. What does Will report this year?
choices: $50,000 of gain and $12,000 of interest income
$24,800 of gain and no interest income
$20,000 of gain and $12,000 of interest income
$62,000 of gain
questions.exp: Only principal payments carry gross profit: $50,000 × 40% = $20,000 of gain. Interest is separately taxed as ordinary income. Applying the gross profit percentage to the interest ($24,800) treats interest as part of the selling price.

questions.q: Xena's relinquished property sells for $900,000 through a qualified intermediary. The QI pays her $40,000 of cash at closing (not reinvested), and $10,000 of exchange expenses (broker commissions and closing costs) are paid from the proceeds. Her realized gain is $300,000. How much gain does she recognize?
questions.exp: Exchange expenses reduce the amount realized and may offset cash boot received: $40,000 − $10,000 = $30,000 recognized under §1031. Ignoring the offset overstates the recognized gain.

questions.q: Yuri sold land for $2,000,000 on the installment method (gross profit percentage 50%), receiving no down payment and a note due in five years. This year he borrows $1,000,000 from a bank and pledges the note as security. The §453A pledge rule applies. How much gain does Yuri recognize this year?
questions.exp: Under §453A, pledging an installment obligation as security for a loan treats the loan proceeds as a payment on the obligation: $1,000,000 × 50% = $500,000. Recognizing $1,000,000 applies the loan proceeds without the gross profit percentage.

questions.q: Zane exchanges land (basis $300,000; FMV $550,000) and $50,000 of cash for a commercial building worth $600,000. What is Zane's basis in the building?
questions.exp: Giving boot does not cause the giver to recognize gain (paying cash is not a sale). Basis = $300,000 old basis + $50,000 cash paid = $350,000, which equals the $600,000 FMV less the $250,000 deferred gain. A $600,000 cost basis ignores the deferral.

questions.q: Mia sold land with a $200,000 basis to her son for $500,000: $50,000 down and a note for the rest, with adequate interest. She reported $30,000 of gain in Year 1. In Year 2, before making any further payments, the son sells the land to an unrelated buyer for $520,000 cash. How much gain must Mia recognize in Year 2?
questions.exp: Under §453, the amount treated as received is the son's amount realized, capped at the $500,000 contract price, less payments already received ($50,000): $450,000 × 60% gross profit percentage = $270,000. Using the $520,000 resale price ignores the contract-price cap.

questions.q: Nell sold her relinquished property for $1,000,000 in a deferred exchange. Which identification of replacement property is valid?
choices: A written identification of three properties delivered on day 50
Five properties with a total FMV of $1,800,000, identified in writing on day 44
An oral identification of three properties to her qualified intermediary on day 40
Four properties with a total FMV of $2,400,000, of which she acquires two worth $1,100,000
questions.exp: Under Reg. 1.1031(k)-1, any number of properties may be identified if their total FMV does not exceed 200% of the relinquished property's value ($2,000,000), in writing within 45 days. Exceeding 200% requires acquiring 95% of the identified value. Oral and late identifications are invalid.

questions.q: Omar exchanges an apartment building (adjusted basis $300,000) for land worth $200,000 and a building worth $600,000, both acquired in the same exchange with no boot. How much of his $300,000 substituted basis is allocated to the building?
questions.exp: When several like-kind properties are received, the substituted basis is allocated by relative FMV: $300,000 × $600,000 ÷ $800,000 = $225,000. Assigning all the basis to the building would overstate depreciation, because land is not depreciable.

questions.q: Pia's warehouse, used in her business, is condemned by the city. She receives the condemnation award on August 1, 2026, and realizes a gain. She is a calendar-year taxpayer. What is the last day she can buy qualifying replacement real property and still defer the gain under §1033?
choices: December 31, 2028
August 1, 2028
August 1, 2029
December 31, 2029
questions.exp: For condemned real property held for business or investment, the replacement period ends three years after the close of the first tax year in which any gain is realized: December 31, 2029. The two-year period (December 31, 2028) applies to other involuntary conversions, such as casualties.

questions.q: Raj owns a rental building that the state condemns. He wants to buy unimproved land to hold for investment as the replacement. Which statement is correct under §1033?
choices: The land qualifies only if Raj builds a rental building on it within the replacement period
The land does not qualify because replacement property must be similar or related in service or use
The land qualifies only if bought within two years
The land qualifies because, for condemned real property held for business or investment, like-kind replacement property suffices
questions.exp: Section 1033 allows like-kind property as a replacement for condemned real property held for business or investment, and improved and unimproved real property are like-kind. The stricter 'similar or related in service or use' test applies to other involuntary conversions.

questions.q: A partnership owns an apartment building. Partner A wants to cash out, while Partners B and C want to defer gain through a §1031 exchange. Which approach is most consistent with the exchange rules?
choices: Partner A exchanges his partnership interest for an interest in another partnership owning real property
The partnership exchanges the building, and Partner A's share of the replacement is treated as his sale
The partnership distributes undivided tenancy-in-common interests in the building to the partners well before the sale, after which A sells his interest and B and C exchange theirs
The partnership completes the exchange and then redeems Partner A with cash from a refinancing on the same day
questions.exp: Partnership interests are not like-kind property, so a 'drop and swap' converts the ownership into direct tenancy-in-common interests that each owner can sell or exchange separately. Doing it well in advance supports the required 'held for investment' intent. Swapping partnership interests fails because they are excluded from §1031.

questions.q: Sue exchanges rental land with a $90,000 basis for other rental land worth $110,000 plus $50,000 of cash. What gain does she recognize?
questions.exp: Her realized gain is $160,000 − $90,000 = $70,000, but under §1031 recognized gain is limited to the lesser of realized gain or boot received, here the $50,000 of cash. Answering $70,000 recognizes the full realized gain and ignores the boot limit.

questions.q: Tom trades in a business pickup truck (adjusted basis $10,000; FMV $25,000) and pays $35,000 cash for a new truck priced at $60,000. What are Tom's recognized gain and basis in the new truck?
choices: $0 gain; $60,000 basis
$0 gain; $45,000 basis
questions.exp: Since 2018, §1031 applies only to real property, so the trade-in is a taxable sale: $25,000 − $10,000 = $15,000 of gain (§1245 ordinary income), and the new truck takes a $60,000 cost basis. The $45,000 substituted basis reflects pre-2018 law.

questions.q: Ula sold land on the installment method last year and reported it that way on her timely filed return. This year, her tax adviser recommends recognizing the entire remaining gain because her other income dropped sharply. Which statement is correct?
choices: She can accelerate the gain only by disposing of the note
She can amend last year's return at any time within three years to elect out
She may revoke the installment method only with IRS consent, which is generally granted only in limited circumstances, so planning should be done by the due date of the year-of-sale return
She can elect out of the installment method on this year's return
questions.exp: Under §453, the election out must be made by the due date (including extensions) of the return for the year of sale, and a late election or revocation requires IRS consent, which is rarely granted for hindsight tax planning. Disposing of the note is a way to trigger the gain, but it is not the only constraint the question tests.

questions.q: Vera exchanges investment real property with a $100,000 basis, worth $400,000, for replacement real property. She receives replacement property worth $350,000 and a $50,000 note from the buyer, payable next year with adequate interest, through her qualified intermediary. Which statement is correct?
choices: The note causes the exchange to fail
The $50,000 note is not boot because it is not cash
The $50,000 note is boot, but the gain it represents may be reported on the installment method when the note is collected
All $300,000 of realized gain is recognized because a note was received
questions.exp: A note received in an exchange is boot, but under §453 and Reg. 1.1031(k)-1 the gain it represents can be reported as payments are received. Treating the note as not boot ignores that it is non-like-kind property, while treating the exchange as failed goes too far.

questions.q: Vale Corp., a C corporation, earns $100,000 of pretax income and distributes all of its after-tax earnings to its sole shareholder as a qualified dividend. The shareholder pays 20% on qualified dividends plus the 3.8% net investment income tax. What is the combined corporate and shareholder tax on the $100,000?
questions.exp: Corporate tax is $100,000 × 21% = $21,000, leaving a $79,000 dividend taxed at 23.8% = $18,802, for a total of $39,802. Adding the two rates to get $44,800 ignores that the shareholder tax applies only to the after-tax amount actually distributed.

questions.q: Birch Corp. has gross income from operations of $200,000, operating expenses of $210,000, and $100,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 30% of the stock. What is Birch's dividends-received deduction?
questions.exp: Taxable income before the DRD is $200,000 + $100,000 − $210,000 = $90,000. The 65% DRD ($65,000) is limited to 65% × $90,000 = $58,500, and the limit applies because taking the full $65,000 would not create an NOL ($90,000 − $65,000 is still positive). The $65,000 answer ignores the taxable income limitation.

questions.q: Cedar Corp. owns 30% of a domestic corporation and receives $100,000 of dividends from it. Cedar also has $200,000 of operating income and $240,000 of operating expenses. How much DRD may Cedar claim?
questions.exp: Taxable income before the DRD is $60,000, and the full 65% DRD of $65,000 would create a $5,000 NOL, so the taxable income limitation does not apply and the full $65,000 is allowed. Answering $39,000 (65% × $60,000) applies the limitation even though the NOL exception overrides it.

questions.q: Dune Corp. has taxable income of $400,000 before any NOL deduction and an NOL carryforward of $500,000 that arose in a tax year beginning after 2020. What is Dune's regular federal income tax for the year?
questions.exp: Post-2017 NOLs may offset only 80% of taxable income, so the deduction is $320,000, leaving $80,000 × 21% = $16,800 of tax and a $180,000 carryforward. A $0 answer wrongly lets the NOL offset 100% of taxable income.

questions.q: Elm Corp. has $300,000 of ordinary income, a $20,000 long-term capital gain and a $50,000 short-term capital loss for the year. How is the net capital loss treated?
choices: It is not deductible this year; it is carried back 3 years and forward 5 years as a short-term capital loss
It is carried back 2 years and forward 20 years as an ordinary loss
It offsets ordinary income in full, reducing taxable income to $270,000
Up to $3,000 offsets ordinary income, and the rest carries forward indefinitely
questions.exp: A corporation may deduct capital losses only against capital gains; the $30,000 net capital loss is carried back 3 years and forward 5 years, always as a short-term loss. The $3,000 ordinary offset and indefinite carryforward are individual rules.

questions.q: Fir Corp., a C corporation, sells a commercial building for $1,100,000. It bought the building for $1,000,000 and took $300,000 of straight-line depreciation. How much of the gain is ordinary income under §291?
questions.exp: The gain is $1,100,000 − $700,000 = $400,000. Section 291 treats 20% of the lesser of the depreciation taken ($300,000) or the gain ($400,000) as ordinary income: 20% × $300,000 = $60,000. Answering $80,000 applies the 20% to the total gain instead of to the depreciation.

questions.q: At the start of the year, Grove Corp. has an accumulated E&P deficit of $50,000. Its current E&P for the year is $30,000, and it distributes $40,000 cash to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $100,000. How much of the distribution is a taxable dividend?
questions.exp: A distribution is a dividend to the extent of current E&P even when accumulated E&P is negative, so $30,000 is a dividend and the remaining $10,000 is a return of basis. Answering $0 wrongly nets the accumulated deficit against current E&P before the year ends.

questions.q: Hale Corp. distributes land to its shareholder as a dividend. The land has a basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $100,000 and is subject to a $120,000 mortgage that the shareholder assumes. What gain does Hale recognize?
questions.exp: When distributed property is subject to a liability greater than its value, the FMV is treated as not less than the liability, so Hale recognizes $120,000 − $30,000 = $90,000. The $70,000 answer uses the $100,000 FMV and ignores the liability rule.

questions.q: Iris Corp. has ample E&P and distributes investment land to its sole shareholder. The land has a basis of $80,000 and an FMV of $50,000. What are the tax results?
choices: Iris recognizes a $30,000 loss; the shareholder has a $50,000 dividend and a $50,000 basis
Iris recognizes no loss; the shareholder has a $50,000 dividend and a $50,000 basis in the land
Iris recognizes no loss; the shareholder has a $50,000 dividend and an $80,000 basis
Iris recognizes no loss; the shareholder has an $80,000 dividend and an $80,000 basis
questions.exp: A corporation cannot recognize a loss on a nonliquidating distribution of property, and the shareholder's dividend and basis both equal the $50,000 FMV, so the $30,000 loss disappears. Better planning would be to sell the land, recognize the loss, and distribute the cash.

questions.q: Jett Corp. has 100 shares of voting common stock outstanding. Amy owns 60 shares, and unrelated individuals own the rest. Jett redeems 30 of Amy's shares. How is the redemption treated?
choices: As an exchange, because Amy's interest falls to about 42.9%, below both 50% and 80% of her prior 60%
As a dividend, because only a complete termination qualifies for exchange treatment
As an exchange, but only if Amy waives family attribution for 10 years
As a dividend, because Amy still owns more than 20% of the stock
questions.exp: After the redemption Amy owns 30 of 70 shares (42.9%). That is under 50% and under 80% × 60% = 48%, so the redemption is substantially disproportionate under §302 and treated as an exchange. Complete termination is only one of several ways to get exchange treatment.

questions.q: Father and Son each own 50 of the 100 outstanding shares of Kite Corp. Kite redeems all of Father's shares for cash. What lets Father treat the redemption as an exchange rather than a dividend?
choices: Father waiving family attribution: no interest other than as a creditor, no reacquisition for 10 years, and a filed agreement
Father receiving a note instead of cash for the shares
Nothing, because Son's shares are always attributed to Father
Father staying on as a paid consultant to keep the business stable
questions.exp: Without a waiver, Father constructively owns Son's shares and so owns 100% after the redemption. Section 302 waives family attribution if Father keeps no interest other than as a creditor (not as an employee or consultant), acquires none for 10 years, and files the agreement.

questions.q: Which statement about the accumulated earnings tax is correct?
choices: It is self-assessed each year on a schedule attached to Form 1120
Earnings retained for documented, reasonably anticipated business needs reduce the amount subject to tax
It applies to S corporations that retain more than $250,000 of earnings
It is imposed at 37% on undistributed taxable income
questions.exp: The 20% accumulated earnings tax reaches only earnings retained beyond the reasonable needs of the business, so a specific, documented plan (such as a plant expansion) is the main defense. It is assessed by the IRS rather than self-reported, and it does not apply to S corporations.

questions.q: Lark Corp., a manufacturer, had accumulated E&P of $180,000 at the end of the prior year. For the current year its accumulated taxable income before the accumulated earnings credit is $200,000, it paid no dividends, and it cannot show any reasonable business needs. What is its accumulated earnings tax?
questions.exp: The minimum credit for a non-service corporation is $250,000 − $180,000 = $70,000, so the tax is 20% × ($200,000 − $70,000) = $26,000. The $40,000 answer ignores the minimum credit, which would be the result for a personal service corporation, whose $150,000 minimum is already exceeded by the $180,000 of accumulated E&P.

questions.q: A closely held C corporation is a personal holding company when which conditions are both met?
choices: At least 60% of taxable income is retained, and five or fewer individuals own more than 50% of the voting stock
At least 50% of gross income is passive, and ten or fewer individuals own more than 80% of the voting stock at year-end
At least 25% of gross receipts are passive investment income, and the corporation has accumulated E&P
At least 60% of adjusted ordinary gross income is PHC income, and five or fewer individuals own more than 50% of the stock value at any time in the last half of the year
questions.exp: The PHC tests are an income test (60% of adjusted ordinary gross income) and an ownership test (more than 50% of value held by five or fewer individuals during the last half of the year). The 25% passive investment income test is an S corporation rule.

questions.q: Mesa Corp. discovers after year-end that it was a personal holding company and owes PHC tax. Which step can reduce its undistributed PHC income for that year even after the year has closed?
choices: A pro rata stock dividend to its common shareholders
A capital contribution by its shareholders
A retroactive election to be taxed as an S corporation
A deficiency dividend paid after the PHC liability is determined
questions.exp: The deficiency dividend procedure lets a PHC pay a dividend after the liability is determined and deduct it for the earlier year, removing the 20% PHC tax (interest and penalties still apply). A stock dividend does not distribute earnings, so it gives no dividends-paid deduction.

questions.q: Nash Corp. is a closely held C corporation that is not a personal service corporation. This year it has $100,000 of net active business income, $30,000 of portfolio income, and a $120,000 loss from a passive rental activity. How much of the passive loss may Nash deduct?
questions.exp: A closely held C corporation that is not a PSC may use passive losses against net active income but not against portfolio income, so it deducts $100,000 and carries $20,000 forward. A personal service corporation could deduct none of the loss.

questions.q: Oak Corp., an accrual-method calendar-year C corporation, accrues a $50,000 bonus on December 31, 2026, for its president, a cash-method individual who owns 60% of its stock. The bonus is paid on March 1, 2027. When may Oak deduct it?
choices: In 2026, because it is paid within 2½ months after year-end
In 2027, when the shareholder includes it in income
Never, because compensation to a majority shareholder is a dividend
In 2026, because all events fixing the liability occurred in 2026
questions.exp: Under §267, an accrual-method corporation cannot deduct an amount owed to a cash-method related party (more than 50% owner) until the payee includes it in income, which is 2027. The 2½-month rule applies only to unrelated employees.

questions.q: Pine Corp. is formed and begins business on July 1 of its first calendar tax year. It incurred $53,000 of organizational expenditures. What is its maximum deduction for organizational expenditures in the first year?
questions.exp: The $5,000 immediate deduction is reduced dollar for dollar by the $3,000 above $50,000, leaving $2,000. The remaining $51,000 is amortized over 180 months: $51,000 / 180 × 6 = $1,700, for a total of $3,700. The $6,700 answer forgets the phase-out of the $5,000 amount.

questions.q: Quill Corp. pays its sole shareholder-employee a salary far above what comparable businesses pay for similar services. On audit, how is the IRS most likely to treat the excess?
choices: As a capital contribution that increases the shareholder's stock basis
As a nondeductible constructive dividend to the extent of E&P
As a loan from Quill to the shareholder that must be repaid
As a deductible salary, because the board approved it
questions.exp: Only reasonable compensation is deductible; the excess paid to a shareholder-employee is recharacterized as a constructive dividend, which the corporation cannot deduct and which is still taxable to the shareholder. In an S corporation the IRS usually challenges the opposite pattern, salaries that are too low.

questions.q: Shareholders of a new C corporation are deciding whether to fund it with part debt and part equity instead of all equity. What is the main tax advantage of including bona fide shareholder debt?
choices: Interest received by the shareholders qualifies for the 20% dividend rate
Interest paid is deductible by the corporation, and principal repayments are a tax-free return of the loan rather than dividends
The debt raises the shareholders' stock basis, allowing them to deduct corporate losses
Repaying the debt is deductible by the corporation in the year paid
questions.exp: Interest is deductible (subject to limits such as §163(j)), and principal repayments are a tax-free recovery of the loan, whereas equity returns come out as nondeductible dividends. If the debt lacks real debt features, the IRS may reclassify it as equity under §385 principles.

questions.q: Parent Corp. owns 70% of Sub Corp.'s voting stock and 70% of its value. Parent wants to offset Sub's operating losses against its own income. What must change for the two to file a consolidated federal return?
choices: Parent must own at least 80% of Sub's voting power and 80% of its value
Parent must own 80% of Sub's voting power; value is irrelevant
Sub must elect to be treated as a personal holding company
Nothing; 50% ownership is enough for a consolidated return
questions.exp: An affiliated group needs a common parent that directly owns stock with at least 80% of the total voting power and at least 80% of the total value of the subsidiary. Once affiliated, members may file a consolidated return that nets one member's losses against another's income.

questions.q: Pratt Corp. owns 100% of Spoke Corp. and completely liquidates it. Pratt's basis in the Spoke stock is $200,000. Spoke's assets have an adjusted basis of $500,000 and an FMV of $900,000, and it has no liabilities. What gain does Pratt recognize, and what basis does it take in the assets?
choices: $0 gain; $200,000 basis
$0 gain; $500,000 basis
$0 gain; $900,000 basis
questions.exp: Under §332, a parent owning at least 80% of the vote and value recognizes no gain or loss on a subsidiary's liquidation, and it takes Spoke's $500,000 carryover basis. The $200,000 stock basis disappears, so it is not the asset basis.

questions.q: Ridge Corp. adopts a plan of complete liquidation and distributes land (basis $100,000, FMV $400,000) to its sole individual shareholder, whose stock basis is $50,000. What gain does Ridge recognize, and what is the shareholder's basis in the land?
choices: $0 gain; $50,000 basis
$0 gain; $100,000 basis
questions.exp: Under §336 a liquidating corporation recognizes gain as if it sold the property at FMV ($400,000 − $100,000 = $300,000). The shareholder is taxed under §331 on the excess of FMV over stock basis and takes a $400,000 FMV basis. The carryover basis applies only to an 80% corporate parent under §332.

questions.q: Stark Corp. had taxable income of over $1 million in one of its three preceding tax years. Which statement about Stark's current-year estimated tax payments is correct?
choices: It must pay 110% of last year's tax to use the prior-year safe harbor
It may base all four installments on 100% of last year's tax
It is not required to make estimated payments if it files by the extended due date
It may use last year's tax only for the first installment and must base the rest on current-year tax
questions.exp: A large corporation (taxable income of $1 million or more in any of the three prior years) may use the prior-year safe harbor only for its first installment and must recapture any shortfall in the second. The 110% rule applies to high-income individuals, not corporations.

questions.q: Which statement about the corporate alternative minimum tax (CAMT) is correct?
choices: It is 20% of adjusted current earnings and applies to all corporations
It applies to every C corporation with financial statement income above $1 million
It is 15% of adjusted financial statement income and generally applies only to corporations averaging more than $1 billion of it
It is 21% of taxable income after adding back tax preference items
questions.exp: The CAMT enacted in 2022 is 15% of adjusted financial statement income (book income with specified adjustments) and generally reaches only corporations whose average annual AFSI over three years exceeds $1 billion. Any CAMT paid creates a minimum tax credit for later years.

questions.q: A publicly traded domestic corporation repurchases $50 million of its stock during the year and issues $20 million of new stock to employees and investors in the same year. What is its stock buyback excise tax?
questions.exp: The excise tax is 1% of the FMV of stock repurchased, reduced by the FMV of stock issued during the year: 1% × ($50 million − $20 million) = $300,000. The $500,000 answer ignores the netting for stock issued.

questions.q: The founder of a profitable C corporation plans to keep the stock until death and let earnings build inside the company for real business needs. Which tax effect makes this a common planning strategy?
choices: Accumulated E&P is eliminated when the founder dies
The heirs' stock basis steps up to FMV, so the shareholder-level tax on the retained earnings can be avoided
The corporation may deduct the value of the founder's stock at death
Retained earnings escape the corporate-level tax
questions.exp: Under §1014, the heirs take an FMV basis in the stock, so a later sale or redemption produces little gain and the second tax on retained earnings may never be paid. The corporation still pays its 21% tax, and its E&P stays intact.

questions.q: A business owner who works full time in her company is comparing a C corporation with an S corporation. Which fringe-benefit advantage does a C corporation offer her?
choices: She may exclude $50,000 of dividends each year as a fringe benefit
Her share of corporate income is taxed only when distributed as salary
Her salary is exempt from FICA tax
Employer-paid health insurance is excluded from her income even though she owns 100% of the stock
questions.exp: A shareholder-employee of a C corporation is an employee for fringe-benefit purposes, so employer-paid health coverage is excluded under §106. A more-than-2% S corporation shareholder is treated like a partner and must include those premiums in wages.

questions.q: Teal Corp. buys 5% of a domestic corporation's stock 10 days before the ex-dividend date, receives a $40,000 dividend, and sells the stock 20 days after the ex-dividend date. How much DRD may Teal claim on the dividend?
questions.exp: The DRD is denied unless the stock is held more than 45 days during the 91-day period beginning 45 days before the ex-dividend date; Teal held it about 30 days. Otherwise the 50% DRD for less-than-20% ownership would have given $20,000.

questions.q: What happens when a C corporation distributes appreciated property, rather than cash, to a shareholder as a nonliquidating distribution?
choices: The corporation recognizes gain, but the shareholder's dividend is limited to the corporation's basis
The corporation recognizes gain as if it sold the property at FMV, which can produce two levels of tax on the appreciation
The corporation recognizes no gain, and the shareholder takes a carryover basis
The corporation recognizes gain only if the shareholder owns more than 50% of the stock
questions.exp: Section 311 taxes the corporation on the appreciation as if it sold the property, and the shareholder also has a dividend equal to FMV (to the extent of E&P) with an FMV basis. That is why appreciated property is usually a poor choice to distribute from a C corporation.

questions.q: In 2025, Ellen, who has AGI of $200,000 and itemizes, gives $150,000 of cash to her church, a public charity. She makes no other contributions. What is her 2025 deduction?
choices: $120,000 deduction; the $30,000 excess is lost
$120,000 deduction; $30,000 carried forward five years
$150,000 deduction; no carryover
$100,000 deduction; $50,000 carried forward five years
questions.exp: Cash gifts to public charities are limited to 60% of AGI: 60% x $200,000 = $120,000, and the $30,000 excess carries forward for five years. The 50% limit applies to noncash property, not cash, and excess contributions are not forfeited.

questions.q: In 2025, Victor, with AGI of $200,000, donates publicly traded stock held for three years (basis $30,000, fair market value $90,000) to a public charity. He makes no other gifts and no special election. What is his current deduction?
choices: $90,000, with no carryover
$100,000, with no carryover
$30,000, with no carryover
$60,000, with a $30,000 carryover
questions.exp: Long-term capital gain property given to a public charity is deductible at fair market value but limited to 30% of AGI: 30% x $200,000 = $60,000, with the $30,000 excess carried forward. The 50% limit would apply only if he elected to deduct basis instead.

questions.q: Same facts as a gift of long-term stock worth $90,000 with a $30,000 basis to a public charity by a donor with $200,000 of AGI, but the donor elects to reduce the contribution to basis. What is the result?
choices: A $30,000 deduction now and a $60,000 carryover
A $30,000 deduction under the 50% limit, and the $60,000 of appreciation is never deducted
A $90,000 deduction under the 50% limit
A $60,000 deduction under the 30% limit and no carryover
questions.exp: The election measures the gift at its $30,000 basis but moves it to the 50% limit ($100,000), so $30,000 is deducted now and the appreciation is permanently lost. It makes sense mainly when appreciation is small or the donor cannot use a carryover.

questions.q: Gina, a sole proprietor who runs a bookstore, donates inventory with a cost of $4,000 and a retail value of $10,000 to a public library. What is her charitable deduction?
questions.exp: Inventory is ordinary income property, so the deduction is reduced by the ordinary income that would have been recognized on a sale, leaving the $4,000 cost. No enhanced inventory deduction applies because the books are not food and are not used to care for the ill, the needy or infants, so $7,000 is not available.

questions.q: Hal donates stock he has held for ten months (basis $6,000, fair market value $10,000) to a public charity. What is his charitable deduction?
questions.exp: Stock held one year or less is short-term capital gain property, treated like ordinary income property, so the deduction is limited to the $6,000 basis. Fair market value is allowed only for property held more than one year.

questions.q: Iris donates a painting she has owned for five years (basis $20,000, fair market value $50,000) to a hospital, which she knows will sell it to raise funds. What is her deduction?
choices: $0, because the hospital is not a museum
$35,000, the average of basis and value
$50,000, limited to 30% of AGI
$20,000, because the property is put to an unrelated use
questions.exp: Long-term tangible personal property whose use is unrelated to the donee's exempt purpose is deductible only at basis, $20,000. Fair market value would be allowed only if the donee used the painting in its exempt function, such as an art museum displaying it.

questions.q: Jack, whose AGI is $400,000, donates a sculpture he has owned for six years (basis $20,000, fair market value $50,000) to an art museum that will display it in its permanent collection. What is his deduction?
choices: $20,000, limited to 50% of AGI
$50,000, limited to 60% of AGI
$30,000, the amount of appreciation
$50,000, limited to 30% of AGI
questions.exp: Because the museum uses the sculpture in its exempt purpose, it is long-term capital gain property deductible at $50,000 fair market value, subject to the 30% limit ($120,000 here). The 60% limit applies only to cash gifts to public charities.

questions.q: Kara donates land held ten years (basis $40,000, fair market value $100,000) to her family's private nonoperating foundation. What are the amount and AGI limit of her deduction?
choices: $40,000, limited to 30% of AGI
$100,000, limited to 20% of AGI
$100,000, limited to 30% of AGI
$40,000, limited to 20% of AGI
questions.exp: Long-term capital gain property given to a private nonoperating foundation is deductible only at basis, $40,000, and is limited to 20% of AGI. Fair market value is allowed only for qualified appreciated stock, meaning publicly traded stock, not land.

questions.q: In 2025, Leon, with AGI of $300,000, donates publicly traded stock held for four years (basis $20,000, fair market value $80,000) to a private nonoperating foundation. What are his deduction and carryover?
choices: $80,000 deduction; no carryover
$60,000 deduction; $20,000 carryover
$20,000 deduction; no carryover
$60,000 deduction; the $20,000 excess is lost
questions.exp: Qualified appreciated stock given to a private foundation is deductible at fair market value, subject to the 20% limit: 20% x $300,000 = $60,000, with the $20,000 excess carried forward five years. Limiting the gift to basis applies to other capital gain property, not publicly traded stock.

questions.q: In 2025, Mona, with AGI of $100,000, gives $40,000 of cash to a private nonoperating foundation and makes no other gifts. What is her deduction?
choices: $40,000, under the 60% cash limit
$20,000, with a $20,000 carryover
$30,000, with a $10,000 carryover
$30,000, with the $10,000 excess lost
questions.exp: Cash gifts to private nonoperating foundations are limited to 30% of AGI: 30% x $100,000 = $30,000, and the $10,000 excess carries forward five years. The 60% cash limit applies only to public charities; 20% applies to capital gain property given to such foundations.

questions.q: In 2025, Ned has AGI of $100,000. He gives $20,000 of cash and long-term stock worth $40,000 (basis $15,000) to his church, a public charity, and makes no elections. What is his total current deduction?
choices: $50,000, with a $10,000 carryover
$40,000, with a $20,000 carryover
$35,000, because the stock is deducted at basis
$60,000, because the overall limit is 60% of AGI
questions.exp: The cash ($20,000) is allowed in full, and the capital gain stock is limited to the lesser of 30% of AGI ($30,000) or 50% of AGI less the cash gift ($50,000 - $20,000 = $30,000). Total is $50,000, with $10,000 of stock carried forward; the 60% limit does not apply to property.

questions.q: A donor has a charitable contribution carryover from a prior year and also makes new contributions this year. How are they applied against this year's limits?
choices: Carryovers may be used only if no current-year gifts are made
Carryovers are used first, oldest first, before current-year gifts
Carryovers and current gifts are prorated against the limit
Current-year contributions are deducted first, then carryovers in the order they arose
questions.exp: Current-year contributions are applied first, then carryovers from the earliest year, each keeping its original percentage-limit character for up to five years. Applying carryovers first is a common error that would let older amounts crowd out new gifts.

questions.q: Owen sells land with a basis of $40,000 and fair market value of $100,000 to a public charity for $40,000, intending the difference as a gift. What gain does he recognize, and what is his contribution?
choices: No gain; $60,000 contribution
$60,000 gain; $100,000 contribution
$24,000 gain; $76,000 contribution
$24,000 gain; $60,000 contribution
questions.exp: In a bargain sale, basis is allocated in proportion to the sale price: $40,000 x ($40,000 / $100,000) = $16,000, so gain is $40,000 - $16,000 = $24,000. The contribution is the $60,000 of value given up; assuming full basis offsets the price ignores the allocation rule.

questions.q: Pia owns stock with a basis of $50,000 and a fair market value of $30,000. She wants to benefit a public charity. Which approach gives her the best tax result?
choices: Donate the stock to a donor-advised fund to preserve the loss
Donate the stock directly and deduct its $50,000 basis
Sell the stock, recognize the $20,000 capital loss and donate the $30,000 cash
Donate the stock directly and deduct $30,000 plus the $20,000 loss
questions.exp: Donating depreciated property yields a deduction of only fair market value and the loss is never recognized, so selling first captures the $20,000 capital loss and still produces a $30,000 cash deduction. A donor-advised fund gift is also a gift of the stock and loses the loss.

questions.q: Quinn holds long-term stock with a basis of $10,000 and a value of $50,000 and plans to give $50,000 to a public charity. Compared with selling the stock and donating the after-tax proceeds plus cash to reach $50,000, what does donating the stock directly accomplish?
choices: It converts the $40,000 gain into ordinary income for the charity
It allows the gain to be deferred until the charity sells
It avoids tax on the $40,000 gain while still producing a $50,000 deduction
It produces a larger deduction of $90,000
questions.exp: Long-term capital gain property is deductible at fair market value and the donor never recognizes the built-in gain, so a direct gift saves tax on $40,000 that a sale would trigger. The charity, being tax-exempt, pays no tax when it later sells, so nothing is merely deferred.

questions.q: Rita pays $500 for a ticket to a charity gala at which she receives a dinner worth $150. What is her deduction, and what must the charity provide?
choices: $350; a written statement disclosing the value of the dinner
$500; a receipt only if the payment exceeds $250
$350; no statement, because the benefit is under $250
$150; a statement of the amount Rita paid
questions.exp: Only the excess of the payment over the value received is deductible: $500 - $150 = $350. A quid pro quo payment over $75 requires the charity to give a written disclosure of the good-faith estimate of the benefit, regardless of the $250 acknowledgment rule.

questions.q: Sean makes a single $1,000 cash gift to a public charity by check. What substantiation must he have to claim the deduction?
choices: A Form 8283 signed by the charity and attached to his return
His canceled check is sufficient for any cash gift
A contemporaneous written acknowledgment from the charity, obtained by the earlier of filing or the return's due date, including extensions
A qualified appraisal attached to his return
questions.exp: A single contribution of $250 or more requires a contemporaneous written acknowledgment stating the amount and whether any goods or services were provided, obtained by the earlier of the filing date or the extended due date. A canceled check alone is not enough at this level, and appraisals and Form 8283 relate to noncash gifts.

questions.q: Which of the following donations requires the donor to obtain a qualified appraisal to support the deduction?
choices: Used clothing in good condition valued at $400
A $20,000 cash gift to a university
Stock of a closely held corporation valued at $12,000
Publicly traded stock valued at $50,000
