questions.exp: Noncash gifts of property (or similar items) claimed at more than $5,000 generally need a qualified appraisal, and closely held stock is not excepted. Publicly traded securities are excepted because their value is readily determinable, and cash never requires an appraisal.

questions.q: Tom donates a used car with a published blue-book value of $6,000 to a charity, which sells it at auction for $2,500 without making any significant use of it or improving it. What is Tom's maximum deduction?
questions.exp: When a donated vehicle claimed at more than $500 is sold by the charity without significant intervening use or material improvement, the deduction is limited to the gross proceeds reported on Form 1098-C, $2,500. The blue-book value is not used, and $500 is only the threshold that triggers the rule.

questions.q: Uma, an attorney, volunteers 20 hours of legal work for a public charity. Her normal billing rate is $300 per hour, and she spends $150 of her own money on supplies used for the project. What is her charitable deduction?
questions.exp: The value of donated services is never deductible, but unreimbursed out-of-pocket expenses incurred while performing services for a charity are deductible, so Uma deducts $150. Treating the forgone $6,000 of fees as a contribution is the common error.

questions.q: Which of the following payments is deductible in 2025 by a calendar-year individual who itemizes?
choices: A check dated December 31, 2025, but mailed on January 5, 2026
A contribution charged to a credit card on December 28, 2025, and paid to the card issuer in January 2026
A note payable to the charity signed in December 2025 and paid in 2026
A written pledge made in December 2025 and paid in February 2026
questions.exp: A charge to a credit card is deductible when charged, even if the card balance is paid the next year. Pledges and the taxpayer's own notes are deductible only when paid, and a check counts when mailed or delivered, which here occurred in 2026.

questions.q: Which of the following is deductible as a charitable contribution by an individual who itemizes?
choices: Membership dues paid to a country club
A gift to a scholarship fund earmarked for a named student
A cash gift to a state university's general scholarship fund
The cost of raffle tickets bought from a church
questions.exp: Gifts to a state university for its own use are deductible because a state institution is a qualified donee. Earmarking a gift for a specific individual makes it a gift to that person, and raffle tickets are purchases of a chance to win rather than gifts.

questions.q: For 2025, Watt Corp. has taxable income of $480,000 after a $20,000 dividends-received deduction but before any charitable deduction. It made $70,000 of qualifying cash contributions and has no NOL or capital loss carrybacks. What is its charitable deduction?
questions.exp: A corporation's limit is 10% of taxable income computed without the charitable deduction or the dividends-received deduction: 10% x ($480,000 + $20,000) = $50,000. The $20,000 excess carries forward five years; computing the limit after the DRD gives $48,000.

questions.q: Which transfer of a partial interest in property produces a charitable deduction outside a trust?
choices: A gift of the right to use a vacation home rent-free for two weeks
A gift of the right to receive rent from a building while the donor keeps the building
A gift of a 10-year term of years in an office building
A gift of a remainder interest in the donor's personal residence
questions.exp: Partial interests are generally nondeductible, but a remainder interest in a personal residence or farm is a specific statutory exception. Rent-free use of property and income interests carved out of property the donor keeps fail the partial interest rule.

questions.q: How does a charitable remainder annuity trust differ from a charitable remainder unitrust?
choices: A CRAT is taxable on its income, while a CRUT is exempt
A CRAT's payout may be as low as 1%, while a CRUT's payout must be at least 10%
A CRAT pays a fixed amount set at creation and cannot accept additional contributions; a CRUT pays a fixed percentage of annually revalued assets
A CRAT pays a fixed percentage of annually revalued assets; a CRUT pays a fixed dollar amount
questions.exp: A CRAT pays a fixed annuity of at least 5% (and not more than 50%) of initial value and may not receive later additions, while a CRUT pays a fixed percentage of its value redetermined each year and may accept additions. Both are tax-exempt, and the 5% minimum payout applies to both.

questions.q: Yara transfers stock with a large built-in gain to a charitable remainder unitrust, which immediately sells it and reinvests the proceeds. What are the income tax consequences?
choices: The trust is generally exempt, so the gain is not taxed on the sale, and Yara's payouts are taxed under a tiered ordering that can carry out the gain over time
Neither the trust nor Yara is ever taxed on the gain
The trust pays capital gains tax on the sale at trust rates
Yara recognizes the gain on the sale because she arranged it
questions.exp: A CRT is exempt from income tax, so a sale inside the trust defers tax on the gain, and distributions are taxed in the order ordinary income, capital gain, other income and then corpus. The gain is not permanently exempt, because it can be carried out to Yara in her annual payments.

questions.q: Zack funds a charitable remainder unitrust with $1,000,000 of property, retaining a lifetime unitrust interest with the remainder to his alma mater. What income tax deduction does he receive in the year of funding?
choices: The present value of the charitable remainder, which must be at least 10% of the value contributed
The present value of his retained unitrust interest
Nothing until the charity receives the remainder at his death
$1,000,000, the full value transferred
questions.exp: The donor deducts the present value of the remainder interest passing to charity, and a CRT must have a remainder of at least 10% of the initial value to qualify. He cannot deduct his own retained payment stream, and the deduction is not deferred until the charity receives the assets.

questions.q: Abby expects unusually high income this year and wants to fund her charitable giving for the next five years while deciding later which charities to support. Which strategy best fits, and why?
choices: Contribute to a donor-advised fund, deducting the gift now at public charity limits while recommending grants later
Create a private nonoperating foundation, because gifts to it receive the highest AGI limits
Transfer property to a charitable lead trust, because the remainder returns to her
Make pledges to several charities, because pledges are deductible when made
questions.exp: A gift to a donor-advised fund is a completed gift to a public charity, deductible in the high-income year, while Abby keeps only advisory privileges over later grants. Pledges are deductible only when paid, and private foundations have lower AGI limits than public charities.

questions.q: Which statement about a qualified charitable distribution from an IRA is correct?
choices: It is excluded from income, may count toward the owner's required minimum distribution and produces no charitable deduction
It is available from any retirement plan, including an active 401(k)
The owner includes the distribution in income and claims an offsetting itemized deduction
It may be made to a donor-advised fund if the owner is at least age 70 1/2
questions.exp: A QCD paid directly from an IRA to an eligible charity by an owner at least age 70 1/2 is excluded from income and can satisfy the RMD, but no deduction is allowed. Donor-advised funds and supporting organizations are not eligible recipients, and QCDs must come from an IRA.

questions.q: Ben transfers property to a charitable lead annuity trust that pays a fixed annuity to charity for 15 years, with the remainder then passing to his children. The trust is structured as a nongrantor trust. Which statement is correct?
choices: Ben receives an immediate income tax deduction for the present value of the annuity
Ben receives no income tax deduction, and the trust deducts its payments to charity
Ben is taxed annually on the trust's income
The children receive an income tax deduction when the remainder vests
questions.exp: With a nongrantor CLT, the donor gets no upfront income tax deduction, and the trust itself deducts the amounts paid to charity from its gross income. The upfront deduction, with the donor taxed on trust income each year, applies only to a grantor lead trust.

questions.q: Kai was granted nonqualified stock options (no readily ascertainable FMV) to buy 1,000 shares at $10 per share. He exercised them when the stock was worth $30 per share and sold the shares 18 months later for $40 per share. How much ordinary income does Kai recognize at exercise?
questions.exp: At exercise of an NQSO, the spread is compensation: ($30 - $10) x 1,000 = $20,000. His basis becomes $30,000, so the later sale produces $10,000 of long-term capital gain.

questions.q: Lia exercised incentive stock options for 1,000 shares at $10 per share when the FMV was $30 per share. She sold the shares for $50 per share more than two years after the grant and more than one year after exercise. What is the regular tax result of the sale?
choices: $40,000 long-term capital gain
$40,000 ordinary income
$50,000 long-term capital gain
$20,000 ordinary income and $20,000 long-term capital gain
questions.exp: In a qualifying ISO disposition, the entire gain over the exercise price is long-term capital gain: ($50 - $10) x 1,000 = $40,000, with no ordinary income. Splitting off the $20,000 spread applies only to a disqualifying disposition.

questions.q: In 2025, Lia exercised ISOs for 1,000 shares at $10 per share when the FMV was $30 per share, and she still held the shares at year-end. What is the effect for alternative minimum tax?
choices: A $20,000 negative AMT adjustment
No effect, because ISOs are tax-free
A $20,000 positive AMT adjustment, giving an AMT basis of $30,000 per share
A $30,000 AMT adjustment
questions.exp: The ISO bargain element ($20 x 1,000 = $20,000) is an AMT adjustment in the year of exercise if the shares are held past year-end, and AMT basis becomes $30 per share. Regular tax has no income at exercise.

questions.q: Max exercised ISOs for 1,000 shares at $10 per share when the FMV was $30 per share, and sold the shares six months later for $45 per share. How much ordinary income does he recognize?
questions.exp: Selling within a year of exercise is a disqualifying disposition, so the bargain element at exercise, ($30 - $10) x 1,000 = $20,000, is ordinary income, and the remaining $15,000 is short-term capital gain. The $35,000 trap treats the whole gain as ordinary income.

questions.q: Nia acquired 500 shares under an incentive stock option, paying the $12 strike price when the market value was $40. The stock then dropped, and three months later she sold all 500 shares for $32 each. What amount must she report as compensation (ordinary) income?
questions.exp: This is a disqualifying disposition, and when the sale price is below the exercise-date value, ordinary income is limited to the actual gain: ($32 - $12) x 500 = $10,000. Reporting the full $14,000 exercise spread is the trap.

questions.q: On one date, Omni Corp. grants Lee ISOs on 15,000 shares with a grant-date FMV of $10 per share, all first exercisable in the same calendar year. Lee has no other ISOs. How many of the options are treated as nonqualified options?
questions.exp: ISO treatment is limited to $100,000 of grant-date value first exercisable in any year: $100,000 / $10 = 10,000 shares qualify, and the other 5,000 are NQSOs. The rule does not disqualify the whole grant.

questions.q: Ann received 10,000 shares of restricted stock subject to a three-year vesting requirement. At grant the FMV was $2 per share, and she paid nothing. She made a timely §83(b) election. The stock was worth $15 per share at vesting. How much ordinary income does Ann recognize because of the election?
choices: $150,000 at vesting
$130,000 at vesting
$20,000 in the year of grant
questions.exp: With an election under §83 to be taxed at grant, the FMV at grant less the amount paid ($2 x 10,000 = $20,000) is ordinary income in the grant year, and nothing more is taxed at vesting. Her capital gain holding period starts at grant.

questions.q: Bo received 10,000 shares of restricted stock worth $2 per share at grant, subject to a three-year vesting requirement. He paid nothing and did not make a §83(b) election. At vesting, the stock was worth $15 per share. What does Bo recognize at vesting?
choices: $130,000 capital gain
$20,000 ordinary income
$150,000 ordinary income
questions.exp: Without an election under §83 to be taxed at grant, property subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture is taxed at vesting at its then FMV: $15 x 10,000 = $150,000 of ordinary income. Capital gain treatment begins only after vesting.

questions.q: Cy made a timely §83(b) election on restricted stock, reporting $20,000 of ordinary income (he paid nothing). He left the company before vesting and forfeited the shares. What is the tax result of the forfeiture?
choices: No deduction or loss, because he paid nothing for the shares
A $20,000 ordinary deduction
An amended return removing the $20,000
A $20,000 capital loss
questions.exp: On forfeiture after an election under §83 to be taxed at grant, the loss is limited to the amount paid for the stock, less any amount realized, which here is zero. The income reported is not recovered, which is the main risk of the election.

questions.q: Dee was granted 2,000 restricted stock units that settle in shares when they vest in three years. She wants to start her capital gain holding period now. What is correct?
choices: RSUs are taxed at grant at FMV
RSUs are taxed only when the shares are sold
She can make an election under §83 to be taxed at grant within 30 days of grant
RSUs are not property transferred at grant, so the §83 election to be taxed at grant is unavailable; she is taxed on the share value at delivery
questions.exp: An RSU is an unfunded promise to deliver stock, so no property is transferred at grant and the §83 election to be taxed at grant does not apply. The FMV of the shares delivered is ordinary income at settlement.

questions.q: Under a §423 employee stock purchase plan, Eve bought 100 shares at 85% of the lower of the offering-date FMV ($20) or the purchase-date FMV ($24). She sold them for $30 per share more than two years after the offering date and one year after purchase. How much ordinary income does she recognize?
questions.exp: The purchase price was 85% x $20 = $17. In a qualifying disposition, ordinary income is the lesser of the actual gain ($13) or the offering-date discount ($20 - $17 = $3): $3 x 100 = $300, with the remaining $1,000 as long-term capital gain.

questions.q: Using the same ESPP facts (purchase price $17 per share, FMV $24 on the purchase date), Eve instead sells the 100 shares for $30 per share four months after purchase. How much ordinary income does she recognize?
questions.exp: In a disqualifying disposition, ordinary income is the purchase-date spread, ($24 - $17) x 100 = $700, whatever the sale price, and the remaining $600 is short-term capital gain. The $300 trap uses the qualifying-disposition formula.

questions.q: A nonqualified deferred compensation plan fails the §409A requirements. Fred's vested deferred amount under the plan is $100,000 for the year. Ignoring the premium interest, what is the federal income tax consequence?
choices: $100,000 included in income plus a 10% additional tax
$100,000 included in income when eventually paid
$100,000 included in gross income plus a 20% additional tax of $20,000
A $20,000 penalty only, with income still deferred
questions.exp: A §409A failure accelerates inclusion of vested deferred amounts and adds a 20% additional tax plus premium interest. The 10% rate is the early distribution penalty for qualified plans.

questions.q: Apex Corp., a publicly held corporation, pays its CEO, a covered employee, a $1,500,000 salary and a $500,000 bonus tied to performance goals. How much of this compensation is nondeductible under §162(m)?
choices: $0, because the bonus is performance-based
questions.exp: Since 2018, §162(m) has had no performance-based exception: deductible compensation is capped at $1,000,000, so $2,000,000 - $1,000,000 = $1,000,000 is nondeductible. The $500,000 trap treats the bonus as exempt.

questions.q: On a change in control, executive Gil receives payments contingent on the change of $1,500,000. His base amount (average annual compensation for the prior five years) is $400,000. What excise tax does Gil owe under §4999?
questions.exp: Payments of $1,500,000 equal or exceed 3 x $400,000 = $1,200,000, so the excess parachute payment is everything above one times base: $1,100,000, and 20% x $1,100,000 = $220,000. The $60,000 trap uses only the excess over three times base.

questions.q: Gil's base amount is $400,000. The acquirer offers a 'best-net' cutback so that no payment is a parachute payment. What is the most that can be paid as change-in-control payments without triggering §280G?
questions.exp: Payments are parachute payments only if they equal or exceed three times the base amount, so the maximum is $1 less than $1,200,000. At exactly $1,200,000, the excess parachute payment would be $800,000.

questions.q: Oak Corp., a calendar-year accrual taxpayer, maintains an unfunded nonqualified deferred compensation plan. In 2025, an executive earns $200,000 of deferred compensation that will be paid to him in 2030. When may Oak deduct it?
choices: Ratably from 2025 through 2030
2030, when the executive includes it in income
2025, if paid within 2.5 months
2025, when earned
questions.exp: Under §404, employers deduct nonqualified deferred compensation in the year the employee includes it in income, regardless of the employer's accounting method. The 2.5-month rule only distinguishes deferred from current compensation.

questions.q: Hart Corp. sets up a rabbi trust to hold assets for its executives' nonqualified deferred compensation. Which statement is correct?
choices: Executives are not taxed currently because the trust assets remain subject to Hart's general creditors
Executives are taxed currently because the assets are set aside
Hart deducts contributions to the trust when made
Trust earnings are tax-exempt
questions.exp: A rabbi trust avoids constructive receipt and economic benefit because the assets are available to the employer's creditors in insolvency, so deferral is kept. Hart deducts only when executives include the amounts, and Hart is taxed on trust earnings as a grantor trust.

questions.q: A tax-exempt hospital provides its CEO an ineligible deferred compensation plan under §457(f). The benefit vests (no longer subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture) in 2025 but is payable in 2028. When is the CEO taxed?
choices: Never, because the employer is exempt
2028, when paid
When the CEO retires
2025, when the substantial risk of forfeiture lapses
questions.exp: Under §457(f), ineligible plan amounts are included in income when there is no longer a substantial risk of forfeiture, even if paid later. Deferral until payment is the rule for eligible §457 plans.

questions.q: Assume for 2025 an elective deferral limit of $23,500 for §401(k) plans and a special catch-up limit of $11,250 for participants who attain age 60 through 63 during the year. Rosa turns 61 in 2025. What is the maximum she may defer into her 401(k)?
questions.exp: Participants aged 60 through 63 use the higher catch-up: $23,500 + $11,250 = $34,750. The $31,000 trap uses the regular $7,500 catch-up for those 50 and older.

questions.q: Assume for 2025 a §415 annual additions limit of $70,000 and an elective deferral limit of $23,500. Sam, age 45, defers $23,500 to his employer's 401(k). Ignoring the compensation limit, what is the most the employer can contribute for Sam this year?
questions.exp: Employee deferrals count toward the §415 annual additions limit, so employer contributions are limited to $70,000 - $23,500 = $46,500. Catch-up contributions, not relevant at age 45, are outside the limit.

questions.q: Tina, age 52, receives $150,000 of employer-paid group-term life insurance. Assume the Table I cost is $0.23 per $1,000 of coverage per month for her age bracket, and she pays nothing toward it. How much is included in her gross income for the year?
questions.exp: Only coverage above $50,000 is taxable: $100,000 / $1,000 x $0.23 x 12 = $276. Applying the rate to all $150,000 gives the $414 trap.

questions.q: Jade works for a privately held corporation and exercises options for stock that she cannot easily sell. The corporation has a qualifying broad-based plan. Which provision may let her defer the income from exercise for up to five years?
choices: §83 election to be taxed at grant
questions.exp: §83(i) lets eligible employees of private companies elect to defer income on qualified equity grants for up to five years, with specific triggering events. The §83 election to be taxed at grant accelerates income, and §423 applies to ESPPs.

questions.q: Lou exercises 1,000 stock-settled stock appreciation rights with a base price of $10 when the stock is worth $25 per share. What is the tax result?
choices: $15,000 of long-term capital gain
No income until the shares are sold
$25,000 of ordinary income
$15,000 of ordinary income to Lou and a $15,000 deduction for the employer
questions.exp: SARs are taxed at exercise on the value received, ($25 - $10) x 1,000 = $15,000 of ordinary compensation income, and the employer deducts the same amount. No capital gain arises at exercise.

questions.q: An employee exercises nonqualified stock options and recognizes $20,000 of compensation income. What is the employer's deduction?
choices: $0, because options are equity
The book expense under ASC 718
$20,000, in the employer's tax year in which the employee's year of inclusion ends
The grant-date fair value, when granted
questions.exp: Under §83, the employer deducts the amount the employee includes, in the tax year in which or with which the employee's tax year of inclusion ends. ASC 718 book expense creates a book-tax difference but does not set the deduction.

questions.q: An employee makes a qualifying disposition of ISO stock, recognizing a $40,000 long-term capital gain. What deduction does the employer get?
choices: The bargain element at exercise
The grant-date value
questions.exp: No employer deduction is allowed for ISOs unless the employee makes a disqualifying disposition and recognizes ordinary income. This lack of an employer deduction is the ISO trade-off.

questions.q: Rex is the sole shareholder and full-time CEO of an S corporation that earns $300,000 a year. He pays himself no salary and takes $300,000 of distributions to avoid employment taxes. What is the most likely IRS position?
choices: The distributions are reclassified as dividends taxed at 20%
The S election is terminated
Distributions are always respected for S corporations
Part of the distributions is recharacterized as reasonable compensation subject to FICA and withholding
questions.exp: The IRS and the courts recharacterize distributions as wages when a shareholder-employee performs substantial services without reasonable compensation. S corporation distributions are not dividends, and the S election is not terminated for this.

questions.q: Una, single, earns $300,000 of wages from one employer in 2025. What is her Additional Medicare Tax on wages?
questions.exp: The 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to wages above $200,000 for a single filer: 0.9% x $100,000 = $900. The $2,700 trap applies it to all wages.

questions.q: Assume a 2025 Social Security wage base of $176,100. Val earns $250,000 of wages in 2025. What is her employee Social Security (OASDI) tax?
questions.exp: OASDI is 6.2% of wages up to the wage base: 6.2% x $176,100 = $10,918. The $13,469 trap combines 7.65% with the wage base, adding Medicare, which has no cap.

questions.q: An employer reimburses employees' business travel. Under which arrangement are the reimbursements excluded from employees' wages?
choices: Flat monthly allowances paid without receipts
An accountable plan requiring a business connection, substantiation and return of excess amounts
A nonaccountable plan with a written policy
Any reimbursement if the employee itemizes deductions
questions.exp: Accountable plan reimbursements are excluded from wages. Nonaccountable payments are taxable wages, and unreimbursed employee expenses are not deductible as itemized deductions.

questions.q: Wynn was granted ISOs on March 1, Year 1, exercised them on February 1, Year 2, and sold the shares on February 15, Year 3, at a gain. How is the sale classified?
choices: A disqualifying disposition, because the sale was not more than two years after the grant date
A disqualifying disposition, because the shares were held less than 18 months after exercise
A qualifying disposition, because she held the options more than one year before exercising
A qualifying disposition, because she held the shares more than one year after exercise
questions.exp: An ISO disposition qualifies only if the sale is more than two years after grant and more than one year after exercise. The one-year test is met (about 12.5 months), but the sale came only about 23.5 months after grant, so the disposition is disqualifying. Meeting only the one-year test is the trap.

questions.q: Xia receives nonqualified options that are actively traded on an established market. When is she taxed?
choices: Never, if she holds them for one year
At sale of the shares
At grant, on the option's FMV, because it has a readily ascertainable value
At exercise, on the spread
questions.exp: Under §83 and Reg. §1.83-7, an option with a readily ascertainable FMV (such as an actively traded one) is taxed when granted, and later exercise is not a taxable event. Most employee options lack such a value and are taxed at exercise.

questions.q: A 55-year-old executive in the 37% bracket expects to be in a much lower bracket after retiring at 60, and her employer is financially strong. What is the key planning trade-off in electing to defer bonus into an unfunded nonqualified plan?
choices: Deferral lets the employer deduct the bonus now
Deferral may lower her tax rate on the bonus, but she becomes an unsecured general creditor of the employer for the deferred amount
Deferral avoids FICA permanently
Deferral lets her roll the amount into an IRA
questions.exp: Nonqualified deferral can lower the rate on the income, but the amount is at risk in the employer's insolvency, and the employer's deduction is deferred too. FICA generally applies when amounts vest under the special timing rule, and NQDC cannot be rolled into an IRA.

questions.q: A startup founder receives restricted founder shares with a current FMV of $0.01 per share, subject to vesting, and the company is expected to grow rapidly. Why is a §83(b) election typically advisable?
choices: It defers all income until vesting
It triggers minimal ordinary income now, and all later appreciation becomes capital gain with a holding period starting at grant
It avoids the need to pay for the shares
It lets the company take a large deduction later
questions.exp: When value is low and growth is expected, the election makes the small current value ordinary income and turns future appreciation into capital gain, which may also start a §1202 holding period. The risk is low when the income at grant is small.

questions.q: A retail store with a 40% gross profit percentage sells a television to an employee for $500. Its normal price to customers is $1,000. How much of the discount is taxable to the employee?
questions.exp: A §132 qualified employee discount on merchandise is excludable up to the gross profit percentage of the price: 40% x $1,000 = $400. The $500 discount exceeds that by $100, which is taxable.

questions.q: Zeta Corp. pays an executive a $1,500,000 change-in-control bonus. His base amount is $400,000, and the bonus is a parachute payment. Disregarding §162(m), how much may Zeta deduct?
questions.exp: §280G denies the deduction for the excess parachute payment, $1,500,000 - $400,000 = $1,100,000, so Zeta deducts $400,000. The excise tax and the disallowance both apply to amounts above one times base, not three times.

questions.q: Under a plan, a bonus vests on December 31, 2025, and is paid on March 1, 2026. How is it treated under §409A?
choices: It violates §409A because it is paid after vesting
It is exempt from §409A as a short-term deferral, because it is paid by March 15 of the year after the year it vests
It is a §457(f) payment
It is deferred compensation that must comply with §409A
questions.exp: The short-term deferral exception covers amounts paid by the 15th day of the third month after the end of the year in which the right vests. Payment after March 15, 2026 would make the plan subject to §409A.

questions.q: Hope receives a lump-sum distribution from her 401(k) that includes employer stock. The plan's basis in the stock is $50,000, and its FMV at distribution is $300,000. She does not roll it over. How much ordinary income does she recognize at distribution, ignoring any early withdrawal penalty?
questions.exp: Under the net unrealized appreciation rules, only the plan's cost basis ($50,000) is taxed at distribution, and the $250,000 of NUA is taxed as long-term capital gain when the stock is sold. Rolling it into an IRA would forfeit NUA treatment.

questions.q: Ana and Ben form Newco. Ana transfers land with a $40,000 basis and a $100,000 FMV and receives Newco stock worth $90,000 plus $10,000 of cash. Ben transfers $90,000 of cash for stock worth $90,000. After the transfers, Ana and Ben own all of Newco's stock. What are Ana's recognized gain and her basis in the Newco stock?
choices: $0 gain; $30,000 basis
questions.exp: The transferors have 100% control, so §351 applies, and Ana recognizes gain up to the $10,000 of boot (realized gain is $60,000). Her stock basis is $40,000 + $10,000 gain − $10,000 cash = $40,000. Answering $50,000 adds the gain but forgets to subtract the boot received.

questions.q: In the same formation, where Ana transferred land with a $40,000 basis (FMV $100,000) to Newco for stock and $10,000 of cash and recognized $10,000 of gain, what is Newco's basis in the land?
questions.exp: Under §362, a corporation's basis in property received in a §351 exchange is the transferor's basis plus gain recognized by the transferor: $40,000 + $10,000 = $50,000. A $100,000 FMV basis would apply only if the exchange were fully taxable.

questions.q: Cara and Dov each transfer property worth $150,000 to a new corporation for 375 shares each. Eli receives 250 shares, worth $100,000, solely for services. Which statement is correct?
choices: Section 351 applies to all three because together they own 100% of the stock
Section 351 fails because the property transferors own only 75% of the stock, so Cara and Dov recognize gain on their property
Eli is treated as a transferor of property because services create goodwill
Section 351 applies to Cara and Dov, and only Eli has income
questions.exp: Stock issued for services is not issued for property, so Eli is not counted. Cara and Dov hold 750 of 1,000 shares (75%), below the 80% control requirement of §368, so §351 fails and they recognize realized gain. Eli has $100,000 of ordinary income either way.

questions.q: Fay transfers a building (adjusted basis $100,000; FMV $500,000), subject to a $150,000 mortgage, to her wholly owned corporation for additional stock. There is a valid business purpose for the mortgage. What are Fay's recognized gain and her basis in the stock received?
choices: $0 gain; $0 basis
$0 gain; negative $50,000 basis
$50,000 gain; $0 basis
questions.exp: Under §357, liabilities assumed in excess of the basis of the property transferred produce gain of $150,000 − $100,000 = $50,000. Stock basis = $100,000 − $150,000 liability + $50,000 gain = $0. Basis can never be negative, which is why the gain is required.

questions.q: Gus transfers equipment with a $200,000 basis and a $120,000 FMV to his newly formed corporation for all of its stock in a §351 exchange. He transfers no other property, and no election is made. What are the corporation's basis in the equipment and Gus's basis in his stock?
choices: Equipment $120,000; stock $200,000
Equipment $120,000; stock $120,000
Equipment $200,000; stock $120,000
Equipment $200,000; stock $200,000
questions.exp: Under §362, when the total basis of property transferred exceeds its total FMV, the corporation's basis is limited to FMV ($120,000), while the shareholder keeps a $200,000 substituted basis in the stock. A joint election could instead reduce the stock basis to $120,000 and let the corporation keep $200,000, but not both.

questions.q: Hal contributes land (basis $30,000; FMV $100,000), subject to a $40,000 mortgage that the partnership assumes, for a 50% interest in a new partnership. Ivy contributes $60,000 of cash for the other 50%. Partners share liabilities equally. What is Hal's basis in his partnership interest?
choices: $0, with $10,000 of gain
questions.exp: Hal's basis is $30,000 less the $40,000 liability assumed by the partnership, plus his $20,000 share of it: $10,000. His net liability relief of $20,000 does not exceed his basis, so §731 gain does not arise. Ignoring his share of the liability produces negative basis and a false gain.

questions.q: Jay contributes a building (basis $10,000; FMV $120,000), subject to a $50,000 nonrecourse mortgage the partnership assumes, for a 50% interest in a partnership. The other partner contributes $70,000 of cash. Partners share the liability equally. How much gain does Jay recognize?
questions.exp: Jay's net decrease in liabilities is $50,000 − $25,000 (his 50% share) = $25,000, treated as a cash distribution under §752. It exceeds his $10,000 basis by $15,000, which is gain under §731, and his basis becomes $0. Answering $40,000 ignores Jay's retained share of the debt.

questions.q: Kim receives a 20% interest in an existing LLC taxed as a partnership in exchange for her future services. If the LLC were liquidated immediately, she would receive $50,000. Which statement is correct?
choices: Kim recognizes income only when she sells the interest
Kim recognizes no income because services are not property
Kim recognizes $50,000 of ordinary income because she received a capital interest for services
Kim recognizes $50,000 of capital gain
questions.exp: An interest that would share in liquidation proceeds is a capital interest, and receiving one for services is compensation income at FMV under §83 and §721 (which does not cover services). A pure profits interest, worth $0 on liquidation, generally produces no income under Rev. Proc. 93-27.

questions.q: A corporation with 60 shareholders is considering an S election. Which fact would make it ineligible?
choices: Some shares carry voting rights and others do not
One shareholder is a nonresident alien
An estate holds shares
A grantor trust owned by a U.S. citizen holds shares
questions.exp: Under §1361, nonresident aliens, partnerships, and most corporations are ineligible shareholders. Grantor trusts and estates are permitted, and differences only in voting rights do not create a second class of stock.

questions.q: Lark Inc., a calendar-year C corporation in existence for several years, wants to be an S corporation. It files a valid Form 2553, with all shareholders' consents, on April 1, 2026, and no relief for late elections is requested. When is the election effective?
choices: January 1, 2027
April 1, 2026
January 1, 2026
July 1, 2026
questions.exp: An election made within the first 2 months and 15 days of the tax year (by March 15 for a calendar year) can be effective for that year; one made later takes effect the following year under §1362. April 1 is too late for 2026 without late-election relief.

questions.q: Mae forms a single-member LLC to run a consulting business and files no entity classification election. Later, she wants S corporation treatment. Which statement is correct?
choices: The LLC is disregarded by default, and it may elect to be taxed as an association and then elect S status (or file Form 2553, which serves as both)
The LLC is a partnership by default and cannot elect S status
The LLC must convert to a state-law corporation to be an S corporation
The LLC is a C corporation by default because it has limited liability
questions.exp: Under the check-the-box regulations, a single-member domestic LLC is disregarded by default and may elect to be taxed as a corporation; a timely Form 2553 is deemed to include that election. State-law conversion is unnecessary, and a single-member LLC cannot be a partnership.

questions.q: A business earns $200,000 of pretax income and distributes all after-tax earnings as qualified dividends to an individual owner taxed at 20% on dividends. Assume a 21% corporate rate and ignore the net investment income tax. What is the combined effective federal tax rate on the income if the business is a C corporation?
questions.exp: The corporation pays 21%, leaving 79%, and the dividend tax takes 20% of that: 21% + (79% × 20%) = 36.8%. Adding the rates (41%) overstates the burden because the dividend tax applies only to after-tax corporate earnings.

questions.q: Nora's business is profitable, and she plans to reinvest nearly all of its earnings for the next 10 years to fund growth, then sell the company. She is in the 37% bracket. Ignoring §1202, which characteristic of a C corporation is most relevant to her?
choices: C corporation losses flow through to shareholders
C corporations may allocate income disproportionately among shareholders
C corporation earnings that are kept in the business are taxed only at the 21% corporate rate until distributed
C corporations are exempt from the accumulated earnings tax
questions.exp: When earnings are retained rather than distributed, the second layer of tax is deferred, so reinvested profits bear only the 21% corporate rate instead of the 37% individual rate. Retention beyond reasonable business needs can trigger the accumulated earnings tax, and C corporation losses do not flow through.

questions.q: Otto's single-member LLC earns $200,000 a year from an active business. He is considering an S election and paying himself a reasonable salary of $120,000. What is the main employment tax planning point?
choices: Otto can avoid employment taxes by taking no salary
All S corporation income is subject to self-employment tax
The S election makes him ineligible for the QBI deduction
Distributions from the S corporation beyond reasonable salary are not subject to FICA or self-employment tax
questions.exp: An S corporation shareholder-employee pays FICA only on wages; the remaining $80,000 of flow-through income and distributions is not subject to employment tax, whereas all of the LLC's net earnings are subject to SE tax. The IRS can recharacterize distributions as wages if salary is unreasonably low.

questions.q: Pax Corp., a calendar-year C corporation, starts business on July 1 and incurs $53,000 of organizational expenditures. It elects to deduct and amortize them under §248. What is its total deduction for organizational expenditures in its first year?
questions.exp: The immediate deduction is $5,000 reduced by the excess over $50,000: $5,000 − $3,000 = $2,000. The remaining $51,000 is amortized over 180 months starting in the month business begins: $51,000 ÷ 180 × 6 = $1,700. Total = $3,700. Forgetting the phase-down of the $5,000 gives $6,700.

questions.q: Quill LLC incurs $20,000 of start-up expenditures before opening for business on January 2. It elects under §195 to deduct and amortize them. What is its start-up cost deduction for its first full year of business?
questions.exp: Section 195 allows an immediate deduction of up to $5,000 (reduced only when costs exceed $50,000), with the remaining $15,000 amortized over 180 months: $15,000 ÷ 180 × 12 = $1,000, for a total of $6,000. Answering $1,333 amortizes all $20,000 and omits the $5,000 immediate deduction.

questions.q: Ray and Sue will acquire rental real estate financed largely with nonrecourse debt and expect large tax losses in the early years. They want to deduct those losses. Which entity choice best supports this goal?
choices: A C corporation, because losses flow through to shareholders
An S corporation, because losses are not subject to basis limits
An S corporation, because shareholders get basis for entity-level debt
An LLC taxed as a partnership, because members include their share of entity liabilities, including qualified nonrecourse financing, in basis and at-risk amounts
questions.exp: Under §752 and §465, partners include their share of partnership debt (including qualified nonrecourse real estate financing) in basis and at-risk amounts, allowing larger loss deductions. S corporation shareholders get basis only for debt the corporation owes directly to them, and C corporation losses do not flow through.

questions.q: Tern Inc. converted from a C corporation to an S corporation two years ago, when it had a net unrealized built-in gain of $300,000. This year it sells land that had a $120,000 built-in gain at conversion, for a recognized gain of $150,000. Taxable income is not a limiting factor. What is Tern's built-in gains tax, assuming a 21% rate?
questions.exp: Under §1374, the recognized built-in gain is limited to the gain that existed at conversion ($120,000), and the tax is $120,000 × 21% = $25,200, well within the NUBIG limit. The $30,000 of post-conversion appreciation is not subject to the tax, so taxing the full $150,000 ($31,500) is wrong.

questions.q: Una is founding a technology startup that she expects to sell in six to eight years for a large gain. She wants to maximize her after-tax proceeds from the sale. Which entity choice gives her access to the §1202 exclusion?
choices: An S corporation
A C corporation, with stock issued to her at formation
An LLC taxed as a partnership
A sole proprietorship that later incorporates by selling its assets to a corporation
questions.exp: Section 1202 applies only to qualified small business stock issued by a C corporation at original issuance, so the gain on a sale after the required holding period can be largely or fully excluded. S corporation stock and partnership interests never qualify.

questions.q: Vale P.C. is a personal service corporation (a qualified PSC) owned by physicians, with average annual gross receipts well above the threshold that normally requires a C corporation to use the accrual method. Which statement is correct?
choices: Vale must use a fiscal year ending September 30
Vale is taxed at a flat 35% rate because it is a personal service corporation
Vale must use the accrual method because its receipts exceed the threshold
Vale may use the cash method because qualified personal service corporations are exempt from the accrual requirement
questions.exp: Section 448 bars C corporations above the gross receipts test from using the cash method but exempts qualified PSCs. Since 2018, PSCs are taxed at the same flat 21% as other C corporations, and they generally use a calendar year unless a business purpose or §444 election applies.

questions.q: Wes contributes land (basis $40,000; FMV $100,000) and Xia contributes $100,000 of cash to form an equal partnership. Two years later, the partnership sells the land for $120,000. How much of the partnership's $80,000 tax gain is allocated to Wes?
questions.exp: Under §704, the $60,000 built-in gain at contribution is allocated entirely to Wes, the contributing partner, and the $20,000 of post-contribution appreciation is shared equally: $60,000 + $10,000 = $70,000. Splitting the whole $80,000 equally ($40,000) ignores the built-in gain rule.

questions.q: Yan contributes a concentrated position in one publicly traded stock to a newly formed partnership, and other investors contribute different publicly traded stocks, producing diversification for each of them. The partnership would be an investment company if incorporated. What is the result?
choices: Yan recognizes gain on the appreciated stock because the transfer to an investment partnership results in diversification
Yan recognizes gain only if he receives cash
The partnership recognizes the gain
No gain is recognized under §721
questions.exp: Section 721 (and §351 for corporations) does not apply to transfers to an investment company that result in diversification of the transferors' interests, so the built-in gain is recognized. This rule blocks exchange funds from diversifying appreciated positions tax-free.

questions.q: Zed owns 60% of Acorn Corp., whose stock is worth $1,000,000 in total. A new investor will contribute cash for a 30% interest. To bring Zed within the control group under §351 as an accommodation transferor under Rev. Proc. 77-37, what is the minimum value of property Zed should contribute in exchange for additional stock?
questions.exp: Under Rev. Proc. 77-37, property transferred by an existing shareholder is not 'of relatively small value' if it is at least 10% of the FMV of the stock he already owns: 10% × $600,000 = $60,000. Using 10% of the corporation's total value ($100,000) misapplies the guideline.

questions.q: Bo transfers equipment held for three years (a §1231 asset) and Cy transfers inventory to a new corporation in a valid §351 exchange. Both receive only stock. Which statement about the holding periods of their stock is correct?
choices: Bo begins a new holding period, while Cy tacks
Bo tacks the equipment's holding period, while Cy's holding period begins on the transfer date
Both begin new holding periods on the transfer date
Both tack the holding periods of the property transferred
questions.exp: Under §1223, stock received for capital assets or §1231 property takes a tacked holding period, but stock received for ordinary-income property such as inventory does not. The corporation's holding period in the property tacks in both cases.

questions.q: Dee contributes appreciated land to a partnership. Eighteen months later, the partnership distributes cash to her that is not a normal operating distribution. What is the main risk?
choices: The distribution reduces the partnership's basis in the land
The distribution is always tax-free as long as it does not exceed her basis
The distribution is treated as a guaranteed payment
The contribution and distribution may be treated as a disguised sale of the land, with gain recognized at the time of the contribution
questions.exp: Under §707 and its regulations, a contribution and a related distribution within two years are presumed to be a sale of the property, which requires gain recognition as of the contribution date unless the facts clearly show otherwise. Relying only on §731 basis recovery ignores the disguised-sale rules.

questions.q: An S corporation's shareholders want the founder to receive a larger share of distributions than her ownership percentage while sharing taxable income pro rata. Which is the likely result?
choices: Disproportionate distributions under the governing provisions may create a second class of stock and terminate the S election
The corporation must file as a partnership
The excess distributions are treated as wages
The arrangement is permitted if documented in a shareholder agreement
questions.exp: Under Reg. 1.1361-1, S corporation shares must confer identical rights to distribution and liquidation proceeds; governing provisions that provide disproportionate distributions create a second class of stock and can terminate the election. Flexible allocations like this require a partnership.

questions.q: Fin is launching a business expected to lose $150,000 in each of its first two years. Fin has $400,000 of salary from another job and will materially participate in the new business. Which entity choice lets Fin use the early losses soonest?
choices: A C corporation, because it can pay Fin a deductible salary
Any entity, because all business losses flow through to owners
A C corporation, because its NOLs can be carried back two years
An S corporation or LLC, because losses flow through and can offset Fin's other income, subject to basis, at-risk, passive, and excess business loss limits
questions.exp: A pass-through entity passes losses to the owner, and with material participation (and within basis and other limits) they offset other income now. A C corporation keeps losses as NOLs usable only against its own future income, and post-2020 NOLs generally cannot be carried back.

questions.q: Gil owns 100% of a profitable C corporation and takes $1,000,000 of salary, far above what comparable executives earn, leaving the corporation with almost no taxable income. On audit, what is the likely result?
choices: Gil's excess salary is excluded from his income
The corporation is converted to an S corporation
The full salary remains deductible because Gil worked full time
The excess salary is reclassified as a dividend: not deductible by the corporation but still taxable to Gil
questions.exp: Only reasonable compensation is deductible under §162; unreasonable compensation to a shareholder-employee is treated as a constructive dividend, which is nondeductible to the corporation and taxable to the shareholder. This is the mirror image of the S corporation issue, where the IRS pushes for more salary.

questions.q: Hu, a physician in a specified service trade or business, has taxable income well above the top of the §199A phase-in range. He is choosing between operating as an S corporation and as a partnership. Which statement about the QBI deduction is correct?
choices: Organizing as a C corporation allows a 20% QBI deduction at the corporate level
The partnership allows a full 20% QBI deduction because guaranteed payments qualify
The S corporation allows a QBI deduction on distributions but not wages
Neither entity yields a QBI deduction for Hu because his SSTB income is excluded above the phase-in range
questions.exp: Above the phase-in range, SSTB income is not qualified business income under §199A, whatever the pass-through form. Guaranteed payments and S corporation wages are never QBI, and C corporations are not eligible for the deduction.

questions.q: Ike transfers fully depreciated equipment (original cost $80,000, basis $0, FMV $50,000) to his new corporation solely for stock in a valid §351 exchange. Which statement is correct?
choices: The corporation recognizes $50,000 of income
Ike recognizes $50,000 of §1245 ordinary income
Ike recognizes $50,000 of capital gain
No gain or recapture is recognized now, but the recapture potential carries over to the corporation
questions.exp: Section 1245 recapture is overridden by §351 nonrecognition except to the extent gain is recognized because of boot. The corporation takes a $0 carryover basis, and the $50,000 recapture potential follows the equipment into the corporation.

questions.q: Jo owns 100% of Pine Corp., worth $900,000. Kai, an unrelated investor, will transfer appreciated land worth $300,000 to Pine for 25% of the stock after the transfer. Jo transfers nothing. What is the result to Kai?
choices: Kai recognizes no gain because he receives only stock
Kai recognizes gain because he does not have 80% control after the exchange
Kai recognizes gain only if Pine pays boot
Kai recognizes no gain because Jo's ownership counts toward control
questions.exp: Section 351 control is measured by the stock owned by the transferors of property immediately after the exchange; Jo is not a transferor, so Kai alone holds 25%, well short of 80%. Kai's realized gain is fully recognized. Jo could join the control group as an accommodation transferor by contributing enough property.

questions.q: Lyn transfers two assets to a corporation in a §351 exchange: Asset X (basis $20,000; FMV $60,000) and Asset Y (basis $50,000; FMV $40,000). She receives $80,000 of stock and $20,000 of cash. What is her total recognized gain or loss?
choices: $12,000 gain and $10,000 loss
questions.exp: Boot is allocated among the assets by relative FMV: 60% ($12,000) to X and 40% ($8,000) to Y. X's realized gain of $40,000 is recognized to the extent of its $12,000 of boot, and Y's $10,000 loss is not recognized under §351. Netting the gain and loss across assets ($30,000 net realized) is not allowed.

questions.q: A newly formed partnership has three partners: an individual with a calendar year, an individual with a calendar year, and a corporation with a June 30 fiscal year. Each owns one-third of profits and capital. Which tax year must the partnership generally use?
choices: A calendar year, because partners owning a majority interest use a calendar year
A fiscal year ending September 30 under a §444 election only
Any year it chooses on its first return
June 30, because a corporate partner controls the choice
questions.exp: Under §706, a partnership must use the tax year of partners owning more than 50% of profits and capital; the two individuals together own two-thirds and use a calendar year. A §444 election or business-purpose year is an exception, not the default.

questions.q: Mo contributes property with an FMV of $100,000 and a basis of $30,000 to a new partnership for a 40% interest. Under the §704 regulations, what are Mo's opening book capital account and his tax basis in his partnership interest, assuming no liabilities?
choices: Book capital $100,000; tax basis $100,000
Book capital $30,000; tax basis $30,000
Book capital $40,000; tax basis $30,000
Book capital $100,000; tax basis $30,000
questions.exp: Book capital accounts record contributed property at FMV ($100,000), while outside tax basis is the contributor's basis under §722 ($30,000). The $70,000 difference is the built-in gain tracked under the contributed-property rules. Using the tax basis for the book account misstates the partners' economic deal.

questions.q: Ned and three other investors form a corporation in a valid §351 exchange. Ned transfers property with a $50,000 basis and an $80,000 FMV and also agrees to perform services worth $20,000, receiving stock worth $100,000. What does Ned recognize, and what is his basis in the stock?
choices: $20,000 ordinary income; $100,000 basis
$20,000 ordinary income; $70,000 basis
$0 income; $50,000 basis
questions.exp: Stock received for services is compensation income ($20,000) even within §351, but the property portion is tax-free. Basis = $50,000 property basis + $20,000 included in income = $70,000. Treating all the stock as received for property ignores the services.

questions.q: Pam wants to bring in investors with different economic deals: one gets a preferred return, another gets 50% of profits but only 20% of losses. She also wants pass-through taxation. Which entity best fits?
choices: A C corporation with two classes of stock
An S corporation with voting and nonvoting stock
An LLC taxed as a partnership
An S corporation
questions.exp: Partnerships may make special allocations that have substantial economic effect under §704, allowing preferred returns and different sharing of profits and losses. S corporations must allocate per share, per day, and may have only one class of stock; voting differences do not change economic rights.

questions.q: Quinn contributes land with a basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $90,000, held as an investment for six years, to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. What are the partnership's basis and holding period in the land?
choices: $30,000 basis; holding period starts on the contribution date
$90,000 basis; holding period starts on the contribution date
$30,000 basis; holding period includes Quinn's six years
$90,000 basis; holding period includes Quinn's six years
questions.exp: Under §723 the partnership takes Quinn's $30,000 carryover basis, and under §1223 its holding period includes Quinn's holding period. A FMV basis would arise only in a taxable transfer.

questions.q: Rex and Sol own an appreciated operating business and expect to split up in 10 years, with each taking some of the business's real estate. They are choosing between a C corporation and an LLC taxed as a partnership. Which statement about a future in-kind distribution of the appreciated real estate is correct?
choices: A C corporation recognizes gain as if it sold the property, while a partnership distribution of property generally triggers no gain to the partnership or partners
A C corporation's liquidating distribution of appreciated property is tax-free to the corporation under §336
A partnership's distribution of appreciated property always triggers gain to the partnership
Both entities may distribute appreciated property without any entity-level or owner-level gain
questions.exp: Under §311 and §336, a corporation recognizes gain on distributing appreciated property, and the shareholders are also taxed, while under §731 a partnership distribution of property generally produces no gain, with the partners taking a carryover basis. That flexibility on exit is a key reason to choose a partnership for appreciating assets.

topics.topic: Estate and trust income tax planning

questions.q: A simple trust earns $30,000 of taxable interest and realizes a $10,000 long-term capital gain that the governing instrument allocates to corpus. A $2,000 trustee fee is charged entirely to corpus, and the trustee distributes the $30,000 of trust accounting income to the beneficiary. What is the trust's taxable income?
questions.exp: DNI is $30,000 - $2,000 = $28,000 (the corpus gain is excluded), so the distribution deduction is the lesser of $30,000 distributed or $28,000 DNI. Taxable income is $30,000 + $10,000 - $2,000 - $28,000 - $300 exemption = $9,700; deducting the full $30,000 distribution ignores the DNI ceiling.

questions.q: Which set of facts allows a trust to be treated as a simple trust for the current year?
choices: The trust must distribute all income currently and also paid a charitable bequest
The trust has only one beneficiary, regardless of its distribution requirements
The trust may accumulate income but made no distributions during the year
The trust must distribute all income currently, has no charitable purpose and distributed no corpus
questions.exp: A simple trust must be required to distribute all income currently, may not provide for charitable contributions and may not distribute corpus during the year. A trust that distributes corpus or makes a charitable payment is complex for that year, and the number of beneficiaries is irrelevant.

questions.q: Which combination correctly states the personal exemptions allowed under §642 on Form 1041?
choices: Estate $100; simple trust $300; complex trust $600
Estate $600; simple trust $100; complex trust $300
Estate $300; simple trust $600; complex trust $100
Estate $600; simple trust $300; complex trust $100
questions.exp: Section 642 allows $600 for an estate, $300 for a trust required to distribute all income currently and $100 for all other trusts. These amounts are not indexed, and the larger trust exemption goes to the trust that must distribute everything, not the complex trust.

questions.q: A simple trust has $40,000 of taxable interest and $10,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest, and no expenses. It distributes all $50,000 of accounting income to its sole beneficiary. How much must the beneficiary include in gross income?
questions.exp: DNI of $50,000 includes the tax-exempt interest, but the distribution keeps its character, so $10,000 stays tax-exempt to the beneficiary and only $40,000 is taxable. The trust's distribution deduction is also limited to the $40,000 taxable portion.

questions.q: A complex trust has trust accounting income and DNI of $60,000, all taxable interest. The instrument requires $40,000 of income to be paid to Ava each year, and the trustee also makes a discretionary $40,000 distribution of corpus to Ben. How much does Ben include in gross income?
questions.exp: Under the tier system, Ava's required income distribution is a first-tier distribution and absorbs $40,000 of DNI first. Only the remaining $60,000 - $40,000 = $20,000 of DNI is carried out to Ben's second-tier distribution; splitting DNI equally ignores the tier ordering.

questions.q: A trust has $60,000 of trust accounting income and $50,000 of DNI because $10,000 of trustee fees are charged to corpus. The instrument requires all income to be paid equally to Cole and Dana, so each receives $30,000. How much does each include in income?
questions.exp: When first-tier distributions ($60,000) exceed DNI ($50,000), DNI is allocated pro rata: $50,000 x ($30,000 / $60,000) = $25,000 each. Including the full $30,000 would tax more than the trust's DNI, which caps what distributions carry out.

questions.q: A calendar-year complex trust had trust accounting income of $80,000 and DNI of $70,000 for 2025, and it distributed $50,000 during 2025. What is the maximum amount of distributions made in the first 65 days of 2026 that the trustee may elect to treat as made in 2025?
questions.exp: The election is limited to the greater of trust accounting income or DNI for the year, reduced by distributions already made in that year: $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000. Using DNI ($70,000 - $50,000 = $20,000) applies the lesser rather than the greater amount.

questions.q: Which statement about the 65-day election is correct?
choices: It applies automatically to every distribution made within 65 days of year-end
Estates and complex trusts may make it on a timely filed return, including extensions
It is made by filing a separate request with the IRS within 65 days of death
It is available only to simple trusts and must be made by January 31
questions.exp: The election is available to estates and complex trusts for distributions in the first 65 days of the following year and is made on the Form 1041 filed by its due date, including extensions. It is not automatic, and simple trusts already must distribute all income currently.

questions.q: Why is the 65-day rule a valuable income tax planning tool for a complex trust?
choices: It allows the trust to defer paying its own tax until the following year
After year-end the trustee knows actual income and can shift it to beneficiaries in lower brackets
It lets the trust avoid the throwback rules on foreign accumulation distributions only
It converts accumulated capital gains into tax-exempt income for the beneficiaries
questions.exp: Trust brackets are highly compressed, so trustees benefit from distributing income to lower-bracket beneficiaries, and the 65-day window lets them do so after the year's income is known. The rule changes who is taxed on the income; it does not defer tax or change character.

questions.q: A complex trust sells stock for a $25,000 long-term capital gain. The governing instrument and local law allocate capital gains to principal, and the trustee makes no distribution of the proceeds. Who is taxed on the gain?
choices: The remainder beneficiaries, in the year the trust terminates
The income beneficiaries, because DNI always includes capital gains
No one, because the trust receives a stepped-up basis each year
The trust, because gains allocated to corpus and not distributed are excluded from DNI
questions.exp: Capital gains allocated to corpus and not paid, credited or required to be distributed are excluded from DNI, so the trust pays the tax. Gains are included in DNI only when allocated to income, consistently treated as distributed, or distributed in the final year.

questions.q: In a trust's final taxable year, deductions exceed gross income and the trust also has an unused capital loss carryover. What happens to these items?
choices: They are carried back to the trust's three prior years
They pass through to the beneficiaries succeeding to the trust property
They pass to the grantor, who reports them on Form 1040
They are lost because the trust no longer exists
questions.exp: Under §642, unused loss carryovers and excess deductions on termination are allowed to the beneficiaries succeeding to the property. They are not forfeited, and a nongrantor trust's items do not revert to the grantor.

questions.q: A complex trust's DNI of $100,000 consists of $60,000 of qualified dividends and $40,000 of taxable interest. The trust distributes $50,000 to its sole beneficiary and the instrument has no special allocation provisions. How does the beneficiary report the distribution?
choices: $30,000 of qualified dividends and $20,000 of interest
$50,000 of qualified dividends, because dividends are deemed distributed first
$25,000 of qualified dividends and $25,000 of interest
$50,000 of ordinary interest income, because interest is deemed distributed first
questions.exp: Absent a specific allocation in the instrument, a distribution carries out each class of income in proportion to its share of DNI: 60% x $50,000 = $30,000 of dividends and 40% x $50,000 = $20,000 of interest. There is no rule that one class is distributed first.

questions.q: A simple trust has $60,000 of taxable interest, $40,000 of tax-exempt interest and a $10,000 trustee fee charged to corpus. It distributes all $100,000 of accounting income. What is the trust's distribution deduction?
questions.exp: 40% of the fee ($4,000) is allocated to tax-exempt income and is nondeductible, so DNI is $90,000, of which $36,000 is net tax-exempt income. The deduction is limited to DNI less net tax-exempt income: $90,000 - $36,000 = $54,000; $60,000 ignores the expense allocated to taxable income.

questions.q: Maria creates a revocable living trust, retaining the right to amend or revoke it at any time. The trust earns $50,000 of dividends this year. Who reports the dividend income?
choices: No one until Maria's death, when the trust becomes irrevocable
The trust, on Form 1041 at compressed trust rates
The remainder beneficiaries, as the income accrues
Maria, because a revocable trust is a grantor trust
questions.exp: A power to revoke makes the grantor the owner of the trust under §676, so Maria reports the income on her own return. The trust is ignored for income tax purposes during her life; income is not deferred until death.

questions.q: A grantor creates an irrevocable trust for her children and retains, in a nonfiduciary capacity, the power to reacquire trust assets by substituting other property of equal value. What is the main planning result?
choices: The trust is a grantor trust, and its assets are included in her gross estate
The power is ignored for both income and transfer tax purposes
The trust is a nongrantor trust, and its assets are included in her gross estate
The trust is a grantor trust for income tax purposes, but its assets are generally excluded from her gross estate
questions.exp: A nonfiduciary swap power under §675 makes the trust a grantor trust, and the IRS has ruled that such a power alone does not cause estate inclusion. This combination is the basis of the intentionally defective grantor trust; income tax and estate tax 'ownership' rules differ.

questions.q: Leo sells stock with a basis of $200,000 and a fair market value of $1,000,000 to his intentionally defective grantor trust in exchange for a $1,000,000 interest-bearing note. How much gain does Leo recognize on the sale?
choices: $800,000, recognized as note principal is collected
$1,000,000, because the trust takes a carryover basis
$800,000, recognized in the year of sale
$0, because a sale to one's own grantor trust is disregarded
questions.exp: Because Leo is treated as owning the grantor trust's assets, a sale to it is a transaction with himself and no gain is recognized; the interest on the note is likewise disregarded. The installment method is irrelevant because there is no sale for income tax purposes.

questions.q: The grantor of an intentionally defective grantor trust pays $120,000 of income tax on the trust's income from her own funds, and the trust instrument does not require reimbursement. What are the gift tax consequences?
choices: A gift that qualifies automatically for the marital deduction
A $120,000 taxable gift to the trust beneficiaries
A gift only to the extent the payment exceeds the trust's income
No gift, because the grantor is paying her own legal obligation
questions.exp: The grantor is legally liable for tax on grantor trust income, so paying it is not a gift to the beneficiaries. This is why grantor trusts are attractive: the tax payments shrink the grantor's estate while the trust grows untaxed.

questions.q: Which retained interest causes a trust to be treated as a grantor trust under §673?
choices: A right to remove the trustee and appoint an unrelated, independent successor
A reversionary interest in corpus worth more than 5% of the trust's value at creation
A right to receive trust income only after the death of an adverse party who must consent
A power held by an independent trustee to sprinkle income among the children
questions.exp: Section 673 treats the grantor as owner of any portion in which he has a reversionary interest exceeding 5% of that portion's value at inception. Powers held by independent trustees and the power to appoint an independent successor trustee do not trigger grantor trust status.

questions.q: An irrevocable trust's income may, without the consent of an adverse party, be used to pay premiums on insurance policies on the grantor's life. What are the income tax consequences?
choices: The trust is taxed on the income at compressed rates
The beneficiaries are taxed whether or not income is distributed
The insurance company is treated as owner of the trust
The grantor is taxed on the trust income under §677
questions.exp: Section 677 treats the grantor as owner of any portion whose income may be applied to premiums on insurance on the grantor's life without an adverse party's consent. Taxing the beneficiaries on undistributed income has no basis here.

questions.q: A trust created by her father gives Nina, a beneficiary, the unrestricted power, exercisable solely by herself, to withdraw all trust income each year. Nina never exercises it. Who is taxed on the trust income?
choices: The trust and Nina equally
Her father, as grantor of the trust
Nina, who is treated as the owner under §678
The trust, because Nina did not withdraw the income
questions.exp: Section 678 treats a person other than the grantor as owner of any portion over which she holds a power exercisable solely by herself to vest income or corpus in herself. Not exercising the power does not change the result, and the father is not the owner unless §§671-677 apply to him.

questions.q: After a decedent's death, the executor and the trustee of the decedent's qualified revocable trust make a §645 election. What is its principal effect?
choices: The trust's assets are excluded from the decedent's gross estate
The trust becomes a grantor trust of the surviving spouse
The trust's income is taxed to the decedent's final Form 1040
The trust is treated and taxed as part of the estate, which may adopt a fiscal year
questions.exp: A §645 election treats the qualified revocable trust as part of the estate, giving it estate benefits such as a fiscal year and the estate's estimated tax relief. It has no effect on estate tax inclusion, and the decedent's final Form 1040 covers only the period before death.

questions.q: Which statement about estimated income tax payments by estates and trusts is correct?
choices: An estate is not required to pay estimated tax for its tax years ending within two years after the decedent's death
Trusts are exempt from estimated tax for the first two years after creation
Neither estates nor trusts are ever required to pay estimated tax
Estates must pay estimated tax beginning with the first fiscal year after death
questions.exp: Section 6654(l) generally requires estates and trusts to pay estimated tax but exempts an estate (and a trust treated as part of it) for tax years ending within two years of death. The two-year relief is for estates, not newly created trusts.

questions.q: A complex trust with DNI of $60,000 distributes stock to a beneficiary. The trust's basis is $20,000 and fair market value is $50,000, and the trustee makes no §643(e) election. What are the beneficiary's basis and the amount of the distribution taken into account?
choices: Basis $20,000; distribution counted at $50,000
Basis $50,000; distribution counted at $50,000
Basis $50,000; distribution counted at $20,000
Basis $20,000; distribution counted at $20,000
questions.exp: Without the election, the beneficiary takes the trust's $20,000 basis and the distribution is counted at the lesser of basis or fair market value, $20,000. Counting it at $50,000 would apply only if the trust elected to recognize the $30,000 gain.

questions.q: Using the same stock (basis $20,000, value $50,000), the trustee instead makes a §643(e) election for the distribution. What is the result?
choices: The beneficiary recognizes the $30,000 gain when the stock is received
The trust recognizes $30,000 of gain, and the beneficiary's basis is $50,000
The trust recognizes no gain, but the beneficiary's basis is stepped up to $50,000
The election applies only to that one asset and only to the extent of DNI
questions.exp: Under the election, the trust recognizes gain as if it sold the property ($50,000 - $20,000 = $30,000), the distribution is counted at $50,000 and the beneficiary's basis is $50,000. The election applies to all in-kind distributions the trust makes that year, not just one asset.

questions.q: A will leaves Sam a pecuniary bequest of $100,000. The executor satisfies it by distributing land with an estate basis of $80,000 (its value at death) and a current fair market value of $100,000. What are the tax consequences?
choices: The estate recognizes $20,000 of gain, and Sam's basis is $100,000
The estate recognizes $20,000 of gain, and Sam's basis is $80,000
No gain is recognized, and Sam takes an $80,000 basis
Sam recognizes $20,000 of gain, and his basis is $100,000
questions.exp: Satisfying a fixed-dollar bequest with appreciated property is treated as a sale by the estate, so it recognizes $100,000 - $80,000 = $20,000 of gain and Sam takes a $100,000 basis. A distribution of specifically bequeathed property, by contrast, triggers no gain.

questions.q: An estate with DNI of $40,000 distributes a painting that the will specifically bequeathed to the decedent's niece. The distribution is made in a single installment. What are the income tax effects?
choices: The estate deducts the painting's value, up to $40,000, and the niece includes it
The estate gets no distribution deduction, and the niece has no income from the distribution
The niece includes $40,000 in income, and the estate deducts $40,000
The estate recognizes gain equal to the painting's appreciation since death
questions.exp: Under §663, a gift or bequest of specific property paid in no more than three installments is excluded from the distribution rules, so it carries out no DNI. No gain arises because the estate is delivering the specific property, not satisfying a dollar amount.

questions.q: A trustee is deciding whether to accumulate or distribute $50,000 of interest and dividend income. The trust's beneficiaries are all in low tax brackets. Which consideration most strongly favors distributing the income?
choices: Trust brackets reach the top rate at a far lower income level, and undistributed investment income may also bear the 3.8% NIIT
A trust cannot deduct any expenses unless it distributes all of its income
Accumulated income is always taxed again when distributed in later years
Distributions reduce DNI to zero for all future years
questions.exp: The compressed trust brackets and the low NIIT threshold for trusts mean accumulated investment income is usually taxed at higher rates than in low-bracket beneficiaries' hands. Domestic trusts are not subject to a second tax on accumulated income when it is later distributed.

questions.q: Which statement about the charitable deduction of a complex trust under §642 is correct?
choices: It is allowed without percentage limit for gross income paid for charitable purposes under the governing instrument
It is allowed only for amounts paid to public charities, not private foundations
It is limited to 60% of the trust's adjusted gross income
It is available to simple trusts for amounts paid out of corpus
questions.exp: Section 642 allows a trust an unlimited deduction for amounts of gross income paid for charitable purposes pursuant to the governing instrument. The individual AGI limits do not apply, and a trust making charitable payments cannot be a simple trust.

questions.q: At his death, Ray was owed a $30,000 final bonus by his employer, which the employer pays to his estate. Estate tax was paid on the estate. How is the bonus treated?
choices: It is excluded from income because the estate's basis was stepped up to $30,000
It is income in respect of a decedent, taxable to the estate, with a §691 deduction for related estate tax
It is taxable to the estate, with no deduction available for estate tax
It is taxable only on Ray's final Form 1040
questions.exp: Amounts Ray earned but had not received are IRD, which gets no basis step-up and is taxed to the recipient when collected. The recipient may deduct the federal estate tax attributable to the IRD under §691, so the item is not taxed on the final return as a cash-basis taxpayer.

questions.q: A calendar-year complex trust has gross income of $5,000. When is its Form 1041 due, and what extension is available?
choices: April 15, with an automatic 5 1/2-month extension by filing Form 7004
No return is required because gross income is below $10,000
April 15, with an automatic 6-month extension by filing Form 4868
March 15, with an automatic 6-month extension
questions.exp: Form 1041 for a calendar-year trust is due April 15, and Form 7004 provides an automatic 5 1/2-month extension (to September 30). A return is required because gross income is at least $600; Form 4868 is the individual extension form.

questions.q: This year Ali has a $50,000 net §1231 gain. In the prior five years he had $30,000 of net §1231 losses, none of which has been recaptured. How is this year's gain characterized?
choices: $20,000 ordinary income and $30,000 long-term capital gain
$50,000 ordinary income
$50,000 long-term capital gain
$30,000 ordinary income and $20,000 long-term capital gain
questions.exp: Under the §1231 five-year lookback, net §1231 gain is ordinary income to the extent of nonrecaptured net §1231 losses from the prior five years ($30,000), and the remaining $20,000 is long-term capital gain. Treating all $50,000 as capital gain ignores the lookback.

questions.q: Bea owns two business assets held for several years: Asset G, with a $100,000 built-in §1231 gain (no depreciation recapture), and Asset L, with a $100,000 built-in §1231 loss. She has no other §1231 transactions in any year and will sell both over the next two years. Which plan gives the most favorable character?
choices: Sell Asset L in Year 1 and Asset G in Year 2
The order makes no difference because the lookback rule equalizes the results
Sell both in the same year
