questions.q: A partnership makes payments to a retiring partner. Some qualify as guaranteed payments under §736(a) and the rest are §736(b) payments for her interest in partnership property. How do the payments affect the remaining partners?
choices: Both types are deductible by the partnership
The guaranteed payments are deductible by the partnership, reducing the remaining partners' income, while the property payments are not
Neither type affects the remaining partners' taxable income
Only the property payments are deductible by the partnership
questions.exp: Guaranteed payments to a retiring partner are deductible by the partnership, so the remaining partners' distributive shares go down. Payments for partnership property are treated as distributions and give no deduction, which is why partners often negotiate over how the payments are classified.

questions.q: A retiring partner with an outside basis of $90,000 will receive $150,000 for her interest in partnership property in three equal annual payments. Absent an election, how is the gain on these distributions recognized?
choices: Basis is recovered first, so no gain is recognized until the third payment, when $60,000 is recognized
One-third of the gain, $20,000, is recognized with each payment
None of the gain is recognized because the payments are deferred
All $60,000 of gain is recognized in the year of retirement
questions.exp: For fixed liquidating payments for partnership property made over several years, the partner recovers her basis first and recognizes gain only after the payments exceed it: $50,000 after year 1, $100,000 after year 2, and $60,000 of gain in year 3. A ratable approach requires an election.

questions.q: In March, Ray buys a 60% interest in a partnership from an existing partner. The partnership's business continues unchanged. Does the partnership terminate for tax purposes?
choices: No, because a partnership terminates only if no part of its business continues to be carried on by any partners
Yes, because 50% or more of the interests changed hands within 12 months
Yes, but only if the partnership has a §754 election
No, unless the buyer was not already a partner
questions.exp: Since technical terminations were repealed for tax years after 2017, a partnership terminates only when no part of its business, financial operation or venture continues by any of its partners in a partnership. The 50%-in-12-months technical termination is no longer law.

questions.q: Why can a distribution that changes a partner's share of the partnership's hot assets cause the partner or the partnership to recognize ordinary income, even though distributions are normally tax-free?
choices: Because a disproportionate distribution under §751 is treated as an exchange of hot assets for other property
Because distributions of inventory are always taxable at FMV
Because the partnership must make a §754 election when hot assets are distributed
Because hot assets cannot be distributed without the IRS's consent
questions.exp: Section 751 treats a distribution that shifts a partner's share of unrealized receivables or substantially appreciated inventory relative to other property as a partial sale or exchange, preventing ordinary income from being converted to capital gain. A distribution proportionate in both classes stays tax-free.

questions.q: Sia's outside basis is $25,000. In a current distribution she receives land with a basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $50,000, subject to a $20,000 mortgage that she assumes. Before the distribution her share of that mortgage, the partnership's only liability, was 50%. What is her basis in the land?
questions.exp: Sia's liability increase ($20,000 assumed) and decrease ($10,000 share removed) are netted, a $10,000 net increase that raises her outside basis to $35,000. The land then takes its $30,000 carryover basis, leaving $5,000 of outside basis; ignoring the netting limits the land to $25,000.

questions.q: Tom is leaving a partnership. His outside basis is only $15,000, and the partnership liquidates his entire interest by giving him a single item: inventory that it carries at a $20,000 basis. What are the tax consequences to Tom?
choices: $5,000 of gain; inventory basis $20,000
No gain or loss; inventory basis $20,000
No gain or loss; inventory basis $15,000
$5,000 of ordinary income; inventory basis $20,000
questions.exp: A partner never recognizes gain on distributed property other than money, and the inventory's basis is reduced to his $15,000 outside basis. The lower basis preserves the ordinary income he will recognize when he sells it.

questions.q: Uma's outside basis is $40,000. She receives a $10,000 cash distribution that does not end her interest in the partnership. What are the results?
choices: $30,000 capital loss; outside basis $0
No gain or loss; outside basis $40,000
No gain or loss; outside basis $30,000
$10,000 capital gain; outside basis $40,000
questions.exp: A partner cannot recognize a loss on a current distribution; the cash simply reduces outside basis to $30,000. A loss may be recognized only in a liquidating distribution of money, unrealized receivables and inventory.

questions.q: Val's outside basis at the start of the year is $10,000. During the year she draws $30,000 of cash as advances against her share of profits, and her distributive share of partnership income for the year is $25,000. What are her gain and ending outside basis?
choices: $20,000 gain; ending basis $25,000
No gain; ending basis $5,000
$5,000 gain; ending basis $0
No gain; ending basis $35,000
questions.exp: Draws against a partner's distributive share are treated as current distributions made on the last day of the year, after basis is increased for the year's income to $35,000. The $30,000 is therefore tax-free and leaves $5,000; testing the draws against the opening $10,000 produces the wrong gain.

questions.q: Which statement about the inventory that §751 treats as a hot asset is correct?
choices: Inventory is a hot asset only if it is worth more than 200% of its basis
All inventory is a hot asset on a sale of an interest, but for disproportionate distributions only substantially appreciated inventory counts
Only substantially appreciated inventory is a hot asset on a sale of an interest
Inventory is never a hot asset if the partnership uses the cash method
questions.exp: Since 1997, all inventory items are hot assets when a partner sells an interest, while the disproportionate distribution rules apply only to inventory whose FMV exceeds 120% of its basis. The cash method affects unrealized receivables, not whether inventory counts.

questions.q: A partner dies, and the partnership makes ongoing payments to her estate that are classified under §736(a). How are those payments treated?
choices: As gifts from the surviving partners
As income in respect of a decedent, ordinary income to the estate with no basis step-up
As capital gain, because they relate to the partner's interest
As tax-free distributions, because the estate's basis was stepped up at death
questions.exp: Payments to a deceased partner's successor that are income payments under §736 are income in respect of a decedent under §753, so the estate reports them as ordinary income and the stepped-up basis does not shelter them. Payments for partnership property are recovered against the stepped-up outside basis.

questions.q: Wes retires from a manufacturing partnership in which capital is a material income-producing factor. Part of his liquidation payment is attributable to his share of unrealized receivables. How is that portion treated?
choices: As capital gain, because the payment is for partnership property
As a guaranteed payment deductible by the partnership
As a tax-free return of capital
As a payment for property that is subject to the hot-asset rules, so it produces ordinary income to Wes
questions.exp: Because capital is a material income-producing factor, the payment for receivables is a payment for partnership property, but the disproportionate distribution rules of §751 still make it ordinary income to Wes. It is not a guaranteed payment, so the partnership gets no deduction.

questions.q: Xia's outside basis of $70,000 includes her $30,000 share of partnership liabilities. In complete liquidation she receives $50,000 of cash and is relieved of her entire share of the liabilities. What does she recognize?
choices: No gain or loss
$10,000 capital gain
$20,000 capital loss
$40,000 capital gain
questions.exp: Relief from her $30,000 share of liabilities is a deemed distribution of money, so total money is $50,000 + $30,000 = $80,000 against a $70,000 basis, giving $10,000 of capital gain. Ignoring the liability relief would produce a $20,000 loss.

questions.q: A partnership distributes land with a tax basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $90,000 to Yan in a current distribution. How does the distribution affect Yan's capital account and her outside basis?
choices: Both are reduced by $30,000
Both are reduced by $90,000
The capital account is reduced by $90,000 after the land is booked up, and outside basis is reduced by $30,000
The capital account is reduced by $30,000, and outside basis is reduced by $90,000
questions.exp: Book capital accounts are reduced by the FMV of distributed property after the partnership books the unrealized gain to all partners, while outside basis is reduced by the land's carryover basis of $30,000. Treating the two the same mixes book and tax rules.

questions.q: Ann contributes land with a basis of $40,000 and an FMV of $100,000 to the AB partnership, and Bo contributes $100,000 of cash. They share profits equally and use the traditional §704(c) method. Two years later the partnership sells the land for $120,000. How is the $80,000 tax gain allocated?
questions.exp: The $60,000 built-in gain at contribution goes to Ann, and the $20,000 of post-contribution (book) gain is shared equally, so Ann has $60,000 + $10,000 = $70,000 and Bo $10,000. Splitting the whole gain equally ignores the §704 contributed-property rules.

questions.q: Cy contributes equipment with an FMV of $100,000 and a tax basis of $40,000 (five years of recovery left, straight-line) to a 50/50 partnership, and Di contributes $100,000 of cash. Annual book depreciation is $20,000 and tax depreciation is $8,000. Under the traditional §704(c) method, how much tax depreciation is allocated to Di each year?
questions.exp: Di should get tax depreciation equal to her $10,000 share of book depreciation, but the ceiling rule limits allocations to the $8,000 of actual tax depreciation, so all $8,000 goes to her and Cy gets none. The $2,000 shortfall is the ceiling-rule distortion that the curative and remedial methods fix.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the remedial method for contributed property with a ceiling-rule limitation?
choices: The partnership reallocates actual tax gain from other partnership property to the noncontributing partner
The contributing partner recognizes the entire built-in gain in the year of contribution
The partnership revalues the property to its tax basis so that book and tax depreciation match
The partnership creates offsetting notional tax items: a remedial deduction for the noncontributing partner and equal remedial income for the contributing partner
questions.exp: The remedial method eliminates ceiling-rule distortions by creating tax items that do not otherwise exist, with remedial deductions to the noncontributing partner offset by remedial income of the same character to the contributor. Reallocating other actual tax items describes the curative method.

questions.q: Eve contributes land with a basis of $40,000 and an FMV of $100,000 to a 50/50 partnership with Fox, who contributes $100,000 of cash. The partnership uses the traditional method and later sells the land for $90,000. How is the $50,000 tax gain allocated?
choices: Eve $25,000 gain; Fox $25,000 gain
Eve $55,000 gain; Fox $5,000 loss
Eve $60,000 gain; Fox $10,000 loss
Eve $50,000 gain; Fox $0
questions.exp: There is a $10,000 book loss (split $5,000 each) but a $50,000 tax gain, and under the ceiling rule the partnership cannot allocate more tax gain or loss than actually exists. All $50,000 of tax gain goes to Eve and Fox gets no tax loss; the $55,000 / $5,000 split would require the remedial method.

questions.q: Gus contributes stock with a basis of $100,000 and an FMV of $60,000 to a partnership. Later Gus sells his entire partnership interest to Hope, and the partnership then sells the stock for $60,000. How much of the partnership's $40,000 tax loss can be allocated to Hope?
questions.exp: Under §704 a built-in loss on contributed property can be taken into account only by the contributing partner; for other partners, including a buyer of his interest, the property's basis is treated as its $60,000 FMV at contribution. Hope has no loss, because Gus's built-in loss is personal to him.

questions.q: In 2023 Ike contributed land with a basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $80,000 to a partnership. In 2026, when the land is worth $90,000, the partnership distributes it to another partner, Jo. How much gain does Ike recognize?
questions.exp: Distributing contributed property to another partner within 7 years causes the contributor to recognize the gain he would have been allocated had the property been sold at FMV, which is his $50,000 precontribution gain ($80,000 − $30,000). The later $10,000 of appreciation is not precontribution gain, so $60,000 is wrong.

questions.q: For a partnership allocation to have economic effect under the basic test of the §704(b) regulations, which requirements must the partnership agreement meet?
choices: Capital accounts must be kept on the tax basis, and all partners must sign each year's allocations
Liquidating distributions must follow profit percentages, and all debt must be nonrecourse
Capital accounts must be maintained under the regulations, liquidating distributions must follow positive capital accounts, and partners with deficits must restore them
Allocations must follow ownership percentages, and capital accounts must be kept on the tax basis
questions.exp: The basic economic effect test requires proper capital account maintenance, liquidation in accordance with positive capital account balances, and an unconditional deficit restoration obligation. Allocations need not follow ownership percentages; that is the point of a special allocation.

questions.q: Kay and Lu each contribute $50,000 to a partnership that buys equipment for $100,000. The agreement allocates all depreciation to Kay, maintains capital accounts properly, liquidates per positive capital accounts, and contains a qualified income offset, but neither partner has a deficit restoration obligation. Depreciation is $30,000 a year and there are no liabilities or other items. How much of year 2 depreciation can be allocated to Kay?
questions.exp: After year 1 Kay's capital account is $50,000 − $30,000 = $20,000. Under the alternate economic effect test an allocation may not create a deficit for a partner with no restoration obligation, so only $20,000 goes to Kay and the other $10,000 is allocated to Lu.

questions.q: A partnership expects $100,000 of tax-exempt interest and $100,000 of taxable dividends each year. Partner Mo is in a high tax bracket and Partner Ned has expiring losses. The agreement allocates all tax-exempt interest to Mo and an equal amount of dividends to Ned, and their capital accounts would be the same as under a 50/50 split. Why will the allocation fail?
choices: It lacks economic effect, because capital accounts are not maintained
It violates the ceiling rule for contributed property
It is a transitory allocation, because it reverses within 5 years
It is not substantial, because it shifts tax consequences within the year without changing the partners' economic results
questions.exp: An allocation is a shifting allocation, and not substantial, when partners' capital accounts end up about the same as without it while their total tax liability goes down. A transitory allocation involves offsetting allocations in different years, not the same year.

questions.q: A partnership agreement allocates $50,000 of income to Partner Ola in year 1 and an offsetting $50,000 of deductions to her in year 2, so her capital account is unchanged by the end of year 2. Ola has an expiring NOL in year 1. When is the allocation likely to fail the substantiality test?
choices: Only when the partners are related to each other
When there was a strong likelihood at the time the allocation became part of the agreement that the offsetting allocation would occur within 5 years
Never, because Ola's capital account reflects both allocations
Only when the offsetting allocation occurs in the same tax year
questions.exp: A transitory allocation is not substantial if, when it is agreed to, there is a strong likelihood that offsetting allocations within 5 years will leave capital accounts about where they would have been while reducing total taxes. Same-year offsets are tested as shifting allocations instead.

questions.q: Why must deductions attributable to partnership nonrecourse liabilities be allocated under special rules rather than the general economic effect test?
choices: Because nonrecourse liabilities do not increase partners' outside basis
Because nonrecourse deductions are not deductible until the debt is repaid
Because the lender, not any partner, bears the economic risk of loss, so the allocations cannot have economic effect
Because nonrecourse deductions must always be allocated equally among the partners
questions.exp: Nonrecourse deductions cannot have economic effect because no partner bears the economic burden; they are deemed to follow the partners' interests if the agreement meets the safe harbor, including a minimum gain chargeback. Nonrecourse liabilities do increase partners' outside basis.

questions.q: The ABC partnership, which has a §754 election in effect and no liabilities, holds cash of $30,000, inventory with a basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $60,000, and land with a basis of $60,000 and an FMV of $90,000. Cal buys Al's one-third interest for $60,000. What is Cal's §743(b) adjustment?
questions.exp: The adjustment is Cal's $60,000 outside basis minus his one-third share of the $120,000 inside basis ($40,000), or $20,000. Under §755 it is allocated $10,000 to the inventory and $10,000 to the land, one-third of each asset's appreciation.

questions.q: Following Cal's purchase of a one-third interest, he has a $10,000 positive basis adjustment allocated to partnership inventory with a basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $60,000. The partnership sells the inventory for $60,000. How much ordinary income does Cal report from the sale?
questions.exp: The partnership's $30,000 gain gives Cal a $10,000 distributive share, which his $10,000 inventory basis adjustment offsets, so he reports $0. Without a §754 election he would have reported $10,000 of ordinary income on appreciation he had already paid for.

questions.q: A partnership with a §754 election has $60,000 of liabilities shared by profit percentages. Dee buys a 25% interest for $50,000 of cash. The partnership's total adjusted basis in its assets is $200,000. What is Dee's §743(b) adjustment?
questions.exp: Dee's outside basis is $50,000 cash plus her $15,000 share of liabilities, or $65,000. Her share of inside basis is 25% × $200,000 = $50,000, so the adjustment is $65,000 − $50,000 = $15,000. Leaving out the liability share wrongly gives $0.

questions.q: A partner dies holding a one-third partnership interest worth $300,000 whose share of inside basis is $120,000. The partnership has no §754 election and later sells its appreciated assets. What is the effect on the heir?
choices: The partnership's inside basis is automatically stepped up by $180,000
The heir's outside basis is $300,000, but the heir is still allocated a share of gain on the sale, creating a mismatch that may reverse only as a loss later
The heir's outside basis stays at $120,000 because there was no election
The heir recognizes no gain on the sale because the death stepped up the inside basis
questions.exp: Section 1014 steps up the heir's outside basis to FMV, but inside basis changes only with a §754 election (or a mandatory adjustment), so the heir is taxed on gain already reflected in the step-up. That excess outside basis is recovered only on a later sale or liquidation of the interest.

questions.q: A partnership without a §754 election holds property with an adjusted basis of $2 million and an FMV of $1.6 million. A partner sells his 25% interest. Which statement is correct?
choices: The buyer may elect a downward adjustment, but it is optional
The partnership must make a §754 election before the sale is valid
A downward §743 adjustment is mandatory because the partnership has a substantial built-in loss
No adjustment is made because no §754 election is in effect
questions.exp: A §743 basis adjustment is mandatory, even without a §754 election, when the partnership has a substantial built-in loss, meaning its adjusted basis exceeds FMV by more than $250,000. Here the $400,000 excess requires the buyer's downward adjustment, preventing a duplicated loss.

questions.q: The ABC partnership, which has a §754 election and no liabilities, holds $60,000 of cash and land with a basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $120,000. Each partner has a one-third interest and an outside basis of $30,000. The partnership distributes $60,000 of cash to Abe in complete liquidation. What is the §734(b) adjustment?
choices: $30,000 increase to the land
No adjustment, because Abe received only cash
$60,000 increase to the land
$30,000 decrease to the land
questions.exp: Abe recognizes $60,000 − $30,000 = $30,000 of capital gain, and the partnership increases the basis of its remaining capital gain property, the land, by the same $30,000. That keeps the gain from being taxed again to the remaining partners when the land is sold.

questions.q: A partnership with a §754 election distributes land with an inside basis of $50,000 to Bea in complete liquidation of her interest. Bea's outside basis is $30,000, so she takes a $30,000 basis in the land. What adjustment does the partnership make to its remaining property?
choices: A $20,000 increase
A $20,000 decrease
A $50,000 increase
No adjustment, because Bea recognized no gain
questions.exp: When a distributee's basis in distributed property is less than the partnership's basis in it, the partnership increases the basis of its remaining property by the difference, here $50,000 − $30,000 = $20,000. That preserves the $20,000 of basis Bea lost.

questions.q: Cruz, whose outside basis is $80,000, retires from a partnership that has a §754 election in effect. In complete liquidation of his interest he receives only a parcel of land that the partnership holds with a $50,000 basis, and he takes an $80,000 basis in it. What must the partnership do to the basis of its remaining property?
choices: A $30,000 decrease
A $80,000 decrease
A $30,000 increase
No adjustment, because the land's basis increased
questions.exp: When the distributee's basis in distributed property exceeds the partnership's basis, the partnership must reduce the basis of its remaining property by the difference, $80,000 − $50,000 = $30,000. Without the reduction the same $30,000 of basis would be used twice.

questions.q: Which statement about making and revoking a §754 election is correct?
choices: The transferee partner makes the election on his own return for the year of purchase
It may be revoked by the partnership at any time without IRS consent
It applies only to the transfer described in the election and must be renewed for each later transfer
It is made by a statement with the partnership's timely filed return and applies to all later transfers and distributions until revoked with IRS consent
questions.exp: The partnership makes the §754 election with its timely filed return (including extensions) for the year of the transfer or distribution, and it applies to all later transfers and distributions. It can be revoked only with IRS approval, which is why partnerships weigh it carefully.

questions.q: Dot buys a one-fourth partnership interest, and a §743(b) increase of $40,000 is allocated to the partnership's depreciable equipment. Who benefits from the extra depreciation on the $40,000?
choices: All partners in proportion to their capital accounts
All partners equally, because the adjustment changes the partnership's common basis
The partner who sold the interest to Dot
Dot alone, because the adjustment is personal to the transferee
questions.exp: A §743 adjustment affects only the transferee partner's basis in partnership property, not the partnership's common basis, so only Dot deducts the extra depreciation. A §734 distribution adjustment, by contrast, changes common basis and benefits all remaining partners.

questions.q: The assets of a partnership with no §754 election have declined substantially in value, though not by enough to trigger a mandatory adjustment. A partner plans to sell his interest. Why might the partnership choose not to make a §754 election?
choices: Because the election would give the buyer a basis step-up the IRS would challenge
Because the election would cause the selling partner to recognize ordinary income
Because the election cannot be made in a year in which a partner sells an interest
Because the election would require a downward adjustment for the buyer and would apply to all later transfers and distributions
questions.exp: A §754 election requires both positive and negative adjustments, so with depreciated assets the buyer's inside basis would be reduced, and the election stays in effect for all later transfers and distributions. The election does not change the seller's gain or loss.

questions.q: Fay joins an existing partnership on July 1 of a calendar year by contributing cash. The partnership had a large loss from January through June. Which allocation is permitted?
choices: Fay may be allocated the January-to-June loss because her contribution funded it
Fay may be allocated losses only for the part of the year after she joined, using an interim closing or proration
Fay may be allocated an equal share of the full-year loss if the partners agree
Fay may be allocated no losses until the following year
questions.exp: Under the varying-interest rules of §706, partnership items must reflect each partner's interest during the year, so retroactive allocations of losses incurred before a partner joins are not allowed. The partnership uses an interim closing of the books or a proration method.

questions.q: A partnership revalues its property when Gil is admitted as a new partner for cash. The property's FMV exceeds its tax basis. How must the partnership later allocate tax items from that property?
choices: Equally among all partners, including Gil, with no special allocations
Under reverse §704 principles, so the existing partners bear the tax on the pre-admission appreciation
Entirely to Gil, because he paid FMV for his interest
Under the §743 rules, with a basis adjustment for Gil
questions.exp: A revaluation creates book-tax differences treated like contributed property (reverse §704 allocations), so the unrealized appreciation at admission is taxed to the existing partners. A §743 adjustment does not apply because Gil acquired his interest by contribution, not by transfer.

questions.q: A partnership agreement allocates all depreciation on a building to Hal and provides that any later gain on the building is first charged back to Hal up to the depreciation he received. Capital accounts are maintained properly and Hal has a deficit restoration obligation. Why is this allocation generally respected?
choices: Because Hal bears no economic risk of the depreciation
Because depreciation allocations are never tested for substantiality
Because the regulations presume a property's value equals its book basis, so the chargeback is not treated as a certain offset
Because a gain chargeback cancels the economic effect of the depreciation
questions.exp: The substantiality rules presume that the value of property equals its adjusted book basis, so a later gain chargeback is not considered likely, and the depreciation allocation is not treated as transitory. Hal bears the economic burden through his capital account and deficit restoration obligation.

questions.q: Ivo buys a partnership interest, creating a total §743(b) adjustment of $10,000. His share of the net appreciation in the partnership's ordinary income property is $15,000, and his share of the net depreciation in its capital gain property is $5,000. How is the adjustment allocated under §755?
choices: $10,000 to ordinary income property; $0 to capital gain property
$10,000 to capital gain property; $0 to ordinary income property
$5,000 to each class
$15,000 increase to ordinary income property; $5,000 decrease to capital gain property
questions.exp: Section 755 first allocates the adjustment between classes based on the gain or loss the transferee would be allocated in a hypothetical sale, so one class can be increased while the other is decreased. The net of +$15,000 and −$5,000 equals the $10,000 total adjustment.

questions.q: Jill contributes $100,000 of cash to a partnership in exchange for a 25% interest. The partnership has a §754 election in effect. Which basis adjustment applies?
choices: A §743 adjustment equal to the difference between her cash and her share of inside basis
A §734 adjustment to the partnership's remaining property
None under §743 or §734, because acquiring an interest by contribution is neither a transfer nor a distribution
A mandatory adjustment, because she paid cash
questions.exp: Section 743 applies only to a sale or exchange of an existing interest or a transfer at death, and §734 applies only to distributions, so a contribution for a new interest triggers neither. The partnership uses a revaluation and reverse allocations to address pre-existing appreciation.

questions.q: Which event can trigger a §734(b) adjustment rather than a §743(b) adjustment for a partnership with a §754 election?
choices: A partner's sale of her interest to an outsider
A distribution of cash in complete liquidation of a partner's interest
A partner's gift of her interest to her child
The death of a partner whose interest passes to an heir
questions.exp: Section 734 adjustments arise from partnership distributions, such as a liquidating cash distribution that produces gain to the distributee. A sale or an inheritance of an interest is a transfer that triggers a §743 adjustment instead.

questions.q: Kim contributed land with a $100,000 built-in gain to a partnership 12 years ago, and the partnership still holds it. If the partnership sells the land this year, how is the built-in gain allocated?
choices: To no one, because the built-in gain expired after 10 years
Among all partners by profit share, because the 7-year period has expired
To Kim, because the contributed-property allocation rules apply for as long as the partnership holds the property
To Kim only if she elects to accept it
questions.exp: The rule requiring built-in gain to be allocated to the contributing partner has no time limit. The 7-year period applies only to the distribution rules that tax the contributor when the property, or other property, is distributed.

questions.q: A partnership with a §754 election and no liabilities holds assets with a total adjusted basis of $300,000 and a total FMV of $240,000. Eli buys a one-third interest from an existing partner for $80,000. What is Eli's §743(b) adjustment?
choices: $20,000 increase
$20,000 decrease
$60,000 decrease
questions.exp: Eli's $80,000 outside basis is less than his one-third share of inside basis ($300,000 / 3 = $100,000), so the election requires a $20,000 downward adjustment. The $60,000 answer uses the partnership's entire built-in loss instead of Eli's one-third share.

topics.topic: Personal financial planning and retirement accounts

questions.q: Ann, single, age 40, is an active participant in her employer's 401(k) plan and has modified AGI of $86,000. Assume the IRA contribution limit is $7,500, and the deduction phase-out range for an active participant filing single is $81,000 to $91,000. What is the maximum deductible traditional IRA contribution she can make?
questions.exp: She is halfway through the $10,000 phase-out range ($5,000 ÷ $10,000), so the deductible limit is reduced by 50%: $7,500 × 50% = $3,750 under §219(g). Answering $0 treats active participation as an absolute bar, but it only triggers the phase-out.

questions.q: Ben, age 45, is an active participant in his employer's retirement plan, and his wife Cara, age 44, has no earned income and no plan coverage. Their joint modified AGI is $200,000, and Ben's wages easily exceed both contributions. Assume the IRA limit is $7,500 per spouse; the joint phase-out range for an active participant is $129,000 to $149,000; and the phase-out range for a spouse who is not an active participant but is married to one is $242,000 to $252,000. What is the total deductible traditional IRA contribution for the couple?
questions.exp: Ben's MAGI exceeds the top of his range, so his deduction is zero; Cara's deduction uses the higher $242,000–$252,000 range under §219(g), so her full $7,500 spousal IRA contribution is deductible. Answering $0 wrongly applies Ben's active-participant range to Cara.

questions.q: Dev, single, has modified AGI of $156,000. Assume the Roth IRA contribution limit is $7,500 and the Roth phase-out range for single filers is $150,000 to $165,000. What is the maximum Roth IRA contribution Dev can make?
questions.exp: Dev is 6/15 (40%) of the way through the phase-out, so his limit is reduced by 40%: $7,500 × 60% = $4,500 under §408A. Answering $3,000 confuses the 40% reduction with the remaining allowable amount.

questions.q: Eva makes a $7,000 nondeductible contribution to a traditional IRA and converts $7,000 to a Roth IRA a week later. On December 31, after the conversion, her only other IRA, a rollover IRA holding pre-tax money, has a balance of $93,000. She has no other IRA basis. How much of the conversion is taxable?
questions.exp: Under the §408 pro rata rule, all traditional IRAs are combined: basis of $7,000 ÷ ($93,000 + $7,000) = 7% of the conversion is nontaxable ($490), so $6,510 is taxable. The 'backdoor Roth' result of $0 holds only if she has no pre-tax IRA balances at year end.

questions.q: Fred, age 52, withdraws $30,000 from his traditional IRA (no basis): $10,000 for his first home purchase (he has never used this exception), $8,000 for his son's qualified college tuition, and $12,000 to pay credit card debt. What additional tax under §72(t) does Fred owe?
questions.exp: IRA distributions for qualified higher education expenses and up to $10,000 of first-time homebuyer costs are exempt from the 10% additional tax, leaving $12,000 × 10% = $1,200. All $30,000 is still subject to regular income tax. Answering $3,000 ignores the IRA-specific exceptions.

questions.q: Gia separated from service at age 56 and wants to draw $40,000 from her former employer's 401(k) plan this year without the 10% additional tax. Which approach accomplishes this?
choices: Roll the entire balance to an IRA, then withdraw $40,000 from the IRA
Roll the balance to an IRA and take the withdrawal after a 60-day holding period
Take the $40,000 from her IRA under the age-55 separation exception
Leave the money in the 401(k) plan and take the $40,000 distribution directly from the plan
questions.exp: The §72(t) exception for separation from service in or after the year the employee turns 55 applies only to distributions from the employer's qualified plan, not to IRAs. Rolling the money to an IRA first forfeits the exception.

questions.q: Hank, age 45, opened a Roth IRA eight years ago. The account holds $30,000 of contributions (no conversions) and $20,000 of earnings. He withdraws $35,000 for a nonqualified purpose. How much of the withdrawal is included in his gross income?
questions.exp: Roth distributions come out of regular contributions first, tax-free, under §408A ordering rules: $30,000 is a return of contributions and the remaining $5,000 is earnings, which are taxable (and subject to the 10% additional tax) because Hank is under 59½. Answering $14,000 prorates earnings as though the pro rata rule for traditional IRAs applied.

questions.q: Iris, age 75, had a traditional IRA balance of $500,000 on December 31 of last year. Her life expectancy factor under the Uniform Lifetime Table for this year is 24.6. What is her required minimum distribution for this year?
questions.exp: The RMD is the prior year-end balance divided by the distribution period: $500,000 ÷ 24.6 = $20,325. Dividing by 25 or using the current year's balance are common errors.

questions.q: Jake failed to take $20,000 of his required minimum distribution this year. He takes the shortfall and files the required return within the correction window allowed under SECURE 2.0. What excise tax applies to the shortfall?
questions.exp: Section 4974 now imposes a 25% excise tax on an RMD shortfall, reduced to 10% when the failure is corrected timely within the correction window: $20,000 × 10% = $2,000. The $10,000 result uses the former 50% rate.

questions.q: Kim died this year at age 68 with a traditional IRA. Under the SECURE Act, which beneficiary may stretch distributions over his or her own life expectancy instead of emptying the account by the end of the tenth year after death?
choices: Kim's 30-year-old niece
Kim's 64-year-old brother, who is not disabled or chronically ill
A see-through trust for Kim's adult grandchildren
Kim's 40-year-old son, who is in good health
questions.exp: An eligible designated beneficiary under §401 includes an individual not more than 10 years younger than the decedent, so the 64-year-old brother qualifies. Adult children, a niece, and trusts for adult grandchildren are non-eligible designated beneficiaries subject to the 10-year rule.

questions.q: Lena, age 61, earns $300,000 and participates in her employer's 401(k) plan. Assume the elective deferral limit is $24,500, the standard catch-up for those age 50 and over is $8,000, and the enhanced catch-up for those ages 60 through 63 is $11,250. What is the maximum elective deferral Lena can make this year?
questions.exp: SECURE 2.0 replaces the standard catch-up with the higher catch-up for participants ages 60–63: $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750. Adding both catch-ups ($43,750) is not allowed. Because her prior-year wages are high, the catch-up must be made as Roth contributions, but the dollar limit is unchanged.

questions.q: Mo is a self-employed consultant with $100,000 of Schedule C net profit and no employees. His deduction for one-half of self-employment tax is $7,065. What is the maximum deductible contribution to his SEP IRA, assuming the 25% contribution rate is the plan maximum?
questions.exp: For a self-employed person, the 25% rate is applied to compensation net of the contribution itself, which works out to 20% of net earnings after the half-SE-tax deduction: ($100,000 − $7,065) × 20% = $18,587. Applying 25% directly to $92,935 ($23,234) ignores the circular reduction.

questions.q: Nora owns a business with 12 employees and wants to set up a SEP IRA that makes a 15% contribution for herself. Which statement about the plan is correct?
choices: She must contribute the same percentage of compensation for every eligible employee
Contributions vest over a six-year graded schedule
Employees may make their own salary-deferral contributions to the SEP
She may limit contributions to herself and key employees
questions.exp: SEP contributions must be made at a uniform percentage of compensation for all eligible employees and are immediately 100% vested under §408(k). New SEPs do not allow elective salary deferrals, which are a feature of 401(k) and SIMPLE plans.

questions.q: In Year 1, Omar made a $3,000 excess contribution to his traditional IRA and did not withdraw it, or its earnings, by the due date of his Year 1 return. What excise tax does Omar owe for Year 1 on the excess?
questions.exp: Section 4973 imposes a 6% excise tax on an excess contribution for each year it remains in the account at year end: $3,000 × 6% = $180, and the tax recurs each year until corrected. The $300 figure uses the 10% early-distribution rate, which is a different penalty.

questions.q: Pia received a check for her entire IRA balance in March and redeposited it into another IRA within 60 days. In November, she wants to move a second IRA to a new custodian. Which method avoids a problem with the rollover rules?
choices: Any method, because the one-rollover rule applies per account
Have the funds moved directly from one IRA trustee to the other
Receive the funds and redeposit them within 30 days
Receive a distribution check and redeposit it within 60 days
questions.exp: An individual may make only one IRA-to-IRA indirect (60-day) rollover in any 12-month period, counted across all of the individual's IRAs. Direct trustee-to-trustee transfers are not rollovers and are unlimited. The limit is per taxpayer, not per account.

questions.q: Raj, age 45, left his job and requested a $100,000 lump-sum distribution of his 401(k) (all pre-tax). The plan withheld 20% and paid him $80,000, which he deposited in a rollover IRA within 60 days. He did not replace the withheld amount. How much is included in his gross income?
questions.exp: Only the $80,000 actually rolled over is excluded; the $20,000 withheld is a taxable distribution and is also subject to the 10% additional tax because Raj is under 55 at separation. Answering $0 assumes withholding is just a credit. To roll over the full amount, he would have had to deposit $20,000 of other funds.

questions.q: Sue receives a lump-sum distribution from her employer's 401(k) that includes employer stock with a plan cost basis of $50,000 and an FMV of $300,000. She moves the stock to a taxable brokerage account and does not sell it this year. How much ordinary income does she recognize this year on the stock?
questions.exp: Under §402(e)(4), on a lump-sum distribution of employer securities, only the plan's cost basis ($50,000) is taxed currently as ordinary income; the $250,000 net unrealized appreciation is taxed as long-term capital gain when the stock is sold. Taxing the full FMV ignores the NUA rule.

questions.q: Tom's full retirement age is 67, and his monthly Social Security benefit at that age would be $2,000. Delayed retirement credits accrue at 8% per year. If he waits until age 70 to claim, what will his monthly benefit be, ignoring cost-of-living adjustments?
questions.exp: Delayed retirement credits are simple, not compounded: 8% × 3 years = 24%, so $2,000 × 1.24 = $2,480. Compounding the credits gives $2,519, which overstates the benefit.

questions.q: Una paid $20,000 to buy an existing $200,000 life insurance policy on the life of an unrelated business acquaintance and then paid $10,000 of premiums. The insured died and Una collected $200,000. No exception applies. How much of the proceeds is taxable to Una?
questions.exp: Under the §101 transfer-for-value rule, the exclusion is limited to the consideration paid plus later premiums: $200,000 − ($20,000 + $10,000) = $170,000 taxable. Excluding all the proceeds ignores the rule, and subtracting only the purchase price ($180,000) ignores the premiums.

questions.q: Vince paid $60,000 for a single-life annuity that pays $10,000 a year. The expected return under the annuity is $100,000. How much of each $10,000 annual payment is included in his gross income?
questions.exp: Under §72, the exclusion ratio is investment ÷ expected return = $60,000 ÷ $100,000 = 60%, so $6,000 of each payment is excluded and $4,000 is taxable. The $6,000 answer reverses the excluded and taxable portions.

questions.q: Wen withdraws $20,000 from her daughter's §529 plan and uses it for a family vacation. Contributions make up 70% of the account and earnings 30%. What are the federal tax consequences of the withdrawal?
choices: $6,000 included in income and no additional tax
$20,000 included in income and a $2,000 additional tax
$6,000 included in income and a $600 additional tax
$0 included in income because contributions are withdrawn first
questions.exp: A nonqualified §529 distribution is prorated between contributions and earnings: the $6,000 earnings portion is taxable under §72, plus the §529 10% additional tax ($600). The 'contributions first' rule applies to Roth IRAs, not to §529 plans.

questions.q: Xavier's §529 account for his daughter has been open for 16 years. She finished college with $30,000 left over. Assume the lifetime limit on §529-to-Roth IRA rollovers is $35,000, and the Roth IRA annual contribution limit is $7,500. Which statement about rolling the leftover funds to a Roth IRA for the daughter is correct?
choices: The full $30,000 can be rolled over this year, regardless of her compensation
Contributions made to the §529 account in the last five years (and their earnings) are not eligible, and the yearly rollover is limited to the Roth annual limit reduced by her other IRA contributions
The rollover is subject to the Roth income phase-out based on the daughter's MAGI
The rollover is permitted only to a Roth IRA owned by Xavier
questions.exp: SECURE 2.0 permits §529-to-Roth rollovers for the beneficiary if the account has been open at least 15 years, excludes contributions from the past five years, and limits each year's rollover to the Roth annual limit less her other IRA contributions, up to the lifetime cap. The Roth income phase-out is waived for these rollovers, but she still needs compensation at least equal to the rollover amount.

questions.q: Yara, age 67, withdraws $10,000 from her HSA to pay for a cruise. She has no medical expenses this year. What is the tax effect of the withdrawal?
choices: $0 included in income because she is over 65
$10,000 included in income and a $1,000 additional tax
$10,000 included in income with no additional tax
$10,000 included in income and a $2,000 additional tax
questions.exp: Under §223, a nonqualified HSA distribution is included in income, but the 20% additional tax does not apply after age 65, death, or disability; after 65 an HSA works like a traditional IRA for non-medical withdrawals. The 20% additional tax applies only to those under 65.

questions.q: Zeke, age 76, has $400,000 in a designated Roth account in his former employer's 401(k) plan. Under current law, what are his required minimum distribution obligations for this account?
choices: He must roll the account to a Roth IRA by age 73 to avoid RMDs
He must take RMDs, but they are tax-free
He has no lifetime RMDs from the designated Roth account
He must take RMDs because Roth 401(k) accounts follow the same rules as pre-tax 401(k) accounts
questions.exp: SECURE 2.0 eliminated pre-death RMDs from designated Roth accounts in employer plans starting in 2024, matching the Roth IRA rules. A rollover to a Roth IRA is no longer needed to avoid lifetime RMDs.

questions.q: Ava, a 58-year-old physician with very high, stable earnings and two young employees, wants to shelter the largest possible deductible amount for herself over the next seven years before she retires. Which type of plan is generally best suited to this goal?
choices: A SEP IRA
A defined benefit or cash balance plan
A SIMPLE IRA
A profit-sharing plan without a 401(k) feature
questions.exp: A defined benefit or cash balance plan funds a target benefit, so contributions for an older owner with a short time horizon can far exceed the §415 defined contribution limit that caps SEP and profit-sharing plans. A SIMPLE IRA has the lowest limits of the four.

questions.q: Ben receives $30,000 of long-term disability benefits this year under a group policy. His employer paid all of the premiums, and they were not included in Ben's income. How much of the benefits is taxable?
choices: $30,000 less his cumulative premiums
questions.exp: Under §105, benefits from employer-paid disability coverage whose premiums were excluded from the employee's income are fully taxable. Had Ben paid the premiums with after-tax dollars, the benefits would be excluded under §104, which is the planning point.

questions.q: Cleo, age 50, converted $40,000 from a traditional IRA (no basis) to a Roth IRA three years ago and paid tax on the conversion then. She has made no other Roth contributions or conversions. This year she withdraws the $40,000. What are the tax consequences?
choices: No income tax and no additional tax
$40,000 of income and a $4,000 additional tax
$40,000 of income and no additional tax
No income tax, but a $4,000 additional tax
questions.exp: Converted amounts come out after regular contributions and are not taxed again, but under §408A a conversion withdrawn within five years by someone under 59½ is subject to the 10% additional tax: $40,000 × 10% = $4,000. The five-year clock for conversions is separate from the clock for qualified distributions.

questions.q: Dan, age 16, earned $4,000 working at a grocery store this year and has no other income. Assume the IRA contribution limit is $7,500. What is the maximum Roth IRA contribution that can be made for Dan this year?
choices: $0, because he is a minor
questions.exp: IRA contributions are limited to the lesser of the annual limit or the individual's taxable compensation, here $4,000. There is no minimum age, and a parent may fund the contribution as long as Dan has earned income.

questions.q: Ella, age 50, is the sole beneficiary of her late husband's traditional IRA. She needs to withdraw $50,000 over the next three years for living expenses. Which approach avoids the 10% early-withdrawal penalty on those withdrawals?
choices: Keep the account as an inherited IRA and take the withdrawals from it
Roll the IRA into her own IRA and take withdrawals from it
Take a lump-sum distribution and roll the unneeded portion into her own IRA after 90 days
Treat the IRA as her own and take the withdrawals as a hardship distribution
questions.exp: Distributions to a beneficiary because of the owner's death are exempt from the 10% additional tax under §72(t), but once a spouse rolls or elects to treat the IRA as her own, she is the owner and must be 59½ for penalty-free withdrawals. She can still treat the account as her own later, after turning 59½.

questions.q: Fay has a vested 401(k) balance of $80,000 and has never borrowed from the plan. The plan permits loans to the maximum extent allowed under §72(p). What is the maximum loan she can take without it being treated as a distribution?
questions.exp: Under §72(p), a plan loan is limited to the lesser of $50,000 or the greater of 50% of the vested balance or $10,000: 50% × $80,000 = $40,000. The $50,000 statutory cap applies only when half the vested balance exceeds it.

questions.q: Gus, age 75, still works for an unrelated employer, owns no stock in it, and participates in its 401(k) plan, which allows the still-working exception. He also has a traditional IRA from a former job. Assume RMDs generally begin at age 73. Which RMDs must Gus take this year?
choices: RMDs from both the current employer's 401(k) and the IRA
An RMD from the current employer's 401(k) only
An RMD from the IRA only
No RMDs until he retires
questions.exp: The still-working exception in §401 delays RMDs from the current employer's plan for a participant who is not a 5% owner, but it never applies to IRAs. Assuming no RMDs at all extends the exception to accounts it does not cover.

questions.q: Hal, a high-income earner, wants to make a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution and convert it to a Roth IRA. He also has $200,000 of pre-tax money in a rollover IRA, and his current employer's 401(k) plan accepts roll-ins. What should he do to make the conversion essentially tax-free?
choices: Wait 60 days between the contribution and the conversion
Convert in a different calendar year from the contribution
Open a new IRA at a different custodian for the nondeductible contribution
Roll the $200,000 pre-tax IRA into the 401(k) before December 31 of the conversion year
questions.exp: The §408 pro rata rule aggregates all of a person's traditional, SEP, and SIMPLE IRA balances at year end, but not employer plan balances. Moving the pre-tax IRA into the 401(k) by December 31 leaves only basis in the IRA. Using a different custodian does not help because all IRAs are aggregated.

questions.q: Ivy holds high-yield corporate bonds, a broad stock index fund, and an aggressive small-cap growth fund she expects to grow fastest. She has a taxable account, a traditional IRA, and a Roth IRA. Which asset placement is generally the most tax-efficient?
choices: Bonds in the Roth IRA, small-cap growth fund in the taxable account, and index fund in the traditional IRA
Equal portions of each holding in every account
Bonds in the traditional IRA, small-cap growth fund in the Roth IRA, and index fund in the taxable account
Bonds in the taxable account, small-cap growth fund in the traditional IRA, and index fund in the Roth IRA
questions.exp: Interest taxed at ordinary rates belongs in tax-deferred accounts, the highest-growth assets belong in the Roth, where growth is never taxed, and tax-efficient index funds, with qualified dividends, low turnover, and a basis step-up at death, suit taxable accounts. Placing bonds in the taxable account exposes their ordinary interest to annual tax.

questions.q: Jill, age 52, began taking substantially equal periodic payments from her IRA under §72(t) two years ago to avoid the 10% additional tax. This year she wants to take an extra $25,000 withdrawal. What is the consequence?
choices: The extra withdrawal is penalty-free because the payment series already qualifies
There is no consequence if she resumes the original payments next year
Only the extra $25,000 is subject to the 10% additional tax
The modification triggers the 10% additional tax, plus interest, on all prior payments in the series as well
questions.exp: Changing a SEPP series before the later of five years or age 59½ triggers a recapture tax equal to the 10% additional tax that would have applied to all prior distributions, plus interest. Penalizing only the extra withdrawal understates the cost.

questions.q: Kai, in the 22% bracket today, expects to be in the 32% bracket in retirement. He is choosing between deferring $10,000 of pre-tax salary to a traditional 401(k) or paying tax now and contributing the after-tax amount ($7,800) to a Roth 401(k). Either account will quadruple before withdrawal. How much more after-tax money does the Roth produce?
questions.exp: Traditional: $40,000 × (1 − 32%) = $27,200 after tax. Roth: $7,800 × 4 = $31,200 tax-free. The Roth wins by $4,000 because it locks in the lower current rate. Answering $0 assumes equal tax rates, which would make the two choices equivalent.

questions.q: Lou, age 50, has a whole life policy that became a modified endowment contract. The policy has $100,000 of cash value, and his premiums paid total $70,000. He takes a $40,000 policy loan. What are the tax consequences?
choices: $40,000 of income and a $4,000 additional tax
$30,000 of income and a $3,000 additional tax
$0 income, because the loan is less than his basis
$0 income, because policy loans are not distributions
questions.exp: Loans from a MEC are treated as distributions taxed income-first under §72(e): the first $30,000 (cash value over premiums) is taxable, and §72(v) imposes a 10% additional tax before age 59½ ($3,000). The remaining $10,000 is a tax-free recovery of basis. Non-MEC policy loans would not be taxable.

questions.q: Mae's employer provides her with $250,000 of group-term life insurance and pays the full premium. The IRS uniform premium table cost for her age is $0.15 per $1,000 of coverage per month. How much must be included in Mae's gross income for the year?
questions.exp: Section 79 excludes the cost of the first $50,000 of coverage; the remaining $200,000 is taxed at table rates: 200 × $0.15 × 12 = $360. Using the full $250,000 of coverage ($450) ignores the $50,000 exclusion.

questions.q: Ned, age 66 and retired, receives $60,000 of pension income, $15,000 of dividends, and Social Security. His wife, age 64, works part time and earns $20,000. They file jointly. Which statement about IRA contributions this year is correct?
choices: Ned may contribute because pension income is treated as compensation
Neither spouse may contribute because Ned has no compensation
Only the wife may contribute, limited to her own $20,000 of compensation
Both spouses may contribute because the wife's compensation is enough to support contributions for both
questions.exp: Under the §219 spousal IRA rule, on a joint return each spouse may contribute up to the annual limit as long as their combined contributions do not exceed the couple's combined compensation, and the wife's $20,000 covers both. Pensions, dividends, and Social Security are not compensation.

topics.topic: S corporation distributions and basis planning

questions.q: Ava is the sole shareholder of an S corporation with no E&P. Her stock basis at the start of the year is $10,000 and she has no debt basis. For the year, the corporation reports $20,000 of ordinary income, $2,000 of tax-exempt interest, $1,000 of nondeductible expenses and a $9,000 long-term capital loss, and it distributes $25,000 to her. No special elections are made. How much of the capital loss can Ava deduct this year?
questions.exp: Basis is increased by income ($10,000 + $20,000 + $2,000 = $32,000), then reduced by the $25,000 distribution ($7,000) and the $1,000 nondeductible expenses ($6,000), and only then by losses. She deducts $6,000 and carries $3,000 forward; answering $7,000 skips the nondeductible expenses, which come before losses.

questions.q: Ben's S corporation stock basis is $5,000 on January 1. In February the corporation, which has no E&P, distributes $30,000 to him. For the full year his share of ordinary income is $40,000. What are the results of the distribution?
choices: No gain; ending basis $15,000
$25,000 capital gain; ending basis $15,000
No gain; ending basis $45,000
$25,000 capital gain; ending basis $40,000
questions.exp: Basis is adjusted at year-end, with the year's income added before distributions are applied, so the $30,000 is measured against $5,000 + $40,000 = $45,000 and is tax-free, leaving $15,000. Comparing the distribution with the January 1 basis ignores this ordering rule.

questions.q: Cole has held his S corporation shares for five years. After this year's income, his stock basis is $12,000. The corporation has never been a C corporation and distributes $20,000 to him. What does Cole report?
choices: $8,000 long-term capital gain
$20,000 long-term capital gain
$8,000 dividend income
$8,000 ordinary income
questions.exp: With no E&P, a distribution is tax-free up to stock basis, and the $20,000 − $12,000 = $8,000 excess is treated as gain from the sale of the stock, long-term because he has held it more than a year. It is not a dividend because there are no earnings and profits.

questions.q: Dana is the sole shareholder of an S corporation with $15,000 of AAA and $10,000 of accumulated E&P from its C corporation years. Her stock basis is $30,000 after this year's income, and she receives a $30,000 distribution. No elections are made. What are her dividend income and ending stock basis?
choices: $10,000 dividend; ending basis $10,000
$10,000 dividend; ending basis $0
$15,000 dividend; ending basis $15,000
$0 dividend; ending basis $0
questions.exp: The first $15,000 comes from AAA and is tax-free (basis falls to $15,000), the next $10,000 is a dividend from E&P that does not reduce basis, and the last $5,000 is a return of basis, leaving $10,000. Ignoring the E&P layer gives the $0 dividend answer.

questions.q: An S corporation with accumulated E&P from its C corporation years wants its distributions to come out of E&P before AAA. Which statement about this election is correct?
choices: It requires the consent of all shareholders who receive distributions during the year, and the E&P distributed is taxable as dividends
It makes the distributions of E&P tax-free because the corporation is now an S corporation
The corporation may make it alone, without shareholder consent
It is available only in the first year after the S election takes effect
questions.exp: The election to distribute E&P first requires consent from every affected shareholder, and the E&P comes out as dividend income. Corporations make it to eliminate E&P, which removes the exposure to the excess passive investment income tax and to termination of the S election.

questions.q: An S corporation with accumulated E&P of $100,000 starts the year with AAA of $50,000. During the year it has a $40,000 ordinary loss and distributes $30,000. Shareholders have ample basis. How much of the distribution comes from AAA, and what is ending AAA?
choices: $30,000 from AAA; ending AAA ($20,000)
$10,000 from AAA; ending AAA $0
$0 from AAA; ending AAA ($20,000)
$30,000 from AAA; ending AAA $0
questions.exp: In a year with a net negative adjustment, distributions are applied to AAA before the loss, so $50,000 − $30,000 = $20,000 covers the full distribution, and the $40,000 loss then takes AAA to ($20,000). Losses, unlike distributions, can make AAA negative; applying the loss first gives the $10,000 answer.

questions.q: Which item increases an S corporation shareholder's stock basis but does not increase the corporation's accumulated adjustments account?
choices: Long-term capital gain
Net §1231 gain
Tax-exempt interest income
Ordinary business income
questions.exp: Tax-exempt income increases stock basis but is tracked outside AAA (in the other adjustments account), so it is not part of the AAA that comes out first when the corporation has E&P. All taxable income items increase both stock basis and AAA.

questions.q: Erin's S corporation stock basis is $10,000. She has lent the corporation $20,000 directly, and she has personally guaranteed a $50,000 bank loan to it. Her share of the corporation's ordinary loss is $45,000. How much of the loss can she deduct, before the at-risk and passive activity limits?
questions.exp: Losses are deductible up to stock basis ($10,000) plus debt basis from loans the shareholder made directly to the corporation ($20,000), for $30,000, with $15,000 suspended. A guarantee of a third-party loan does not create debt basis unless she actually pays on it.

questions.q: Last year losses reduced Finn's stock basis to $0 and the basis of his $20,000 loan to his S corporation to $12,000. This year his share of ordinary income is $15,000, there are no distributions, and the loan has not been repaid. What are his ending stock basis and debt basis?
choices: Stock $0; debt $27,000
questions.exp: A net increase in basis first restores debt basis to its face amount: $8,000 brings the loan back to $20,000, and the remaining $7,000 increases stock basis. Debt basis can never exceed the face amount of the loan, so $27,000 is impossible.

questions.q: Gail's S corporation stock basis is $0, and her $20,000 loan to the corporation has a reduced basis of $5,000. This year her share of ordinary income is $10,000 and she receives a $10,000 cash distribution. What are the results?
choices: The distribution is tax-free; stock basis is $0 and debt basis stays at $5,000
The distribution is tax-free; stock basis is $10,000 and debt basis is $5,000
Debt basis is restored to $15,000, and the distribution reduces it back to $5,000
Debt basis is restored to $15,000, and the $10,000 distribution is capital gain
questions.exp: Debt basis is restored only by a net increase, which is income minus distributions and losses; here that is $0. The $10,000 of income raises stock basis and the distribution then takes it back to $0 tax-free, leaving debt basis at $5,000.

questions.q: Hal lent his S corporation $20,000 three years ago in exchange for a formal written note. Losses have reduced the note's basis to $5,000, and this year the corporation repays the full $20,000. What does Hal recognize?
choices: $20,000 of long-term capital gain
$15,000 of ordinary income
$15,000 of long-term capital gain
No gain, because loan repayments are a return of capital
questions.exp: Repaying a debt whose basis has been reduced by losses produces gain of $20,000 − $5,000 = $15,000. Because the debt is a note held as a capital asset for more than a year, the gain is long-term capital gain.

questions.q: A shareholder advanced funds to her S corporation on an open account, with no written note. Losses reduced the debt basis, and the corporation now repays the advances in full. How is the shareholder's gain on the repayment characterized?
choices: As dividend income to the extent of AAA
As a tax-free return of capital, because there is no note
As capital gain, because the debt is a capital asset in her hands
As ordinary income, because repayment of an open account is not a sale or exchange
questions.exp: Repaying an open account debt is not a sale or exchange, so gain from repaying reduced-basis open account advances is ordinary income. A formal note held as a capital asset would instead produce capital gain on repayment.

questions.q: Ivy's S corporation will produce large first-year losses, but her stock basis is small. The corporation can borrow $200,000 from a bank if she guarantees it. Which arrangement gives her basis for the losses?
choices: The corporation borrows from a partnership in which she is a partner
She borrows $200,000 from the bank personally and lends it to the corporation
She pledges her personal residence as collateral for the corporation's loan
She guarantees the bank loan to the corporation
questions.exp: Debt basis arises only from bona fide debt the corporation owes directly to the shareholder, so a back-to-back loan through the shareholder creates basis. A guarantee or pledge does not create basis until the shareholder actually pays the corporation's debt.

questions.q: A corporation's S election terminated at the end of last year, when the shareholder had $30,000 of suspended losses, $0 stock basis and $10,000 of debt basis. Which statement about deducting the suspended losses is correct?
choices: They are deductible at any time in the future up to her stock and debt basis
They are deductible immediately up to her $10,000 of debt basis
They are lost on termination and can never be deducted
They are deductible during the post-termination transition period up to her stock basis at the end of that period
questions.exp: Suspended losses are treated as incurred on the last day of the post-termination transition period, but only to the extent of stock basis at that time; debt basis does not count. The shareholder can make a capital contribution during the period to create the basis.

questions.q: Jon has $25,000 of losses from his S corporation suspended for lack of basis. He sells all of his shares to an unrelated buyer. What happens to the suspended losses?
choices: They expire unused; suspended losses are personal to Jon and do not transfer to the buyer
They pass to the buyer along with the shares
They become a capital loss carryforward that Jon may deduct in later years
They increase Jon's basis in the shares sold
questions.exp: Losses suspended under the basis limitation can be used only by the shareholder who incurred them and are lost when the shares are sold to an unrelated party. A transfer to a spouse or incident to divorce is the main exception, so a shareholder planning a sale should restore basis first.

questions.q: A C corporation elected S status effective January 1, 2024, with a net unrealized built-in gain of $100,000. In 2026 it sells equipment for $95,000 that had a basis of $30,000 and an FMV of $90,000 on January 1, 2024. Its 2026 taxable income computed as a C corporation is $80,000. What is the built-in gains tax?
questions.exp: Only the appreciation at conversion is built-in gain: $90,000 − $30,000 = $60,000, and the post-conversion $5,000 is not taxed. The tax is $60,000 × 21% = $12,600, which falls within both the $80,000 taxable income limit and the $100,000 NUBIG limit; $13,650 taxes the whole $65,000 gain.

questions.q: In the third year after converting from a C corporation, an S corporation has a $60,000 net recognized built-in gain, but its taxable income computed as if it were a C corporation is only $40,000. Its remaining net unrealized built-in gain is ample. What is the result?
choices: Built-in gains tax of $12,600; nothing carries forward
Built-in gains tax of $4,200 on the $20,000 excess
Built-in gains tax of $8,400; the $20,000 excess carries forward to later years in the recognition period
Built-in gains tax of $8,400; nothing carries forward
questions.exp: The recognized built-in gain taxed is limited to taxable income, so the tax is $40,000 × 21% = $8,400. The $20,000 excess is treated as recognized built-in gain in the next year, but only if that year is still within the recognition period.

questions.q: A C corporation's S election took effect January 1, 2020. In February 2026, it sells land that was worth $200,000 more than its basis on January 1, 2020. Is the sale subject to the built-in gains tax?
choices: No, because the 5-year recognition period ended December 31, 2024
Yes, because the recognition period is 10 years
Yes, because the land was held on the conversion date
No, because land is never subject to the built-in gains tax
questions.exp: The recognition period is the 5 years beginning on the first day of the first S year, here 2020 through 2024, so a 2026 sale escapes the tax. Waiting until the period ends is the simplest built-in gains planning; the 10-year period is an outdated rule.

questions.q: An S corporation owned 100% by Kim recognizes a $60,000 §1231 gain that is all built-in gain and pays $12,600 of built-in gains tax on it. What net §1231 gain passes through to Kim?
questions.exp: The built-in gains tax paid is treated as a loss to the shareholders with the same character as the gain that caused it, so Kim's net §1231 gain is $60,000 − $12,600 = $47,400. Passing through the full $60,000 ignores this rule and taxes the tax.

questions.q: During its recognition period, a former C corporation sells an asset at a gain. The IRS treats the entire gain as built-in gain. Which planning step at the time of the S election is most important in rebutting this?
choices: Obtaining a reliable appraisal of the corporation's assets as of the conversion date
Contributing additional capital to raise shareholder basis
Electing a calendar year for the S corporation
Distributing all accumulated E&P before the election takes effect
questions.exp: Gain recognized in the recognition period is presumed to be built-in gain unless the corporation shows the asset was acquired later or the gain exceeds the appreciation at conversion. A contemporaneous appraisal is the main evidence; distributing E&P addresses the passive investment income tax, not this one.

questions.q: In year 4 of its recognition period, an S corporation sells a built-in gain asset on the installment method and collects payments in years 4 through 8. How is the built-in gain treated?
choices: Built-in gain recognized from all of the payments, including those after the period ends, is subject to the tax
Only payments received in years 4 and 5 are subject to the built-in gains tax
None of the gain is taxed because the sale was not paid in full during the period
The installment method is not allowed for built-in gain assets
questions.exp: Under the regulations, a sale made during the recognition period keeps its built-in gain character, so installment gain recognized after the period ends is still subject to the tax. An installment sale therefore does not avoid the built-in gains tax.

questions.q: Lena's stock basis in her wholly owned S corporation is $70,000 before a distribution. The corporation, which has no E&P, distributes land with a basis of $40,000 and an FMV of $100,000 to her. What are the results?
choices: $60,000 gain passed through; land basis $100,000; stock basis $30,000
$60,000 gain passed through; land basis $40,000; stock basis $90,000
No gain; land basis $40,000; stock basis $30,000
$60,000 gain passed through; land basis $100,000; stock basis $0 and $30,000 capital gain
questions.exp: The corporation recognizes $60,000 of gain as if it sold the land, which passes through and raises Lena's basis to $130,000. The $100,000 FMV distribution then reduces it to $30,000 tax-free, and she takes a $100,000 basis in the land; the capital gain answer forgets the basis increase from the pass-through gain.

questions.q: An S corporation owns investment land with a basis of $90,000 and an FMV of $50,000 and plans to give it to its sole shareholder. What is the better tax plan?
choices: Distribute the land, because the shareholder takes a $90,000 basis
Sell the land to the shareholder, because the loss is allowed on related-party sales
Sell the land to an unrelated buyer, recognize the $40,000 loss, and distribute the cash
Distribute the land, because the $40,000 loss passes through to the shareholder
questions.exp: A corporation recognizes no loss on distributing depreciated property, and the shareholder's basis is only the $50,000 FMV, so the loss vanishes. A sale to a more-than-50% shareholder is disallowed under §267, so selling to an unrelated buyer preserves the loss.

questions.q: When can an S corporation become liable for the tax on excess net passive income?
choices: Whenever its passive investment income exceeds 25% of gross receipts, even with no E&P
When any shareholder has passive losses from other activities
When it has accumulated E&P and its passive investment income exceeds 50% of taxable income
When it has accumulated E&P from C years at year-end and its passive investment income exceeds 25% of gross receipts
questions.exp: The tax applies only if the corporation has accumulated E&P at year-end and passive investment income above 25% of gross receipts; three consecutive such years also terminate the S election. An S corporation that never had E&P is never subject to it.

questions.q: An S corporation's governing documents give every share identical rights to distributions. One year, the corporation distributes cash to some shareholders a few months before distributing equal amounts per share to the others. What is the effect on the S election?
choices: The early recipients must treat their distributions as dividends
The election terminates because the corporation now has a second class of stock
There is no second class of stock, because the governing provisions confer identical rights, though the timing differences should be corrected
The late recipients may deduct the delay as a loss
questions.exp: Whether a second class of stock exists depends on the governing provisions; differences in the timing of actual distributions under identical rights do not create one, although the IRS may recharacterize them. Making distributions pro rata per share and on the same dates avoids the question.

questions.q: Max is the sole shareholder and full-time CEO of a profitable S corporation. He takes no salary and instead receives $300,000 of distributions. What is the main tax risk?
choices: The IRS may recharacterize part of the distributions as wages subject to employment taxes
The corporation will lose its deduction for the distributions
The distributions will be taxed as dividends because the corporation is profitable
The S election will terminate for paying disproportionate distributions
questions.exp: A shareholder who performs significant services must receive reasonable compensation, and distributions that substitute for salary can be treated as wages subject to FICA and withholding. Distributions to a sole shareholder cannot be disproportionate.

questions.q: Nia's S corporation stock basis is $10,000 after this year's income. Her share of nondeductible, noncapital expenses is $4,000 and her share of ordinary loss is $10,000. She elects to reduce basis by losses before nondeductible expenses. How much loss can she deduct this year?
questions.exp: With the election, the $10,000 loss reduces her $10,000 basis first and is fully deductible, and the $4,000 of nondeductible expenses carries forward to reduce future basis. Without the election, the expenses come first and only $6,000 of loss is deductible.

questions.q: An LLC taxed as a partnership and an S corporation each borrow $500,000 from a bank on a recourse basis for their operations, and in each case the owner contributed $50,000. Why can the S corporation owner usually deduct less of the business's early losses?
choices: S corporation losses are deductible only against S corporation income
S corporation losses are limited to 50% of stock basis
Entity-level debt is not included in an S shareholder's basis, while a partner's basis includes a share of partnership liabilities
S corporation shareholders cannot carry suspended losses forward
questions.exp: A partner's outside basis includes a share of partnership liabilities, but an S shareholder gets basis only for stock and for loans made directly to the corporation. The S owner's loss capacity is therefore $50,000 plus any direct shareholder loans.

questions.q: An S corporation has accumulated E&P of $20,000 and begins the year with AAA of ($10,000). This year it has $15,000 of ordinary income and distributes $12,000 to its sole shareholder, who has ample basis. How much of the distribution is a dividend?
questions.exp: The year's income brings AAA to −$10,000 + $15,000 = $5,000, so $5,000 of the distribution is from AAA and the remaining $7,000 comes from E&P as a dividend. Treating the full $15,000 of income as AAA ignores the negative opening balance.

questions.q: Omar sells all of his 40% interest in a calendar-year S corporation to Pia on July 1. Most of the corporation's income for the year was earned after June 30. Absent any election, how is the year's income allocated between them?
choices: Entirely to Omar, who owned the shares on January 1
Entirely to Pia, who owns the shares at year-end
Pro rata on a per-share, per-day basis over the whole year
According to the income actually earned before and after July 1
questions.exp: S corporation items are allocated per share, per day unless the corporation elects, with the consent of all affected shareholders, to close its books on the date of the sale. That election would assign Omar only the income actually earned through June 30.

questions.q: Labco uses the regular research credit. Its current-year qualified research expenses (QREs) are $2,000,000. Its fixed-base percentage times average annual gross receipts for the prior four years produces a base amount of $1,200,000. What is Labco's regular research credit?
questions.exp: The base amount is the greater of $1,200,000 or the 50% minimum base ($1,000,000), so the credit is 20% x ($2,000,000 - $1,200,000) = $160,000. The $200,000 trap uses the 50% minimum base even though the computed base is higher.

questions.q: Biotek elects the alternative simplified credit (ASC). Its current-year QREs are $1,000,000, and its QREs for the three prior years were $600,000, $700,000 and $800,000. What is the ASC?
