questions.exp: The ASC is 14% of QREs above 50% of the prior three-year average: 50% x $700,000 = $350,000, and 14% x ($1,000,000 - $350,000) = $91,000. The $42,000 trap subtracts the full $700,000 average instead of 50% of it.

questions.q: Newgen began research in the current year and had no QREs in any of the three preceding tax years. Its current-year QREs are $500,000, and it elects the alternative simplified credit. What is its credit?
questions.exp: When a taxpayer has no QREs in any of the three preceding years, the ASC is 6% of current QREs: 6% x $500,000 = $30,000. The $70,000 trap applies the normal 14% rate with a zero base.

questions.q: Tecno's U.S. research activities this year incurred: $800,000 of taxable wages to employees doing qualified research, $100,000 of supplies used in experimentation, $200,000 paid to an unrelated contractor for qualified research, $50,000 of depreciation on lab equipment, and $40,000 of lab utilities and rent. What are Tecno's total QREs?
questions.exp: QREs are wages ($800,000) + supplies ($100,000) + 65% of contract research ($130,000) = $1,030,000; depreciation, rent and utilities are not QREs under §41. The $1,100,000 trap counts 100% of the contract research.

questions.q: Which of the following activities is most likely qualified research for the §41 credit?
choices: Modifying an existing product to meet one customer's specifications using known techniques after commercial production began
Developing a new manufacturing process through a process of experimentation to resolve technical uncertainty about its design
Customer surveys to see which product features buyers prefer
Research performed at the company's lab in Germany
questions.exp: Qualified research must be technological in nature, aim to develop a new or improved business component, and involve a process of experimentation to eliminate uncertainty. Surveys, adaptation after commercial production and foreign research are excluded by statute.

questions.q: Startco, a qualified small business, has a $700,000 research credit this year and no income tax liability. It makes the maximum payroll tax election, which for this year is $500,000. How much of the credit remains available as an income tax credit carryforward?
questions.exp: Up to $500,000 of the credit can be elected against employer payroll taxes, and the remaining $700,000 - $500,000 = $200,000 stays a general business credit that can be carried forward. Nothing is forfeited, so $0 is wrong.

questions.q: Which company is most likely eligible to elect to apply its research credit against employer payroll taxes for its 2025 tax year?
choices: A company with $8 million of 2025 gross receipts that was formed in 2023
A company formed in 2022 with $3.2 million of 2025 gross receipts and no gross receipts before 2022
A company formed in 2015 with $3 million of 2025 gross receipts
A company with no gross receipts that has been profitable from investment income since 2018
questions.exp: A qualified small business must have gross receipts under $5 million for the year and no gross receipts in any year before the five-year period ending with the current year. The 2015 company fails the five-year test, and the $8 million company fails the receipts test.

questions.q: For its 2025 tax year, Corp X has a $100,000 research credit and elects the reduced credit so its §174A research deduction is not reduced. With a 21% corporate rate, what is the amount of the reduced credit?
questions.exp: Under the §280C election, the credit is reduced by the credit times the maximum corporate rate: $100,000 x (1 - 21%) = $79,000. The $65,000 trap confuses this with the 65% contract research rule.

questions.q: Assume that for tax years beginning after 2024, domestic research and experimental expenditures are deductible in full under §174A, while foreign research expenditures are amortized over 15 years beginning at the midpoint of the year paid. In 2025, a calendar-year corporation incurs $900,000 of domestic and $300,000 of foreign research expenditures. What is its 2025 deduction for these costs?
questions.exp: Domestic costs are deducted in full ($900,000), and foreign costs give half a year of 15-year amortization: $300,000 / 15 x 1/2 = $10,000, for a total of $910,000. The $920,000 trap takes a full year of foreign amortization.

questions.q: A large calendar-year corporation has $600,000 of unamortized domestic research expenditures capitalized under §174 in 2022 through 2024. Assume that for its first tax year beginning after 2024 it may elect to deduct the remaining amount either entirely in 2025 or ratably over 2025 and 2026. If it chooses the ratable option, how much does it deduct in 2025?
questions.exp: Ratably over the two-year period means $600,000 / 2 = $300,000 in 2025 and $300,000 in 2026. The $40,000 trap continues the old five-year amortization pattern instead of the accelerated recovery.

questions.q: In 2025, Sunco places in service energy property costing $1,000,000 and claims a 30% investment tax credit. Under §50, by how much must Sunco reduce the property's depreciable basis?
questions.exp: Depreciable basis is reduced by 50% of the energy investment credit: 50% x $300,000 = $150,000, leaving $850,000. Reducing basis by the full $300,000 credit is the trap.

questions.q: Delta claimed a $300,000 energy investment credit on property placed in service on January 1, Year 1. Delta sells the property on July 1, Year 3, which is after two full years but before three full years of service. How much of the credit is recaptured?
questions.exp: The recapture percentage falls by 20 points for each full year of service: disposition in the third year gives 60%, and 60% x $300,000 = $180,000. The $120,000 trap uses 40%, which applies only after three full years.

questions.q: A clean electricity investment credit facility costing $2,000,000 meets the prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements (raising the base rate from 6% to 30%) and also qualifies for the 10-percentage-point energy community bonus. No other bonus applies. What is the credit?
questions.exp: With PWA met, the rate is 30% + 10 points = 40%, and 40% x $2,000,000 = $800,000. The $640,000 trap treats the bonus as 10% of the 30% rate (32%) rather than an additional 10 percentage points.

questions.q: Buyco, a calendar-year C corporation, pays $920,000 in cash to buy $1,000,000 of transferable clean energy credits under §6418 from an unrelated developer and uses them against its 2025 tax. What are Buyco's tax consequences?
choices: It claims a $920,000 credit, limited to the cash paid
It claims the $1,000,000 credit and reports $80,000 of ordinary income
It deducts the $920,000 and claims a $1,000,000 credit
It claims the $1,000,000 credit; the $920,000 is not deductible, and the $80,000 discount is not income
questions.exp: Under §6418, the buyer claims the full credit, cannot deduct the cash paid, and does not recognize income on the discount, while the seller excludes the cash from income. The credit is not limited to the amount paid.

questions.q: A tax-exempt hospital installs solar energy property eligible for a clean energy investment credit. It has no federal income tax liability. How can it benefit from the credit?
choices: It can sell the credit only through a §6418 transfer
It can make an elective payment election under §6417 and receive the credit amount as a refund
It cannot benefit, because exempt organizations owe no income tax
It can claim the credit against its payroll tax withholding
questions.exp: §6417 lets applicable entities such as tax-exempt organizations and governments treat certain clean energy credits as tax payments refundable in cash. Transfer under §6418 is for entities that are not applicable entities, so it is not the exempt hospital's route.

questions.q: A C corporation that is not subject to the corporate AMT has regular tax liability of $210,000 and $200,000 of general business credits for the year. The §38 limitation allows credits up to net income tax minus 25% of net regular tax liability above $25,000. How much of the credit can it use this year?
questions.exp: The limit is $210,000 - 25% x ($210,000 - $25,000) = $210,000 - $46,250 = $163,750, so $36,250 carries over. The $200,000 trap ignores the limitation.

questions.q: A corporation has $36,250 of general business credits it cannot use this year because of the §38 limitation. What are the carryover rules?
choices: Carry back 1 year, then forward 20 years
Carry forward indefinitely, with no carryback
Carry back 2 years, then forward 5 years
Carry back 3 years, then forward 15 years
questions.exp: Under §39, unused general business credits are carried back 1 year and forward 20 years. Indefinite carryforward applies to post-2017 NOLs, not business credits.

questions.q: Maria is a partner in a partnership with average annual gross receipts of $40 million over the prior three years, which passes a research credit through to her. She is subject to the individual AMT. Which statement is correct?
choices: The credit must be applied against payroll tax
The credit cannot offset AMT because research credits never offset AMT
As an eligible small business, the partnership's research credit can offset Maria's AMT
The credit is converted into a deduction for AMT purposes
questions.exp: Under §38, research credits of an eligible small business (average gross receipts of $50 million or less) can offset AMT, and the test is applied at the partnership and partner levels. The payroll offset is for qualified small businesses with under $5 million of receipts and is elective.

questions.q: Engco performs development work for a customer under a fixed-price contract. Engco is paid whether or not the research succeeds, and the customer gets all rights to the results. How do the research costs affect Engco's research credit?
choices: They are QREs for Engco because Engco performs the work
They are not QREs for Engco because the research is funded
65% of the costs are QREs for Engco
They are QREs for Engco only if it also pays the employee wages
questions.exp: Research is funded, and excluded for the performer, when payment does not depend on success or when the performer keeps no substantial rights. Here both conditions apply, so Engco has no QREs, and the 65% rule applies to the customer instead.

questions.q: Retailco develops software solely for internal general and administrative use (an internal accounting system). Beyond the usual four-part test, what additional standard must the software development meet to qualify for the research credit?
choices: It must be developed outside the United States
It must be sold to third parties within one year
The high threshold of innovation test: it must be innovative, involve significant economic risk, and not be commercially available
It must be funded by a government grant
questions.exp: Internal-use software must also satisfy the high threshold of innovation test under the regulations. Software developed for sale or license does not face this extra test.

questions.q: A developer is deciding between a production tax credit (per kWh over 10 years) and an investment tax credit (percentage of basis) for a new renewable facility. Which factor most favors electing the PTC?
choices: High expected electricity production relative to the facility's capital cost
A plan to sell the facility in Year 2
A very high construction cost with low expected output
A need for the largest possible credit in the year placed in service
questions.exp: The PTC rewards output, so efficient, high-production facilities generally do better with it, while the ITC favors costly projects with modest output and gives an upfront benefit. Selling early also creates ITC recapture risk, which does not support the PTC choice.

questions.q: Assume a production tax credit rate of 3.0 cents per kWh for a facility that meets the prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements. In 2025 the facility produced 50,000,000 kWh, sold 45,000,000 kWh to unrelated utilities, and used 5,000,000 kWh on site. What is the PTC?
questions.exp: The PTC applies only to electricity produced and sold to an unrelated person: 45,000,000 x $0.03 = $1,350,000. The $1,500,000 trap includes the electricity used on site.

questions.q: In 2025, when the §25D residential clean energy credit was 30% of qualified costs, the Lees installed solar panels for $24,000 and battery storage for $6,000 at their home. Their 2025 tax liability before credits is $5,000, and they have no other credits. What is their 2025 credit and the amount carried forward?
choices: $7,200 used; $0 carried forward
$5,000 used; $4,000 carried forward
$5,000 used; $0 carried forward
$9,000 used; $0 carried forward
questions.exp: The credit is 30% x ($24,000 + $6,000) = $9,000. It is nonrefundable, so $5,000 offsets the 2025 tax and the unused $4,000 carries forward under §25D. Batteries of at least 3 kWh capacity qualify.

questions.q: For 2025, assume the §25C energy efficient home improvement credit is 30% of costs, with a $2,000 annual limit for heat pumps, a separate $1,200 aggregate annual limit for other items, and a $600 limit for windows. The Parks spent $10,000 on a qualifying heat pump, $2,000 on qualifying windows and $1,000 on insulation. What is their credit?
questions.exp: Heat pump: 30% x $10,000 = $3,000, limited to $2,000. Windows: $600 (30% x $2,000 = $600). Insulation: $300. The non-heat-pump items total $900, under $1,200, so the credit is $2,000 + $900 = $2,900. The $3,900 trap ignores the heat pump cap.

questions.q: In 2025, Grill Co. hired three Work Opportunity Tax Credit-certified employees. Assume the credit is 40% of first-year wages up to $6,000 for employees who work at least 400 hours, and 25% for those who work 120 to 399 hours. Ann worked 500 hours and earned $9,000; Bo worked 300 hours and earned $5,000; Cy worked 100 hours and earned $1,500. What is the WOTC?
questions.exp: Ann: 40% x $6,000 = $2,400; Bo: 25% x $5,000 = $1,250; Cy: nothing (under 120 hours). The total is $3,650. The $4,400 trap gives Bo the 40% rate.

questions.q: Grill Co. paid $120,000 of wages to WOTC-certified employees and claims a $3,650 Work Opportunity Tax Credit. What is the effect on its wage deduction?
choices: The wages must be capitalized
The wage deduction is reduced by $3,650 to $116,350
No effect, because credits and deductions are independent
The wage deduction is reduced by 21% of the credit
questions.exp: §280C requires the wage deduction to be reduced by the amount of the WOTC, to prevent a double benefit. The 21% reduction is how the reduced research credit election works, not this rule.

questions.q: A startup in its third tax year (so its fixed-base percentage is 3%) has $800,000 of QREs and average annual gross receipts of $10,000,000 for the computation period. What is its regular research credit?
questions.exp: The computed base is 3% x $10,000,000 = $300,000, but the base cannot be less than 50% of current QREs ($400,000), so the credit is 20% x ($800,000 - $400,000) = $80,000. The $100,000 trap uses the $300,000 computed base.

questions.q: Which of the following costs incurred in a qualified U.S. research project is a qualified research expense?
choices: Wages paid to researchers working in the company's Canadian lab
The cost of land purchased for a new research campus
Supplies consumed in building and testing prototypes
Depreciation on lab equipment
questions.exp: Supply QREs include tangible property used and consumed in qualified research, other than land and depreciable property. Foreign research is excluded, so Canadian wages are not QREs.

questions.q: For its 2025 tax year, assume §280C requires the §174A deduction for domestic research expenditures to be reduced by the research credit unless the taxpayer elects a reduced credit. A corporation has $1,000,000 of domestic research expenditures and a $100,000 research credit and does not make the election. What is its §174A deduction?
questions.exp: Without the election, the deduction is reduced by the full credit: $1,000,000 - $100,000 = $900,000. Electing the reduced credit instead gives a $79,000 credit with the full $1,000,000 deduction.

questions.q: A corporation's QREs have grown quickly, but it lacks reliable gross receipts records for the 1984 through 1988 base period, and its gross receipts have grown sharply since then. Which planning recommendation is most appropriate?
choices: Use the payroll tax election to avoid computing a base
Use the regular credit, because it always gives the larger credit
Elect the alternative simplified credit, which depends only on the prior three years' QREs and not on gross receipts
Claim no credit, because base-period records are required for every method
questions.exp: The ASC avoids the fixed-base percentage and gross receipts history altogether, and often beats the regular credit for companies with growing receipts. The payroll election is limited to qualified small businesses and does not remove the need to compute a credit.

questions.q: Parent and its two wholly owned subsidiaries form a controlled group. Only Sub 2 conducts research. How is the group's research credit determined?
choices: Only Sub 2 computes a credit, using its own gross receipts
The group is treated as a single taxpayer for computing the credit, and the credit is allocated among the members
Parent claims the entire credit as the common parent
Each member computes its own credit separately, with no aggregation
questions.exp: Under §41 and its regulations, all members of a controlled group are treated as a single taxpayer to compute the credit, which is then allocated among them based on their stand-alone QREs. This stops companies from manipulating the base by moving research among entities.

questions.q: A taxpayer is preparing an amended return to claim a research credit refund. Under current IRS requirements, which information must the claim include?
choices: Only the total QRE amount and the computed credit
Copies of all payroll records for the year
A signed statement from an engineer certifying the research
The business components, the research activities for each, the individuals who performed them, and the information each sought to discover
questions.exp: The IRS requires refund claims for the research credit to identify each business component, the research activities, the individuals involved and the information sought, along with the QRE totals. Totals alone make the claim deficient.

questions.q: A corporation has research credits in three categories: a carryforward from 2020, a carryforward from 2022, and a current 2025 credit. Its §38 limitation allows only part of them to be used this year. In what order are they used?
choices: 2020 carryforward, then 2022 carryforward, then the 2025 credit
Pro rata among all three
The 2025 credit first, then carryforwards from newest to oldest
The taxpayer may choose any order
questions.exp: General business credits are applied first-in, first-out under §38: carryforwards (oldest first), then current-year credits, then carrybacks. This ordering reduces the risk that old credits expire.

questions.q: Jill, single, has AGI of $150,000 and owns an interest in a low-income housing project that generates a passive low-income housing credit. Her taxable income stays in the 24% bracket even after a $25,000 reduction, and she has no passive income. Under §469, credits are allowed up to the tax on a $25,000 deduction equivalent, phasing out for AGI above $200,000. What is the most credit she can use this year?
choices: $0, because she has no passive income
questions.exp: The deduction equivalent of $25,000 at her 24% marginal rate supports $6,000 of credits, and her AGI is below the phase-out. The low-income housing credit does not require active participation, and $25,000 is a deduction equivalent, not a credit amount.

questions.q: Solarco sells clean energy investment credits to Buyco under §6418. Two years later, Solarco's facility has a recapture event. Who is generally liable for the recapture tax?
choices: Buyco, the transferee, though Solarco must notify Buyco of the event
Solarco, the original owner
Solarco and Buyco equally
Neither, because transferred credits cannot be recaptured
questions.exp: Under §6418 and its regulations, ITC recapture falls on the transferee taxpayer, and the transferor must notify it of the recapture event. Buyers manage this risk through indemnities and insurance in the purchase agreement.

questions.q: A domestic manufacturing company has a $250,000 research credit and $90,000 of regular tax after other credits. Its tentative minimum tax is zero, and it is not a qualified small business. With a 21% rate, which planning action best recovers value from the research credit this year?
choices: Making a payroll tax election
Switching from the ASC to the regular credit
Accelerating taxable income (for example, by forgoing bonus depreciation or other elections) so the credit offsets more tax, if the time value of the credit justifies it
Making an elective payment election under §6417
questions.exp: Because the §38 limitation and low tax liability keep the credit from being used, raising taxable income lets more of the credit be used now. The payroll election requires qualified small business status, and the research credit is not an elective payment credit for a for-profit company.

questions.q: Assume a research credit employee is treated as performing qualified services for 100% of their wages if at least 80% of their time is spent on qualified services (the 'substantially all' rule), and otherwise in proportion to their time. Engineer Kai earned $150,000 and spent 85% of his time on qualified research; technician Lu earned $100,000 and spent 50% of her time on qualified research. What are the wage QREs?
questions.exp: Kai meets the 80% substantially all threshold, so all $150,000 counts; Lu counts 50% x $100,000 = $50,000; the total is $200,000. The $177,500 trap prorates Kai's wages at 85%.

questions.q: Startco, a qualified small business, elects to apply $400,000 of its research credit against payroll taxes. Assume the election offsets employer Social Security tax up to $250,000 first, then employer Medicare tax up to $250,000, and that Startco's employer Social Security tax for the relevant periods is $300,000 with enough Medicare tax to absorb any remainder. How much of the credit offsets employer Medicare tax?
questions.exp: The Social Security portion is capped at $250,000 even though $300,000 of tax is available, so the remaining $400,000 - $250,000 = $150,000 offsets Medicare tax. The $0 trap ignores the $250,000 Social Security cap.

questions.q: Buyer Corp. is negotiating to acquire Target Inc., a C corporation whose assets have a fair market value far above their tax basis. From Buyer's tax perspective alone, what is the main advantage of a taxable asset purchase over a stock purchase?
choices: Buyer can deduct the entire purchase price in the year of acquisition
Buyer inherits Target's net operating losses without any limitation
Buyer takes a cost basis in the assets, producing larger depreciation and amortization deductions
Buyer avoids the need to allocate the purchase price among the assets
questions.exp: In an asset purchase the buyer's basis is its cost, stepping up the assets and generating future cost recovery. Tax attributes such as NOLs stay with the seller in an asset deal, and the price must be allocated under §1060.

questions.q: Tango Corp., a C corporation owned entirely by Hector (stock basis $1,000,000), sells all its assets (basis $2,000,000) for $5,000,000 cash and then liquidates, distributing the after-tax cash to Hector. Assuming a 21% corporate rate and no liabilities, what gain does Hector recognize on the liquidation?
questions.exp: Tango pays 21% x ($5,000,000 - $2,000,000) = $630,000, distributing $4,370,000; Hector's gain is $4,370,000 - $1,000,000 = $3,370,000. Ignoring the corporate-level tax gives $4,000,000 and overlooks the double taxation of a C corporation asset sale.

questions.q: In an applicable asset acquisition, Buyer pays $5,000,000 for a business with cash of $200,000, receivables of $300,000, inventory of $500,000, equipment worth $1,500,000 and a customer list worth $1,000,000. How much of the price is allocated to goodwill and going concern value?
questions.exp: Under the §1060 residual method, price is allocated to Class I through VI assets at fair market value ($3,500,000 total), and the remainder, $5,000,000 - $3,500,000 = $1,500,000, goes to Class VII goodwill. Adding the customer list to goodwill gives $2,500,000, but the list is a separate Class VI intangible.

questions.q: Continuing the acquisition, Buyer allocated $1,000,000 to an acquired customer list and $1,500,000 to goodwill. What is Buyer's amortization of these intangibles for a full year?
questions.exp: Both are §197 intangibles amortized ratably over 15 years: ($1,000,000 + $1,500,000) / 15 = $166,667. Amortizing only goodwill gives $100,000, and $62,500 reflects an outdated 40-year book life.

questions.q: As part of an asset acquisition, Buyer pays the selling owner $300,000 for a three-year covenant not to compete. How is the payment treated?
choices: Ordinary income to the seller; amortized by Buyer over 15 years
Capital gain to the seller; amortized by Buyer over three years
Capital gain to the seller; added to Buyer's goodwill basis
Ordinary income to the seller; deducted by Buyer over three years
questions.exp: A noncompete is ordinary income to the recipient, and one entered into in connection with acquiring a business is a §197 intangible amortized over 15 years regardless of its stated term. Deducting it over the three-year term is the common error.

questions.q: Pace Corp. buys 100% of the stock of Loss Co. for cash and makes no §338 election. Which statement describes the tax result to Pace and Loss Co.?
choices: Loss Co.'s NOLs are eliminated because of the change in ownership
Loss Co.'s asset bases are stepped up to reflect the purchase price
Pace may amortize the stock purchase premium over 15 years
Loss Co. keeps its historical asset bases, and its NOLs carry forward subject to §382
questions.exp: A stock purchase does not change the target's inside basis, and its tax attributes remain, with NOL use limited by §382 after the ownership change. Stock is not an amortizable asset, so any premium over inside basis yields no deduction.

questions.q: Pine Corp. makes a qualified stock purchase of Target, a standalone C corporation owned by individuals, and unilaterally makes a regular §338 election. Which statement is correct?
choices: Target is treated as selling its assets, so Target's gain is taxed in addition to the shareholders' gain on their stock
Target recognizes no gain, but Pine still obtains a stepped-up basis
Only the selling shareholders are taxed; Target recognizes nothing
The election must be made jointly with the selling shareholders
questions.exp: Under a regular §338 election, old Target is deemed to sell its assets and recognizes gain, a tax the buyer economically bears, while the sellers are still taxed on their stock sale. That double tax is why such elections are usually made only when the target has NOLs to absorb the deemed-sale gain.

questions.q: In which acquisition may the parties make a joint §338(h)(10) election?
choices: A corporation buys 100% of a standalone C corporation's stock from individual shareholders
A corporation buys 60% of an S corporation's stock from its shareholders
An individual buys 100% of the stock of a subsidiary from its corporate parent
A corporation buys 100% of an S corporation's stock from its shareholders within 12 months
questions.exp: A §338(h)(10) election requires a qualified stock purchase by a corporation of a target that is an S corporation or a member of a selling consolidated or affiliated group. A purchase by an individual is not a qualified stock purchase, 60% fails the 80% test, and a standalone C corporation owned by individuals is not eligible.

questions.q: Parent sells all the stock of its consolidated subsidiary, Sub, to Acquirer for $10,000,000. Parent's basis in the Sub stock is $4,000,000, and Sub's assets have a basis of $6,000,000. Ignoring liabilities, what gain does the Parent group recognize if a §338(h)(10) election is made?
questions.exp: With the election, Sub is treated as selling its assets ($10,000,000 - $6,000,000 = $4,000,000 gain) and then liquidating tax-free into Parent, and the stock sale is ignored. Without it Parent would recognize $6,000,000 on the stock, so the election here both reduces the seller's gain and gives Acquirer a stepped-up basis.

questions.q: What constitutes a qualified stock purchase for purposes of §338?
choices: Acquisition by purchase by a corporation of stock meeting the 80% vote and value test within a 12-month period
Acquisition by a corporation of all of the target's assets for cash
Acquisition by a corporation of at least 80% of the target's stock in a tax-free reorganization
Acquisition by any person of more than 50% of the target's stock within three years
questions.exp: A qualified stock purchase is the purchase by a corporation of stock with at least 80% of the voting power and 80% of the value within a 12-month acquisition period. Stock received in a reorganization is not acquired by purchase, and the more-than-50% three-year test belongs to §382.

questions.q: Target merges into Acquirer under state law. Target's shareholders receive consideration worth $10,000,000, half in Acquirer common stock and half in cash. Which statement is correct?
choices: The merger can qualify as a Type A reorganization, but shareholders recognize gain to the extent of the cash received
The merger is fully taxable because more than 20% of the consideration is cash
The merger qualifies only if all the consideration is voting stock
The merger qualifies, and the shareholders recognize no gain at all
questions.exp: A statutory merger allows flexible consideration as long as continuity of interest is met, and the regulations treat 40% stock consideration as sufficient, so 50% stock qualifies. The cash is boot, taxable to the extent of realized gain; the solely-voting-stock rule applies to Type B, not Type A.

questions.q: Acquirer wants to obtain 90% of Target's stock directly from Target's shareholders in a Type B reorganization. Which consideration is permitted?
choices: Solely Acquirer voting stock, with control held immediately after
Acquirer voting stock plus Acquirer bonds
Acquirer voting stock plus up to 20% cash
Acquirer nonvoting preferred stock only
questions.exp: A Type B reorganization requires the acquisition of stock solely for voting stock, with the acquirer in control (80%) immediately afterward. Any boot, apart from cash for fractional shares, disqualifies it; the 20% boot allowance applies to Type C.

questions.q: In a qualifying reorganization, Uma exchanges Target stock with a basis of $100,000 for Acquirer stock worth $250,000 plus $50,000 of cash. The cash is not treated as a dividend. What gain does Uma recognize, and what is her basis in the Acquirer stock?
choices: $0 gain; $100,000 basis
questions.exp: Realized gain is $300,000 - $100,000 = $200,000, recognized only to the extent of $50,000 of boot. Her stock basis is $100,000 + $50,000 gain recognized - $50,000 cash = $100,000; adding the gain without subtracting the boot gives $150,000.

questions.q: Vic held Target shares with a $270,000 basis. When Target merged into Acquirer in a transaction meeting all §368 requirements, he received $50,000 cash and Acquirer shares valued at $250,000. How much gain must Vic report?
questions.exp: Realized gain is $300,000 - $270,000 = $30,000, and recognized gain is the lesser of realized gain or boot ($50,000), so $30,000. Recognizing the full $50,000 of boot ignores the cap at realized gain.

questions.q: Wes surrenders his Target shares, basis $400,000, in a tax-free statutory merger and gets Acquirer common shares valued at $250,000 together with $50,000 cash. What loss does he recognize, and what basis does he take in the new shares?
choices: A $100,000 recognized loss and a $250,000 stock basis
A $50,000 recognized gain and a $400,000 stock basis
No recognized loss and a $350,000 stock basis
No recognized loss and a $400,000 stock basis
questions.exp: Losses are never recognized in a reorganization exchange, even when boot is received, so the $100,000 realized loss is deferred. Basis is $400,000 - $50,000 boot + $0 gain = $350,000, which preserves the deferred loss.

questions.q: In a Type A merger of Target into Acquirer, what are the consequences to the two corporations?
choices: Target recognizes no gain, but Acquirer takes a fair market value basis
Target recognizes gain on its appreciated assets, and Acquirer takes a fair market value basis
Target recognizes no gain, Acquirer takes Target's asset bases and inherits Target's tax attributes
Acquirer recognizes gain on the stock it issues, and Target's NOLs expire
questions.exp: Target recognizes no gain under §361, Acquirer recognizes nothing on issuing its stock under §1032 and takes a carryover basis under §362, and Target's attributes pass to Acquirer under §381. A stepped-up basis would be inconsistent with nonrecognition.

questions.q: Which requirement for a tax-free reorganization does the continuity of business enterprise doctrine impose?
choices: The acquirer must continue Target's historic business or use a significant portion of its historic business assets
The acquirer must have conducted an active business for five years before the deal
Target's management must remain in place after the acquisition
Target's shareholders must keep their acquirer stock for at least five years
questions.exp: Continuity of business enterprise requires the acquirer to continue a significant historic business of the target or use a significant portion of its historic business assets. Shareholder retention relates to continuity of interest, and the five-year active business test belongs to §355.

questions.q: Which feature describes a Type C reorganization?
choices: The acquirer obtains at least 80% of Target's stock solely for voting stock
Target changes only its state of incorporation
Target distributes the stock of a subsidiary to its shareholders
The acquirer obtains substantially all of Target's assets mainly for voting stock, and Target generally must liquidate
questions.exp: A Type C is an acquisition of substantially all the target's properties for voting stock, with limited boot permitted (liabilities count as boot when other boot is used), and the target must distribute the consideration and liquidate. A stock-for-stock acquisition is Type B, a mere change of domicile is Type F and a spin-off is a §355 transaction.

questions.q: Acquirer creates a merger subsidiary that merges into Target, so Target survives as Acquirer's wholly owned subsidiary. Which requirement applies to qualify as a reverse triangular merger?
choices: Acquirer must already own at least 50% of Target before the merger
Target must transfer substantially all its assets to Acquirer's parent
Target's shareholders may receive any mix of consideration as long as 40% is stock
Target shareholders must exchange stock constituting control of Target for Acquirer voting stock
questions.exp: Under the reverse triangular merger rules, former Target shareholders must exchange an amount of Target stock constituting control (80%) for voting stock of the controlling corporation, and Target must hold substantially all its and the merger subsidiary's assets. The 40% stock rule of thumb applies to direct and forward triangular mergers, not this structure.

questions.q: For §382 purposes, when does an ownership change occur?
choices: When the loss corporation issues new stock equal to at least 80% of its value
When any shareholder acquires more than 50% of the loss corporation's stock in a single year
When the percentage of stock owned by 5% shareholders increases by more than 50 percentage points over their lowest holdings within a three-year testing period
When the loss corporation changes its principal business activity
questions.exp: An ownership change occurs when one or more 5% shareholders increase their combined ownership by more than 50 percentage points over their lowest percentage during the three-year testing period. A change in business is relevant to the continuity of business enterprise requirement, not the definition of an ownership change.

questions.q: Loss Co., which has a $2,000,000 NOL carryforward, undergoes an ownership change when its stock is worth $10,000,000. Assume the long-term tax-exempt rate is 3%. What is the annual §382 limitation?
questions.exp: The annual limitation is the value of the old loss corporation's stock immediately before the change times the long-term tax-exempt rate: $10,000,000 x 3% = $300,000. Applying the rate to the NOL ($2,000,000 x 3% = $60,000) uses the wrong base.

questions.q: Loss Co.'s annual §382 limitation is $300,000. In the first year after the ownership change it has only $100,000 of taxable income before NOLs. In the second year it has $800,000 of taxable income before NOLs. Assuming ample pre-change NOLs and that the 80%-of-taxable-income limit does not bind, how much pre-change NOL can it use in the second year?
questions.exp: Unused limitation carries forward: year one uses $100,000 of the $300,000, so $200,000 is added to year two's $300,000 limit, for $500,000. The 80% limit would allow $640,000, so it does not bind; ignoring the carryforward of unused limitation gives $300,000.

questions.q: Loss Co. has a net unrealized built-in gain at the time of its ownership change, and it sells an appreciated asset it held on the change date two years later. How does §382 treat the recognized built-in gain?
choices: It reduces the §382 limitation for that year
It is taxed at a special 35% rate
It increases the §382 limitation for that year, allowing more pre-change NOLs to offset it
It is excluded from income because it accrued before the change
questions.exp: Recognized built-in gain during the five-year recognition period increases the annual limitation, since that gain economically accrued while the loss corporation's old owners held it. Built-in losses, by contrast, are treated like pre-change losses subject to the limitation.

questions.q: Buyer Corp. pays an investment banker a $1,000,000 success-based fee for a covered acquisition, and it elects the safe harbor of Rev. Proc. 2011-29. How much of the fee may it deduct?
questions.exp: The safe harbor lets the taxpayer treat 70% of a success-based fee as not facilitating the transaction and deduct it, so $700,000 is deductible and $300,000 is capitalized. Without the election the taxpayer must document which portion is not facilitative, which defaults to capitalization.

questions.q: Cove Inc. converted from a C corporation to an S corporation three years ago, when its assets had built-in gain. A buyer now proposes to buy Cove's assets for cash. What tax issue is most significant?
choices: The shareholders cannot use the installment method
The gain is exempt because S corporations are pass-through entities
The sale terminates Cove's S election retroactively to its conversion date
Cove may owe corporate-level tax under §1374 on net recognized built-in gain because the sale falls within the five-year recognition period
questions.exp: A former C corporation that sells assets within five years of its S election pays corporate-level tax on net recognized built-in gain, in addition to the pass-through of the gain to shareholders. After the recognition period, an S corporation asset sale generally produces only one level of tax.

questions.q: Why do individual shareholders of a C corporation usually prefer to sell their stock rather than have the corporation sell its assets?
choices: A stock sale lets them deduct the corporation's NOLs personally
A stock sale generally produces one level of tax, usually capital gain, instead of corporate tax followed by shareholder tax
A stock sale gives the buyer a stepped-up basis at no cost to the sellers
A stock sale is always tax-free to the selling shareholders
questions.exp: Selling stock generally results in a single level of tax at capital gain rates, while an asset sale followed by liquidation taxes the gain at both the corporate and shareholder levels. The trade-off is that the buyer gets no basis step-up, which often leads to a lower price.

questions.q: In an asset sale, an S corporation sells equipment with an original cost of $500,000 and an adjusted basis of $200,000 for $600,000. How is the gain characterized?
choices: $400,000 of ordinary income
$100,000 of ordinary income and $300,000 of §1231 gain
$300,000 of ordinary income and $100,000 of §1231 gain
questions.exp: Section 1245 recaptures depreciation as ordinary income up to the lesser of depreciation taken ($300,000) or gain ($400,000), so $300,000 is ordinary and the remaining $100,000 is §1231 gain. Treating all gain as §1231 ignores recapture, which applies in asset deals but not stock sales.

questions.q: In connection with a change in control, an executive with a base amount of $200,000 receives a $700,000 payment contingent on the change. What are the §280G and §4999 consequences?
choices: $100,000 is nondeductible, and the executive owes a $20,000 excise tax
No consequences, because the payment is less than five times the base amount
$700,000 is nondeductible, and the executive owes a $140,000 excise tax
$500,000 is nondeductible, and the executive owes a $100,000 excise tax
questions.exp: The payment equals or exceeds three times the base amount ($600,000), so the excess parachute payment is the amount over one times the base: $700,000 - $200,000 = $500,000. The corporation loses that deduction and the executive owes a 20% excise tax of $100,000; measuring from three times the base gives $100,000.

questions.q: Parent wants to distribute the stock of its subsidiary to its shareholders tax-free under §355 before a planned acquisition of Parent. Which requirement must be met?
choices: Both Parent and the subsidiary must be engaged in an active trade or business conducted for at least five years before the distribution
The subsidiary must have been formed within the last five years
The distribution must be pro rata among all shareholders
Parent must distribute at least 50% of the subsidiary's stock
questions.exp: Section 355 requires active businesses conducted for five years before the distribution, distribution of control (80%), a business purpose and that the transaction not be a device to distribute earnings. Non-pro-rata split-offs can qualify, and a 50% distribution falls short of the control requirement.

questions.q: A tax researcher finds four sources addressing the same issue. Which ranking lists them from greatest to least authoritative weight?
choices: Internal Revenue Code, private letter rulings, Treasury regulations, revenue rulings
Treasury regulations, Internal Revenue Code, revenue rulings, private letter rulings
Internal Revenue Code, Treasury regulations, revenue rulings, private letter rulings
Internal Revenue Code, revenue rulings, Treasury regulations, private letter rulings
questions.exp: The Code is the primary statutory source, regulations interpret it, revenue rulings are IRS administrative positions with less weight than regulations, and PLRs apply only to the requesting taxpayer. Regulations can never override the statute they interpret.

questions.q: A provision of a U.S. income tax treaty conflicts with a provision of the Internal Revenue Code. Which rule generally resolves the conflict?
choices: The treaty always prevails because treaties are ratified by the Senate
The Code always prevails because it is enacted by both houses of Congress
The provision more favorable to the taxpayer always controls
Neither has preferential status, and the one adopted later in time generally controls
questions.exp: The Code provides that neither treaties nor statutes have preferential status by reason of being one or the other, so the later-in-time rule generally applies. A treaty therefore does not automatically override the Code, and taxpayers must disclose treaty-based return positions.

questions.q: Which statement about a private letter ruling is correct?
choices: It has the same weight as a Treasury regulation
It binds the IRS for all taxpayers with similar facts once it is published
It is not considered authority for any purpose
It binds the IRS only for the taxpayer that requested it and may not be cited as precedent, although it counts as authority for substantial authority purposes
questions.exp: A PLR applies only to the requesting taxpayer and by statute may not be used or cited as precedent, but the regulations list PLRs among the authorities considered in evaluating substantial authority. Revenue rulings, not PLRs, may be relied on by all taxpayers with substantially similar facts.

questions.q: How does a revenue procedure differ from a revenue ruling?
choices: A revenue procedure is issued by Congress, while a revenue ruling is issued by Treasury
A revenue procedure applies only to one taxpayer, while a revenue ruling applies to all
A revenue procedure states procedures and practices, while a revenue ruling applies the law to a specific set of facts
A revenue procedure is binding on courts, while a revenue ruling is not
questions.exp: Both are published in the Internal Revenue Bulletin; a revenue ruling gives the IRS's conclusion on how the law applies to particular facts, while a revenue procedure announces procedures, such as how to request a ruling or method change. Neither binds the courts.

questions.q: Which statement about proposed Treasury regulations is correct?
choices: They are binding on taxpayers from the date they are proposed
They automatically expire after three years
They carry more weight than final regulations because they are more recent
They are not binding, but they may be considered authority for substantial authority purposes
questions.exp: Proposed regulations generally have no binding effect until finalized, but they reflect Treasury's views and are listed as authority for substantial authority. The three-year sunset applies to temporary regulations, not proposed ones.

questions.q: Which statement describes temporary Treasury regulations issued under current law?
choices: They are issued without any corresponding proposed regulations
They are not binding and serve only as guidance
They remain in force until Congress repeals them
They are binding when issued, must also be issued as proposed regulations, and expire within three years
questions.exp: Temporary regulations have the force of final regulations when issued, must simultaneously be issued as proposed regulations, and expire three years after issuance. Treating them as nonbinding confuses them with proposed regulations.

questions.q: After the Supreme Court's 2024 decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, how does a court review a Treasury regulation interpreting an ambiguous Code provision?
choices: The court may not consider the regulation at all
The court must defer to any reasonable Treasury interpretation
The court must defer to the IRS's litigating position
The court exercises its own independent judgment on the best reading of the statute rather than deferring because the statute is ambiguous
questions.exp: Loper Bright overruled Chevron, so courts no longer defer to an agency's reasonable interpretation merely because a statute is ambiguous; they decide the best reading themselves. Courts may still respect agency views and must honor express delegations of authority within constitutional limits.

questions.q: A taxpayer residing in a state within the Ninth Circuit litigates a deficiency in the U.S. Tax Court. The Ninth Circuit has ruled on the precise issue, but the Tax Court has previously reached the opposite result in another taxpayer's case. Which precedent will the Tax Court follow?
choices: Whichever decision is more favorable to the IRS
Its own prior decision, because the Tax Court is a national court
The decision of the Federal Circuit
The Ninth Circuit decision, because an appeal would lie to that circuit
questions.exp: Under the Golsen rule, the Tax Court follows the precedent of the court of appeals to which the case would be appealed when that circuit has squarely ruled on the issue. Otherwise it follows its own precedent; the Federal Circuit hears appeals from the Court of Federal Claims.

questions.q: A taxpayer has received a notice of deficiency, does not want to pay the tax before litigating, and wants judges who specialize in tax law. Which forum should she choose?
choices: U.S. Tax Court
U.S. Court of Federal Claims
U.S. District Court
U.S. Court of Appeals
questions.exp: The Tax Court is the only trial forum that does not require payment of the disputed tax first, and its judges specialize in tax. The District Court and Court of Federal Claims are refund forums that require payment, and the courts of appeals do not hear cases at trial.

questions.q: A taxpayer wants a jury to decide a factual issue in his tax dispute. In which forum is a jury trial available?
choices: U.S. Court of Federal Claims
The IRS Independent Office of Appeals
U.S. Tax Court
U.S. District Court
questions.exp: Only a U.S. District Court refund suit offers a jury trial, and the taxpayer must first pay the tax and file a refund claim. Tax Court and Court of Federal Claims cases are decided by judges, and Appeals is an administrative settlement function, not a court.

questions.q: A taxpayer in the Fifth Circuit faces an unfavorable Fifth Circuit precedent on her issue but favorable Federal Circuit precedent. She is willing to pay the tax first and does not need a jury. Where should she file suit?
choices: U.S. Tax Court
U.S. District Court in her home district
The U.S. Supreme Court
U.S. Court of Federal Claims
questions.exp: The Court of Federal Claims is a refund forum whose decisions are appealed to the Federal Circuit, so it follows Federal Circuit rather than Fifth Circuit precedent. The Tax Court and her local District Court would be bound by the Fifth Circuit, and the Supreme Court does not hear tax cases at trial.

questions.q: Which statement about the Tax Court's small tax case procedure is correct?
choices: Its decisions are binding precedent for later Tax Court cases
Its decisions are appealable to the regional court of appeals
It is available when the amount in dispute for a year does not exceed $50,000, and its decisions are not appealable
It is available for any deficiency if the taxpayer is an individual
questions.exp: The taxpayer may elect the informal small case procedure when the deficiency, including penalties, is $50,000 or less for a tax year; the decision is final and cannot be appealed or cited as precedent. The procedure is not limited to individuals, nor available for unlimited amounts.

questions.q: What does the IRS communicate when it announces a nonacquiescence in a court decision it lost?
choices: That the decision is binding on the IRS nationwide
That it disagrees with the decision and will not follow it in other taxpayers' cases
That the decision has been reversed on appeal
That it agrees with the decision and will follow it for all taxpayers
questions.exp: A nonacquiescence signals that the IRS will not follow an adverse decision in disputes with other taxpayers, though the decision still binds the parties to that case. An acquiescence, in contrast, means the IRS accepts the result.

questions.q: In determining whether a return position is supported by substantial authority under the accuracy-related penalty regulations, which of the following is not considered authority?
choices: The Joint Committee on Taxation's General Explanation of a tax act
An article in a respected tax treatise or journal
A proposed Treasury regulation
A private letter ruling issued to another taxpayer
questions.exp: The regulations exclude conclusions in treatises, legal periodicals and opinions of tax professionals, although the authorities they cite may be considered. PLRs, proposed regulations and the Joint Committee's General Explanation (the Blue Book) are expressly treated as authority.

questions.q: Which list ranks the reporting standards from the lowest to the highest likelihood of a position being sustained?
choices: More likely than not, substantial authority, reasonable basis
Substantial authority, reasonable basis, more likely than not
Reasonable basis, substantial authority, more likely than not
Reasonable basis, more likely than not, substantial authority
questions.exp: Reasonable basis is a relatively low standard (significantly higher than not frivolous), substantial authority is higher, and more likely than not requires a greater than 50% likelihood of success. Substantial authority is less stringent than more likely than not.

questions.q: An individual reported tax of $70,000, but the correct tax is $80,000. The position had neither substantial authority nor disclosure. What is the accuracy-related penalty for substantial understatement?
choices: $0, because the understatement does not exceed 10% of the correct tax
questions.exp: For an individual, an understatement is substantial if it exceeds the greater of 10% of the correct tax ($8,000) or $5,000; the $10,000 understatement qualifies, so the penalty is 20% x $10,000 = $2,000. Comparing $10,000 to 10% of the reported tax rather than the correct tax is a common error, and $4,000 uses the 40% gross valuation rate.

questions.q: How can an individual taxpayer avoid the substantial understatement penalty for a position that is not a tax shelter item?
choices: By having a reasonable basis for the position, without disclosure
By showing the position is not frivolous and disclosing it
By having substantial authority for the position, or a reasonable basis plus adequate disclosure
By obtaining any written opinion from a tax adviser
questions.exp: The understatement is reduced for items supported by substantial authority, or for items adequately disclosed (for example, on Form 8275) that have a reasonable basis. Reasonable basis alone, without disclosure, is not enough, and a nonfrivolous disclosed position fails the reasonable basis threshold.

questions.q: A paid preparer takes an undisclosed position on a client's return that is not a tax shelter or reportable transaction. To avoid the §6694 preparer penalty for an unreasonable position, what standard must the position meet?
choices: Reasonable basis
Substantial authority
More likely than not
Realistic possibility of success
questions.exp: Under §6694, an undisclosed position must have substantial authority, while a disclosed position needs only a reasonable basis; tax shelters and reportable transactions require a reasonable belief the position is more likely than not correct. Reasonable basis alone suffices only with disclosure.

questions.q: A preparer who charged a $3,000 fee for preparing a return is liable for the §6694 penalty for an unreasonable position, with no willful or reckless conduct. What is the penalty?
questions.exp: The unreasonable position penalty is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived from the return: 50% x $3,000 = $1,500. The $5,000 minimum applies to the separate penalty for willful or reckless conduct.

questions.q: While preparing a client's current-year return, a CPA who practices before the IRS discovers that the client omitted income on a prior-year return. Under Circular 230, what must the CPA do?
choices: Promptly advise the client of the noncompliance and its consequences
Amend the prior-year return without the client's consent
Notify the IRS of the omission within 30 days
Withdraw immediately from all engagements with the client
questions.exp: Circular 230 requires a practitioner who knows of a client's noncompliance or omission to promptly advise the client of it and of the consequences of not correcting it. The practitioner has no duty to inform the IRS and cannot amend a return without the client.

questions.q: Which list correctly states the original due dates of calendar-year returns for these entities?
choices: Partnership March 15; S corporation March 15; C corporation April 15
Partnership April 15; S corporation March 15; C corporation March 15
Partnership April 15; S corporation April 15; C corporation April 15
Partnership March 15; S corporation April 15; C corporation March 15
questions.exp: Partnership and S corporation returns are due the 15th day of the third month after year-end (March 15), and C corporation returns are due the 15th day of the fourth month (April 15). The C corporation due date moved to April 15 for most corporations under 2015 legislation.

questions.q: An individual files Form 4868 by April 15 but makes no tax payment with it. Which statement is correct?
choices: No penalties or interest apply until October 15
The time to file and the time to pay are both extended to October 15
The return is due October 15, but interest and the failure-to-pay penalty run on unpaid tax from April 15
The extension is invalid unless at least 50% of the tax is paid
questions.exp: An automatic extension extends only the time to file, so interest and the failure-to-pay penalty accrue on unpaid tax from the original due date. The extension remains valid without payment, and the failure-to-file penalty is avoided if the return is filed by October 15.

questions.q: An individual owed $10,000 of tax for the year, filed no extension, and filed the return and paid the entire balance on June 10 (due date April 15). There was no reasonable cause. Ignoring interest, what are the combined failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties?
questions.exp: The return is two months late (a partial month counts as a full month). The failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5% x 2 x $10,000 = $100, and the 5% per month failure-to-file penalty ($1,000) is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty for the same months to $900, for a total of $1,000. Adding the two without the offset gives $1,100.

questions.q: An individual whose return is due April 15 of Year 1 files it on February 10 of Year 1. Absent fraud or a substantial omission, when does the general period for the IRS to assess additional tax expire?
choices: February 10 of Year 4
April 15 of Year 4
October 15 of Year 4
April 15 of Year 7
questions.exp: The general assessment period is three years from the later of the filing date or the due date, because an early return is treated as filed on its due date, so it runs to April 15 of Year 4. The six-year period applies only to substantial omissions of gross income.

questions.q: A taxpayer reported gross income of $400,000 and omitted $120,000 of gross income from the return, with no fraud. What is the assessment period?
choices: Three years, because there was no fraud
Unlimited, because income was omitted
Seven years, because the omission exceeds 25% of gross income
Six years, because the omission exceeds 25% of the gross income reported
questions.exp: The six-year period applies when omitted gross income exceeds 25% of the gross income stated on the return: $120,000 is more than 25% x $400,000 = $100,000. The unlimited period requires fraud or failure to file, and seven years relates to bad debt and worthless securities refund claims.

questions.q: A taxpayer filed a return on time but paid an additional assessment two years later. Within what period must she file a refund claim to recover that payment?
choices: Within the later of three years from filing the return or two years from paying the tax
Within six years from the original due date
Within three years from the payment only
Within two years from the filing date
questions.exp: A refund claim must be filed within three years from the time the return was filed or two years from the time the tax was paid, whichever is later, and a claim filed in the two-year window recovers only tax paid during it. Using only one of the two periods misstates the rule.

questions.q: A taxpayer mails her return by U.S. Postal Service first-class mail with a postmark of April 15, its due date, and the IRS receives it on April 19. When is the return considered filed?
choices: April 19, the date the IRS received it
It is late unless sent by certified mail
April 16, the next business day after mailing
April 15, because a timely postmarked return is treated as filed on the postmark date
questions.exp: Under the timely mailing rule, a properly addressed return with a timely U.S. postmark (or a designated private delivery service's record) is treated as filed when mailed. Certified mail is not required, though it provides proof of mailing.

questions.q: Zoe's prior-year AGI was $200,000 and her prior-year tax was $40,000 for a full 12-month year. She expects $60,000 of tax this year. What is the minimum annual amount of estimated tax and withholding she must pay timely to avoid an underpayment penalty?
questions.exp: The required annual payment is the lesser of 90% of current-year tax ($54,000) or prior-year tax, which must be 110% because prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000: 110% x $40,000 = $44,000. Using 100% of prior-year tax ($40,000) applies only when prior-year AGI was $150,000 or less.

questions.q: A CPA is asked to research whether a client's transaction qualifies for nonrecognition. What should be the first step in the research process?
choices: Search for court cases that reached a favorable result
Draft the client communication describing the conclusion
Establish the relevant facts and identify the tax issues they raise
Locate the applicable Treasury regulations
questions.exp: Tax research starts by gathering the facts and framing the questions, because the facts determine which authorities are relevant. Locating and evaluating authority, reaching a conclusion and communicating it follow; searching only for favorable cases is a biased approach.

questions.q: A taxpayer living in the United States receives a statutory notice of deficiency. What must he do to contest the deficiency in the Tax Court without paying it first?
choices: Request a conference with the IRS Independent Office of Appeals within 30 days
Pay the tax and file a refund claim within two years
File Form 1040-X within 60 days
File a petition with the Tax Court within 90 days of the notice's mailing
questions.exp: The notice of deficiency (90-day letter) is the taxpayer's ticket to the Tax Court, and he must petition within 90 days (150 days if addressed to a person outside the United States). The 30-day letter precedes it and offers an Appeals conference; paying and claiming a refund leads to the refund forums instead.
